As you ascend to the 3rd floor of the Hanoi Museum, the "Hanoi in the 19th-20th centuries" exhibition space unfolds like a stroll through the city's most profound transformations. This was the era when Hanoi, the capital of Vietnam, transitioned from a feudal capital to a modern metropolis, with Western-style streets rising alongside ancient tiled roofs, trams clanging through the streets, and a new pace of life gradually taking shape in the heart of the old land.

The exhibition space recounts this journey through multiple layers of memory, from Hanoi during the Nguyen Dynasty, when the Bac Thanh citadel stood tall, to the French colonial period, when European architecture, schools, theaters, and urban systems began to shape the city's appearance. The space is filled with everyday artifacts, documentary photos, and ancient maps, weaving a narrative of a Hanoi that went through wars, the subsidy period, and then transformed itself dynamically in the modern era.

Old radios, bicycles, ration stamps, and familiar household items often make elderly visitors pause for a long time, as if reuniting with a part of their own youth. Young visitors are often fascinated to see a very different Hanoi in black-and-white photos, while Hanoians sometimes find here a touch of nostalgia for the sound of trams, street-corner tea stalls, or the slow pace of life that has long since receded.

The exhibition space is brought to life with numerous black-and-white archival photos, urban life artifacts, and models of old streets arranged chronologically. Wood-brown and deep gray tones combined with soft lighting evoke a sense of nostalgia. Prominent highlights include familiar items such as old bicycles, radios, ration stamps, or models of Hanoi trams. The setting often features photo panels of the Old Quarter, French architecture, and corners recreating the daily life of former urban residents.

As you wander through the exhibition, you can almost hear the sounds of trams clanging, the aroma of street food wafting through the air, and the chatter of pedestrians on the streets. The lingering feeling is often one of deep emotion for a city that has gone through so many changes yet still retains its own unique soul.

description:
Upon reaching the 4th floor of the Hanoi Museum, the exhibition theme "Building Socialism" opens up like a special slice of modern history, telling the story of Hanoi's journey through challenging years to reconstruct life after the war. This space recreates a period when the capital was not only the political center of the country, but also a place carrying the aspirations for construction, development, and stability amidst the major changes of the 20th century.

Through documentary photographs, daily life artifacts, propaganda posters, ration coupons, production machinery, or memories of collective housing areas, viewers can gradually visualize the atmosphere of Hanoi during the subsidy period and the process of building a new society. This was a period when factories operated day and night, labor and production movements spread widely, and the collective spirit became a familiar part of the lives of the capital's residents. Stories of sharing, thriftiness, and the will to overcome difficulties often make many elderly people pause longer, as if they are revisiting a part of their own memories.

Many young visitors find here a Hanoi very different from the present – simple, lacking, yet rich in community spirit. Upon leaving the exhibition area, what remains is often a sense of deeper understanding of the generations of people who contributed to shaping the face of Hanoi today from the most simple and resilient things.
description_vi:
Khi lên tới tầng 4 của Bảo tàng Hà Nội, chủ đề trưng bày “Xây dựng xã hội chủ nghĩa” mở ra như một lát cắt đặc biệt của lịch sử hiện đại, kể về hành trình Hà Nội bước qua những năm tháng đầy thử thách để kiến thiết lại cuộc sống sau chiến tranh. Không gian này tái hiện một giai đoạn mà thủ đô không chỉ là trung tâm chính trị của đất nước, mà còn là nơi mang theo khát vọng dựng xây, phát triển và ổn định trong bối cảnh đổi thay lớn của thế kỷ XX.

Qua những bức ảnh tư liệu, hiện vật đời sống, áp phích cổ động, tem phiếu, máy móc sản xuất hay ký ức về các khu tập thể, người xem dần hình dung được bầu không khí của Hà Nội thời kỳ bao cấp và công cuộc xây dựng xã hội mới. Đây là giai đoạn mà những nhà máy hoạt động ngày đêm, các phong trào lao động sản xuất lan rộng và tinh thần tập thể trở thành một phần quen thuộc trong đời sống người dân thủ đô. Những câu chuyện về sự sẻ chia, tiết kiệm và ý chí vượt khó thường khiến nhiều người lớn tuổi dừng lại lâu hơn, như đang gặp lại một phần ký ức của chính mình.

Không ít du khách trẻ tìm thấy ở đây một Hà Nội rất khác với hiện tại – giản dị, thiếu thốn nhưng giàu tinh thần cộng đồng. Khi rời khu trưng bày, điều còn đọng lại thường là cảm giác hiểu hơn về những lớp người đã góp phần xây dựng diện mạo Hà Nội hôm nay từ những điều bình dị và bền bỉ nhất.

description:

description_vi:
Ở tầng 4 của Bảo tàng Hà Nội, chủ đề trưng bày “Hà Nội hướng tới tương lai” giống như chương cuối của một cuốn biên niên sử dài, nơi câu chuyện nghìn năm của Thăng Long không khép lại trong hoài niệm mà tiếp tục mở ra bằng nhịp sống của một đô thị đang không ngừng chuyển mình. Sau khi đi qua những lớp ký ức từ kinh thành cổ, phố phường xưa đến thời kỳ kiến thiết đất nước, du khách bước vào không gian này như đang nhìn thấy Hà Nội của hôm nay và ngày mai cùng hiện diện trong một bức tranh rộng lớn.

Không gian trưng bày kể về hành trình hiện đại hóa của thủ đô với những quy hoạch đô thị mới, hệ thống giao thông phát triển, công trình kiến trúc hiện đại và tầm nhìn xây dựng một thành phố xanh, văn minh, thông minh. Những hình ảnh về các đại lộ, khu đô thị, trung tâm văn hóa – khoa học hay sự chuyển đổi công nghệ được lồng ghép như lời kể tiếp nối cho khát vọng vươn lên của một thành phố từng được chọn làm nơi “rồng bay”. Cái tên “Hà Nội hướng tới tương lai” vì thế không chỉ mang ý nghĩa phát triển vật chất, mà còn gợi về một hành trình gìn giữ ký ức trong khi vẫn mở lòng với đổi mới.

Nhiều du khách trẻ thường dừng lại khá lâu ở khu vực mô hình quy hoạch hoặc màn hình tương tác để hình dung diện mạo Hà Nội mai sau. Khi rời khỏi tầng trưng bày này, cảm giác đọng lại thường là sự đối chiếu thú vị giữa một Hà Nội cổ kính vừa đi qua và một Hà Nội đang tiếp tục lớn lên phía trước.

description: Welcome travelers from afar to step into a wondrous space called the Banana Garden on the 4th floor of the Hanoi Museum. Nestled quietly halfway up the inverted pyramid architectural structure on Pham Hung Street, the garden emerges like a miniature painting of the Northern Vietnamese countryside in the heart of the bustling metropolis. It was no coincidence that at the moment of the museum's inauguration on the occasion of the Millennial Anniversary of Thang Long, these familiar banana plants were chosen to be nurtured here. Legend has it that this plant embodies the simple and loyal character of the Vietnamese people, always reminding descendants of their roots no matter how high they fly or how far they reach. Amidst the hustle and bustle of life, the garden becomes a peaceful sanctuary, where the elderly emotionally reminisce about their childhood memories, while young visitors delight in lingering to immerse themselves in the atmosphere of the folk culture exhibition vividly recreated under the cool canopy. More than just a decorative miniature landscape, this green space is a deep spiritual imprint, a rustic quietude that gently lulls those souls yearning to reconnect with their national roots amidst the contemporary exhibition space.
description_vi: Chào mừng những người lữ khách phương xa bước vào một không gian đầy ngỡ ngàng mang tên Vườn chuối trên tầng 4 của Bảo tàng Hà Nội. Nằm tĩnh lặng nơi độ cao lưng chừng của khối kiến trúc kim tự tháp ngược trên đường Phạm Hùng, khu vườn hiện lên như một bức tranh thu nhỏ của làng quê Bắc Bộ giữa lòng đô thị phồn hoa. Không phải ngẫu nhiên mà vào khoảnh khắc khánh thành bảo tàng nhân dịp Đại lễ ngàn năm Thăng Long, những gốc chuối thân thuộc lại được chọn để ươm mầm nơi đây. Tương truyền rằng, loài cây này mang trong mình cốt cách dung dị, thủy chung của người Việt, luôn nhắc nhở con cháu về cội nguồn dẫu có bay cao, vươn xa đến đâu. Giữa nhịp sống hối hả, khu vườn trở thành chốn dừng chân bình yên, nơi những cụ già bồi hồi tìm về hoài niệm thuở ấu thơ, còn du khách trẻ tuổi lại thích thú nán lại thả hồn vào không khí triển lãm văn hóa dân gian được tái hiện sống động dưới tán lá mát. Hơn cả một tiểu cảnh trang trí, mảng xanh này là một dấu ấn tâm thức sâu sắc, một khoảng lặng mộc mạc ru êm những tâm hồn đang khao khát tìm lại cội nguồn dân tộc giữa không gian trưng bày đương đại.

The 4th Floor: Vườn Chuối relic site is a significant archaeological site that has recently been recognized for its profound historical and cultural value. On November 9, 2025, the Hanoi Department of Culture and Sports organized a ceremony to award the relic site its official designation as a historical and cultural heritage site. This event was held at the Hanoi Museum, marking a milestone in the recognition of the site's importance to the history of Thang Long-Hanoi during early state formation periods.

The ceremony was attended by prominent figures such as Professor Dr. Bui Hoai Son, a member of the National Assembly’s Cultural and Social Committee, Mr. Nguyen Thanh Binh, Head of the Cultural and Social Committee of the Hanoi People's Council, and Ms. Bach Lien Huong, Deputy Secretary of the Hanoi Municipal Party Committee and Director of the Hanoi Department of Culture and Sports. Additionally, representatives from the Hoai Duc Commune Party Committee, local government officials, and scholars specializing in archaeology were also present. The event attracted a large number of residents from Lai Xa village and media outlets to witness this important moment in the preservation and promotion of cultural heritage.

At the event, Mr. Dao Vuong Long, Chief of the Hanoi Department of Culture and Sports Office, announced the decision made by the Hanoi People's Committee to officially rank the Vườn Chuối archaeological site as a historical and cultural heritage site. This decision underscores the significance of the site in understanding the early development of Vietnamese society and its cultural evolution over time.

Since April 2025, the Hanoi Museum has collaborated with the Institute of Archaeology and the Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities at Vietnam National University, Hanoi, to refine and study the collection of artifacts and relics gathered from the excavation conducted in the western part of Vườn Chuối in 2024. These efforts have revealed a detailed picture of the settlement patterns and lifestyle of the ancient inhabitants of Vườn Chuối, highlighting the continuous expansion and development of the village through various historical periods.

The archaeological findings indicate that the initial settlement was established on elevated landforms, surrounded by natural waterways, which gradually expanded into lower areas. This transition reflects the sophisticated organization of the community, with evidence of specialized labor and advanced social structures. The site includes residential areas, burial grounds, and workshops, providing a comprehensive view of life in the region during the Bronze Age.

The Vườn Chuối site is a testament to the presence of early Vietnamese agricultural societies that settled and developed the Red River Delta nearly 4,000 years ago. It represents a crucial period in the formation of early Vietnamese states, showcasing the continuity of cultural practices and technological advancements across different epochs, including the Phung Nguyen, Dong Dau, Go Mun, Dong Son, and Post-Dong Son cultures.

The exhibition at the Hanoi Museum, titled "Discoveries from Vườn Chuối," comprises five sections: the journey of discovery, the convergence and crystallization of cultural traditions, the protection and promotion of the Vườn Chuối heritage, the contributions of scientists to the site, and an interactive experience area where visitors can simulate the work of an archaeologist. The exhibition features nearly 1,000 documents, artifacts, images, and maps, offering a vivid portrayal of the daily life and cultural practices of the ancient inhabitants of Vườn Chuối.

Utilizing advanced technologies such as 3D projection and 3D mapping, the exhibition brings to life the daily activities and living conditions of the pre-Dong Son and Dong Son era communities. Visitors can immerse themselves in the recreated scenes of ancient life, gaining a deeper appreciation for the historical context and cultural significance of the Vườn Chuối site.

To complement the exhibition, the organizing committee released a book titled "Discovering Vườn Chuối (Hanoi) Through Excavations in 2024-2025." This publication delves into the journey of discovery, presenting new insights and findings from recent excavations and research, reinforcing the site's role as a repository of early Vietnamese culture and its enduring relevance in contemporary society.

This event is part of the broader Thang Long-Hanoi Festival 2025, themed "Heritage-Connection-Era," aimed at celebrating the archaeological heritage and fostering connections between the past, present, and future of the thousand-year-old capital city. The 4th Floor: Vườn Chuối relic site stands as a vital link to the ancient roots of Vietnamese civilization, offering visitors a unique opportunity to explore the rich tapestry of cultural heritage embedded within its layers of history.

The 4th Floor: Vườn Chuối relic site stands as a testament to the rich archaeological heritage of Hà Nội and northern Vietnam, offering visitors a glimpse into the ancient civilization that thrived nearly 4,000 years ago. The site, which was first discovered in 1969, has been the subject of extensive archaeological excavations conducted by the Hà Nội Department of Culture and Sports in collaboration with specialized institutions. Over the years, these excavations have uncovered a wealth of artifacts and structures that provide invaluable insights into the lives of the people who lived in this area during various prehistoric periods, including the Phùng Nguyên, Đồng Đậu, Gò Mun, Đông Sơn, and Post-Eastern Sơn cultures.

One of the most significant findings from the recent excavation campaign, which began in March 2024 and is set to conclude in March 2025, is the discovery of a village that developed continuously over nearly 4,000 years. This excavation, covering an area of 6,000 square meters, has revealed important traces of daily life, residential areas, workshops for crafting stone and wooden tools, burial sites, and numerous artifacts characteristic of the Pre-Eastern Sơn and Eastern Sơn periods. Among the remarkable discoveries are jade greenstone axes, symbolic of the power of tribal leaders, and other precious relics that have never before been recorded in the archaeological research of the Metal Age in northern Vietnam and Hà Nội.

The site's importance is further underscored by the variety of artifacts found, including jade ornaments such as necklaces, earrings, beads, and pendants that were likely worn by the elite members of society. These items not only reflect the artistic skills of the ancient inhabitants but also provide clues about their social structure and beliefs. Additionally, the excavation has unearthed a range of tools and pottery, which offer a window into the daily activities and technological advancements of the time.

To celebrate and share these findings with the public, the Hà Nội Museum organized a special exhibition titled "Discoveries from the Vườn Chuối Archaeological Site" in November 2024. This exhibition, part of the Thăng Long-Hà Nội Festival in 2025, showcases nearly 1,000 documents, artifacts, images, and maps that reconstruct the life and culture of the ancient village. Utilizing advanced technologies like 3D projection and 3D mapping, the exhibition aims to bring the past to life, allowing visitors to visualize the daily routines and social dynamics of the ancient inhabitants.

The exhibition also pays tribute to the local community of Lai Xá village, Hoài Đức district, whose residents have played a crucial role in protecting and preserving the archaeological site. Their contributions are highlighted through displays that honor the scientists and individuals who have dedicated themselves to the study and conservation of the Vườn Chuối site. Visitors can see firsthand the significance of the relics found beneath their own village, fostering a sense of pride and connection to their ancestral heritage.

The 4th Floor: Vườn Chuối relic site continues to be a focal point for archaeological research, with ongoing excavations expected to yield further insights into the history and culture of ancient Hà Nội. Despite its recognized value, the process of officially designating it as a historical site has been slow, leaving many to wonder about the reasons behind this delay. Nonetheless, the site remains a vital resource for understanding the development of human civilization in northern Vietnam, and its preservation ensures that future generations will have the opportunity to learn from and appreciate the legacy of those who came before them.

Right at the center of the Hanoi Museum, the main atrium emerges as the "breathing" space of the entire building, where almost every gaze is unconsciously drawn upon first stepping into the museum. This space spans across multiple floors, connecting the exhibition areas with an impressive open structure, giving visitors the feeling of standing in the heart of a colossal architectural structure. Within the building featuring a signature inverted pyramid shape, the atrium not only plays a connecting role but also becomes part of the narrative of Hanoi – a place where the past, present, and future seem to meet in a shared space.

Completed alongside the building on the occasion of the 1000th Anniversary of Thang Long - Hanoi in 2010, the main atrium was designed to harness natural light and create a sense of continuous movement between floors. Many visitors often linger at the railings to look down at the central void or look up at the layered floors above, as if observing a flow of time constructed through architecture. Many of the museum's most beautiful photographs are taken here, where light, shapes, and spatial depth blend together in a captivating way.

What lingers in the main atrium is not just the overwhelming scale, but also a very special feeling: standing in the midst of it, one feels as though they are at the very intersection of Hanoi's thousand-year story.
description_vi:
Ngay tại trung tâm của Bảo tàng Hà Nội, sảnh thông tầng chính hiện lên như khoảng không gian “thở” của toàn bộ công trình, nơi mọi ánh nhìn gần như đều vô thức hướng về khi vừa đặt chân vào bảo tàng. Không gian này trải dài xuyên suốt nhiều tầng, kết nối các khu trưng bày bằng một cấu trúc mở đầy ấn tượng, khiến du khách có cảm giác như đang đứng giữa trái tim của một kiến trúc khổng lồ. Trong công trình mang hình dáng kim tự tháp ngược đặc trưng, sảnh thông tầng không chỉ giữ vai trò liên kết mà còn trở thành một phần của câu chuyện kể về Hà Nội – nơi quá khứ, hiện tại và tương lai như cùng gặp nhau trong một khoảng không chung.

Được hoàn thiện cùng công trình nhân dịp Đại lễ 1000 năm Thăng Long – Hà Nội năm 2010, sảnh thông tầng chính được thiết kế để tận dụng ánh sáng tự nhiên và tạo cảm giác chuyển động liên tục giữa các tầng. Nhiều du khách thường dừng lại thật lâu ở lan can để nhìn xuống khoảng trống trung tâm hoặc ngước lên các tầng xếp lớp phía trên, như đang quan sát một dòng chảy thời gian được dựng bằng kiến trúc. Không ít bức ảnh đẹp nhất của bảo tàng cũng được chụp tại đây, nơi ánh sáng, hình khối và chiều sâu không gian hòa vào nhau đầy cuốn hút.

Điều đọng lại ở sảnh thông tầng chính không chỉ là sự choáng ngợp về quy mô, mà còn là cảm giác rất đặc biệt: đứng giữa nơi ấy, người ta như thấy mình đang ở chính điểm giao nhau của câu chuyện nghìn năm Hà Nội.

Nestled within the front courtyard of the Hanoi Museum on Pham Hung Street, the Dong Buồm exhibition emerges as a very different slice in the heart of the modern metropolis, where architecture is not just to be looked at but also to tell stories. In the middle of the spacious courtyard, bamboo sails rise high as if catching the wind, creating a scene that evokes the ancient voyages of the Vietnamese people, when the desire to go far always went hand in hand with the spirit of preserving their roots.

The exhibition was introduced in 2025 within the framework of the Top 10 Awards, as a creative space connecting architecture, culture, and indigenous memories. The name “Dong Buồm” evokes the image of setting sail—a highly symbolic expression of movement, exploration, and faith in the future. But the interesting thing is that the rustic bamboo material keeps that journey from being separated from mother earth, as if every step forward carries the shadow of Vietnamese tradition.

During the days the exhibition is open, residents and tourists often stroll leisurely around the bamboo structures, take photos, observe the displayed architectural projects, or simply stand under the shade of the “sails” to feel the harmony between art and public space. Leaving this place, people often carry with them a sense of lightness, as if just reminded that a modern city can still grow from very simple materials and deeply Vietnamese memories.

Nép mình trong khuôn viên phía trước Bảo tàng Hà Nội trên đường Phạm Hùng, triển lãm Dong Buồm hiện lên như một lát cắt rất khác giữa lòng đô thị hiện đại, nơi kiến trúc không chỉ để ngắm mà còn để kể chuyện. Giữa khoảng sân rộng, những cánh buồm tre vươn cao như đang đón gió, tạo nên một khung cảnh khiến người ta liên tưởng đến những chuyến hải trình xưa của người Việt, khi khát vọng đi xa luôn song hành cùng tinh thần gìn giữ cội nguồn.

Triển lãm được giới thiệu vào năm 2025 trong khuôn khổ Top 10 Awards, như một không gian sáng tạo kết nối kiến trúc, văn hóa và ký ức bản địa. Tên gọi “Dong Buồm” gợi hình ảnh căng buồm ra khơi – một cách nói đầy biểu tượng về sự chuyển động, khám phá và niềm tin vào tương lai. Nhưng điều thú vị là chất liệu tre mộc mạc lại khiến hành trình ấy không tách rời đất mẹ, như thể mỗi bước tiến đều mang theo bóng dáng truyền thống Việt Nam.

Những ngày triển lãm mở cửa, người dân và du khách thường thong thả dạo quanh các cấu trúc tre, chụp ảnh, quan sát những đồ án kiến trúc trưng bày hay đơn giản là đứng dưới bóng các “cánh buồm” để cảm nhận sự giao hòa giữa nghệ thuật và không gian công cộng. Rời nơi này, người ta thường mang theo cảm giác nhẹ nhõm, như vừa được nhắc nhớ rằng một thành phố hiện đại vẫn có thể lớn lên từ những vật liệu rất đỗi bình dị và ký ức rất Việt Nam.

The inauguration of the "Dong buồm" Pavilion at the Hanoi Museum on May 22, 2026 marked a significant milestone in contemporary Vietnamese architecture. This event not only celebrated the opening of the pavilion but also witnessed the awarding of the Top 10 Awards 2025, which has been organized by KIENVIET MEDIA since its inception in 2018. The ceremony was attended by a multitude of architects, designers, and industry experts, reflecting the growing importance of this annual event in the field of architecture and interior design in Vietnam.

The Top 10 Awards, now in its eighth year, has established itself as a reputable platform for recognizing excellence in architectural and interior design projects across the country. This year's awards continued to focus on three main categories: Top 10 Houses, Top 10 Interior Designs, and Top 10 Green Projects, highlighting the prominent trends in contemporary architecture that emphasize creativity, sustainability, and cultural identity. The organizers announced plans to expand the awards from 2026, introducing two new categories: Top 10 Social Housing and Top 10 C-Solutions, aimed at addressing current issues such as community housing development and sustainable material solutions.

Designed by Dplus Vietnam, the "Dong buồm" Pavilion stands out as a remarkable structure that embodies the spirit of Vietnamese architecture. Inspired by the image of a full sail, the pavilion symbolizes the ambition of Vietnamese architecture to venture into international waters while preserving local cultural values. The design is centered around a core concept known as the "Heritage Core," from which radiates the three fundamental values of the Top 10 Awards: locality, innovation, and humanity. The pavilion's construction features a lattice of bamboo, creating a dynamic visual effect that represents the evolving nature of contemporary Vietnamese architecture.

description:
Hanoi Old Quarter, often simply called phố cổ, is an ancient historical area located in the heart of Hanoi, famous for its system of 36 phố phường formed hundreds of years ago. This quarter began to develop strongly during the Lý and Trần dynasties, when it became a bustling commercial center of the ancient Thăng Long imperial city.
A special feature of the Old Quarter is that each street is often associated with a traditional craft, reflected in names such as Hàng Bạc, Hàng Mã, Hàng Đào… clearly reflecting the economic and cultural life of Hanoians through different periods. Therefore, this place is not just a residential area but also a living museum of urban history and traditional handicrafts of Vietnam.
Having gone through many upheavals, the Old Quarter has largely retained its structure and characteristic way of life, becoming a unique cultural symbol. This is also where many cultural activities and festivals take place, and it is especially vibrant during Tết Nguyên Đán, when the streets are brightly decorated and filled with a traditional atmosphere.
An interesting fact is that despite its small area, the Old Quarter contains an extremely high population density and business activity, creating a dense and colorful pace of life. When strolling here, you are not just exploring a neighborhood, but also stepping into a centuries-long flow of history, where the past and present intertwine in every rhythm of daily life.

Phố cổ Hà Nội, thường được gọi đơn giản là “phố cổ”, là khu vực lịch sử lâu đời nằm ở trung tâm Hà Nội, nổi tiếng với hệ thống “36 phố phường” hình thành từ hàng trăm năm trước. Khu phố này bắt đầu phát triển mạnh từ thời nhà Lý và nhà Trần, khi nơi đây trở thành trung tâm buôn bán sầm uất của kinh thành Thăng Long xưa.
Điểm đặc biệt của phố cổ là mỗi con phố thường gắn với một nghề truyền thống, thể hiện qua tên gọi như Hàng Bạc, Hàng Mã, Hàng Đào… phản ánh rõ nét đời sống kinh tế và văn hóa của người Hà Nội qua từng thời kỳ. Chính vì vậy, nơi đây không chỉ là một khu dân cư mà còn là bảo tàng sống về lịch sử đô thị và nghề thủ công truyền thống của Việt Nam.
Trải qua bao biến động, phố cổ vẫn giữ được phần lớn cấu trúc và nét sinh hoạt đặc trưng, trở thành một biểu tượng văn hóa độc đáo. Đây cũng là nơi diễn ra nhiều hoạt động văn hóa, lễ hội và đặc biệt sôi động vào dịp Tết Nguyên Đán, khi các con phố được trang hoàng rực rỡ và tràn ngập không khí truyền thống.
Một điều thú vị là dù diện tích không lớn, phố cổ lại chứa đựng mật độ dân cư và hoạt động kinh doanh cực kỳ cao, tạo nên một nhịp sống dày đặc và đầy màu sắc. Khi dạo bước nơi đây, bạn không chỉ đang khám phá một khu phố, mà còn đang bước vào dòng chảy lịch sử kéo dài hàng thế kỷ, nơi quá khứ và hiện tại hòa quyện trong từng nhịp sống thường ngày.

Each street in the Old Quarter carries the legacy of a specific trade, evident from names like Hàng Bạc (Silver Street), Hàng Mã (Paper Goods Street), and Hàng Đào (Sandalwood Street), which reflect the economic and cultural life of Hanoians across various epochs.

Despite enduring numerous historical upheavals, the Old Quarter has managed to preserve much of its original layout and lifestyle, making it a unique cultural emblem of the city.

This historic district is not only a residential area but also a dynamic center for cultural activities and festivals. It comes alive particularly during Tết Nguyên Đán, when the streets are festively adorned with decorations and filled with the traditional atmosphere of the Vietnamese New Year. The Old Quarter's small area contrasts sharply with its extremely high population density and intense business activity, contributing to a lively and colorful urban scene. Visitors can experience the interplay between past and present as they wander through the narrow lanes, where the echoes of centuries-old trades blend seamlessly with modern-day commerce.

In addition to its historical and cultural significance, the Old Quarter is a popular tourist destination, offering a glimpse into the daily life of Hanoi. The area around the Hanoi Old Quarter Night Market buzzes with energy as evening falls, illuminated by the glow of streetlights and the sounds of music and chatter. Here, visitors can sample local cuisine from street vendors who set up tables and chairs on the sidewalks, serving dishes that waft with the enticing aromas of Vietnamese street food. The Old Quarter thus stands as a testament to the enduring spirit of Hanoi, where tradition and modernity coexist in a harmonious and dynamic balance.

Article Title: Old Quarter, Hanoi

The Hanoi Old Quarter, also known as Phố cổ Hà Nội, is the historical civic urban core of Hanoi, Vietnam, situated outside the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long. Historically, this area served as the residential, manufacturing, and commercial center, with each street specializing in a distinct type of manufacturing or commerce. Another common name for this area is the 36 streets (Hà Nội 36 phố phường), reflecting the original 36 streets or guilds that comprised the urban area of the city.

The official boundaries of the Hanoi Old Quarter were established by a 1995 decision from the Vietnamese Ministry of Construction. The northern boundary is defined by Hàng Đậu street, while the western boundary is set by Phùng Hưng street. To the south, the limits are marked by Hàng Bông street, Hàng Gai street, Cầu Gỗ street, and Hàng Thùng street. In the east, the area is bounded by Trần Quang Khải street and Trần Nhật Duật street. However, several historically significant streets lie outside these official borders due to their preservation of historical character and density of historical streets.

The Hanoi Old Quarter is part of the Hoàn Kiếm District and covers an area of approximately 100 hectares, encompassing 76 streets distributed across 10 wards. Its history dates back to the Lý and Trần dynasties when it was located east of the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long and along the Red River. Scholar Nguyễn Trãi noted the specialization of certain areas during the Lê dynasty, and the area was fortified with a defensive wall and several gates.

During the Lê dynasty, the area included several lakes and wetlands, notably Thái Cực lake, which were connected to Hoàn Kiếm lake and the Red River. By the late 19th century, these water bodies became isolated. Migration from the surrounding plains and an influx of Chinese traders during the Lê dynasty contributed to the formation of the densest urban area in the city. The French colonial period saw partial rebuilding, including the demolition of two small markets to construct Đồng Xuân Market and the introduction of a tramway. This era also brought French and Indian businessmen to the area for trade.

The Hanoi Old Quarter is renowned for its guild streets, each named after a specific trade, such as Hàng Tre (bamboo wares) and Hàng Đồng (copper wares). While some streets retain their traditional trades, others have shifted to different specialties. For instance, Hàng Buồm (sails street) is now known for Vietnamese cakes and candy. Researchers have documented the cultural evolution of the area during the early 20th century.

Historic sites within the Hanoi Old Quarter include temples, pagodas, and assembly halls. Communal temples, often used for commerce, were common, though many have been lost over time. Notable surviving temples include Mã Mây and Kim Cổ. City gates, except for the Quan Chưởng gate, have largely disappeared. The architectural style of the commercial area features traditional shophouses with slanted tile roofs, predominantly built in the 18th and 19th centuries. Since the late 20th century, the number of traditional houses has declined due to ongoing demolitions and rebuildings.

Preservation efforts have been initiated to restore the deteriorating historic remnants of the Hanoi Old Quarter. In preparation for the 1000th anniversary of Hanoi in 2010, the Hanoi People's Committee allocated 50 billion VND for refurbishing seven key areas.

The Hanoi Old Quarter, also known as Hanoi’s Old Quarter, is a historic district located in the heart of Hoan Kiem District, near Hoan Kiem Lake, and is a must-visit destination for tourists exploring the vibrant city of Hanoi. This ancient area covers approximately 100 hectares and encompasses 76 streets within ten different wards. The southern boundary includes streets such as Cau Go, Hang Gai, Hang Bong, and Hang Thung, while the eastern edge is marked by Tran Nhat Duat and Tran Quang Khai streets. Each street in this quarter is named after traditional crafts and trades that have been practiced here since ancient times, with names like Hang Than, Hang Gai, Hang Bong, and Hang Dao reflecting the historical significance of these areas.

The Hanoi Old Quarter was established during the Ly and Tran dynasties, serving as a bustling hub for commerce and transportation in the ancient capital of Thang Long. The architecture of the old quarter is characterized by narrow, winding streets lined with small houses featuring sloping roofs and yellow-painted walls, which evoke a sense of nostalgia and historical continuity. These structures are typical of traditional Vietnamese architecture, with each house often no more than three stories high and built closely together, creating a dense urban landscape that reflects the city's past.

Visitors to the Hanoi Old Quarter can immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of local culture and history. Walking through the streets, one can easily imagine the lively scenes of daily life from centuries ago, as the quarter continues to thrive with its unique blend of old-world charm and modern vibrancy. The streets are filled with shops selling traditional goods, ranging from handmade crafts to specialty foods, each contributing to the distinctive atmosphere of the area. For instance, Hang Ma Street specializes in decorative items for festivals and holidays, while Hang Buom Street is known for its sweets and snacks, and Hang Quat Street sells religious paraphernalia.

One of the highlights of visiting the Hanoi Old Quarter is the opportunity to experience its diverse culinary offerings. Tourists can indulge in a variety of local delicacies, including famous dishes like bun dau mam tom (rice noodle with tofu and shrimp paste), nem chua ran (fried spring rolls), and kem Trang Tien (Trang Tien ice cream). These traditional foods not only satisfy the palate but also provide a deeper understanding of the local cuisine and its cultural significance. Additionally, there are numerous cafes scattered throughout the quarter where visitors can relax and enjoy a cup of coffee while taking in the picturesque surroundings. Popular spots include Phê La, Café Giảng, and Vintage 1976 Café, each offering a unique ambiance and stunning views of the historic neighborhood.

For those interested in immersing themselves further into the cultural heritage of the Hanoi Old Quarter, there are several notable landmarks and attractions to explore. One of the most iconic sites is the Hoan Kiem Lake, surrounded by the serene beauty of the Ngoc Son Temple, which offers a tranquil setting for reflection and contemplation. Another significant location is the Bai Ma Temple, where visitors can pay their respects and learn about the spiritual traditions that have been preserved over generations. Additionally, the Dong Xuan Market is a bustling hub of activity, especially in the morning when locals gather to buy fresh produce and traditional goods.

Exploring the Hanoi Old Quarter also involves engaging with the dynamic nightlife and street culture. The Ta Hien Street, known as the "street that never sleeps," is a popular spot for young people to socialize and enjoy the energetic atmosphere well into the night. Similarly, the night markets and pedestrian zones offer a glimpse into the vibrant evening scene, where vendors sell everything from souvenirs to street food, creating a lively and festive atmosphere.

To fully appreciate the Hanoi Old Quarter, visitors should consider renting bicycles or cyclos to navigate the narrow streets and soak in the sights and sounds of the area. This method of transportation not only provides a leisurely way to explore but also allows for a closer interaction with the local community and the charming architecture of the old quarter. Moreover, purchasing traditional gifts such as candied fruits, rice cakes, and lotus tea can serve as a meaningful souvenir, capturing the essence of the Hanoi Old Quarter and its enduring cultural legacy.

In summary, the Hanoi Old Quarter is a living testament to the rich history and cultural heritage of Vietnam, offering a unique blend of historical significance, traditional crafts, and contemporary life. Whether it's through tasting local delicacies, visiting historical sites, or simply wandering through the narrow streets, the Hanoi Old Quarter promises an unforgettable experience that encapsulates the spirit of the city.

The Hanoi Old Quarter, a vibrant tapestry of ancient charm and modern vibrancy, is one of the most captivating destinations in the bustling heart of Vietnam's capital city. Spanning approximately 100 hectares, this historic district is home to 76 streets within ten wards, each contributing to a labyrinthine network that encapsulates the essence of traditional Vietnamese architecture and culture. The Old Quarter, often referred to as the "36 streets," is not merely a relic of the past but a living museum where history and contemporary life intertwine seamlessly.

The origins of the Hanoi Old Quarter trace back to the Lý and Trần dynasties, specifically the 11th century, when it served as the commercial hub of the imperial city of Thăng Long. This period saw the establishment of numerous trades and crafts, giving rise to a unique urban layout characterized by narrow, winding streets lined with small, distinctive houses. These structures, typically featuring sloping roofs covered in red tiles and painted in warm hues, reflect the architectural styles of the time, embodying the essence of traditional Vietnamese design.

Today, the Hanoi Old Quarter stands as a testament to its storied past, preserving a wealth of historical and cultural significance. The government and local residents have made concerted efforts to maintain and promote the traditional values embedded in the quarter, ensuring that its rich heritage remains intact for future generations. Each street and alleyway in the Old Quarter tells a story, weaving together the threads of history, culture, and daily life into a vivid narrative that transports visitors through time.

Among the many attractions in the Hanoi Old Quarter, none is more iconic than Hoàn Kiếm Lake, also known as the Lake of the Returned Sword. This serene body of water, situated at the heart of the Old Quarter, is not only a natural landmark but also a spiritual symbol deeply intertwined with the city’s identity. According to legend, the lake earned its name from the tale of King Lê Thái Tổ returning his magical sword to the Golden Turtle God, a story that resonates with the national spirit of independence and patriotism.

Surrounding the lake are several notable landmarks, including the Temple of Literature and the Ngoc Son Temple, both of which offer insights into the religious and educational traditions of old Hanoi. The lake itself is a tranquil oasis amidst the bustling streets, providing a picturesque setting for leisurely strolls and moments of reflection. Its central location makes it a focal point for both locals and tourists, who come to enjoy the serene ambiance and the stunning views of the Thap Rua Pagoda and the Turtle Tower, two enduring symbols of the city’s cultural heritage.

Another must-visit destination within the Hanoi Old Quarter is Hàng Mã Street, renowned for its vibrant atmosphere and traditional crafts. Historically, this street was famous for producing paper goods and ritual objects, a tradition that continues today alongside a thriving market for modern souvenirs and decorative items. During festive seasons such as Tet and Mid-Autumn Festival, Hàng Mã transforms into a dazzling spectacle of colors and lights, with vendors selling an array of lanterns, decorations, and flowers that create a festive and enchanting atmosphere.

Nearby, the lively atmosphere of Tạ Hiện Street offers a different kind of experience. Known colloquially as the "beer street," Tạ Hiện is a popular gathering place for young people and tourists alike, especially in the evenings. The street’s history is rooted in its former role as the site of the Quang Lac Theater, but today it thrives as a hub for socializing and enjoying the nightlife. With its mix of traditional architecture and contemporary energy, Tạ Hiện presents a dynamic scene that perfectly captures the essence of modern Hanoi.

Chợ Đồng Xuân, or Dong Xuan Market, is another cornerstone of the Hanoi Old Quarter, offering a glimpse into the city’s bustling commercial life. Established in 1804, the market has undergone significant changes over the years, particularly after a major fire in 1995, which led to extensive renovations and expansions. Today, it stands as one of the largest markets in northern Vietnam, housing over 2,000 stalls that cater to a wide range of needs, from fresh produce and traditional handicrafts to trendy fashion and household goods.

description: Nestled in the bustling heart of Hanoi's Old Quarter, Hang Bac street stretches like a shimmering silk ribbon, fully preserving the essence of the imperial capital's goldsmithing craftsmanship. Tracing back history to the fifteenth century, talented artisans from Chau Khe and Dinh Cong villages were summoned by the imperial court to Thang Long to cast silver ingots. Enduring countless ups and downs of the times, they gathered here, opening forging and casting workshops, carving gold and silver, and lit up the name Hang Bac, renowned far and wide. The breath of life here always shines with vibrancy and overflows with vitality. Day after day, tourists from all directions bustle back and forth, strolling, captivatedly watching artisans meticulously hammering and casting exquisite jewelry pieces behind glass windows. Especially during the death anniversary of the goldsmithing ancestors or Tet holidays, the entire street seems to be infused with new life, brilliant with flags and flowers, and fragrant with reverent incense smoke before ancient communal houses and temples. Wandering amidst shops overflowing with metallic gleam, one's heart is suddenly filled with a profound sense of appreciation. The experience of witnessing firsthand exquisite goldsmithing works brings a deep admiration, helping us fully understand the exquisite talent and enduring vitality of a traditional craft street in the heart of a prosperous city.
description_vi: Nằm nếp mình giữa trung tâm khu phố cổ Hà Nội nhộn nhịp, phố Hàng Bạc vươn mình tựa một dải lụa lấp lánh lưu giữ trọn vẹn tinh hoa chế tác kim hoàn của mảnh đất kinh kỳ. Ngược dòng lịch sử về thế kỷ mười lăm, những người thợ tài hoa từ làng Châu Khê, Định Công đã được triều đình gọi về Thăng Long đúc bạc nén. Trải qua bao thăng trầm thời cuộc, họ quần tụ lại chốn này, mở lò rèn đúc, chạm khắc vàng bạc và thắp lên cái tên Hàng Bạc vang danh bốn phương. Hơi thở đời sống nơi đây luôn ánh lên sự rộn rã và cuộn trào sức sống. Ngày ngày, du khách thập phương tấp nập ngược xuôi dạo bước, say sưa ngắm nhìn các nghệ nhân tỉ mẩn gò đúc những món trang sức tinh xảo sau khung cửa kính. Đặc biệt trong những dịp giỗ tổ nghề kim hoàn hay lễ Tết, cả con phố như được tiếp thêm sinh khí, rực rỡ cờ hoa và ngào ngạt khói nhang thành kính trước các đình miếu cổ. Lạc bước giữa những cửa hiệu ngập tràn ánh kim, lòng người bỗng dâng lên một niềm cảm khái sâu sắc. Trải nghiệm tận mắt chiêm ngưỡng những tác phẩm kim hoàn sắc sảo mang lại một sự ngưỡng mộ thẳm sâu, giúp ta thấu hiểu trọn vẹn tài hoa tuyệt mỹ và sức sống trường tồn của một con phố nghề cổ truyền giữa lòng đô thị phồn hoa.

documents.content:
Hang Bac Street, also known as Phố Hàng Bạc, is a vibrant and historic thoroughfare nestled in the heart of Hanoi's Old Quarter. This charming street stretches like a shimmering silk ribbon, preserving the essence of the imperial capital's goldsmithing craftsmanship, which dates back to the 15th century. The street's name, Hang Bac, is derived from the gold and silver shops that once lined its length, earning it a reputation as a hub of artisanal excellence.

As one wanders down Hang Bac Street, the eye is immediately drawn to the sparkling white of metal jewelry, intertwined with the brilliant yellow lights from the display cases. The unique identifying feature of the street is the multitude of large gold and silver shop and foreign currency exchange signs, placed side-by-side, covering the entire facade. This bustling scene is nestled within a tangled network of alleys and lanes, bordering the narrow sidewalks always bustling with people and vehicles moving back and forth.

The street's history is deeply rooted in the imperial court's summons of talented artisans from Chau Khe and Dinh Cong villages to Thang Long to cast silver ingots. Over the centuries, these artisans gathered here, opening forging and casting workshops, carving gold and silver, and earning the street its reputation as a center of excellence. The street's cultural significance is further underscored by the numerous ancient communal houses and temples that line its length, their ornate facades and intricate carvings a testament to the region's rich cultural heritage.

During the death anniversary of the goldsmithing ancestors or Tet holidays, the entire street comes alive with vibrant colors, as flags and flowers adorn the streets, and the air is filled with the sweet scent of incense smoke wafting from the ancient temples. Visitors from all directions flock to Hang Bac Street, captivated by the artisans' meticulous craftsmanship, as they hammer and cast exquisite jewelry pieces behind glass windows. The experience of witnessing firsthand the exquisite goldsmithing works brings a deep admiration, helping visitors fully understand the enduring vitality of a traditional craft street in the heart of a prosperous city.

As the sun sets, the street takes on a magical quality, with the soft glow of lanterns and the sound of hammering and chiseling creating a symphony of sights and sounds that transport visitors back in time to an era of imperial grandeur. Hang Bac Street is a true gem of Hanoi's Old Quarter, a testament to the city's rich cultural heritage and its enduring ability to preserve and celebrate its traditions.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Bac Street
documents.content:
Hang Bac Street is located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi. During the late 19th century under French colonial rule, it was known as Rue des changeurs (Street of Money Exchangers). In 1945, the street was renamed Hang Bac.

Previously, Hang Bac Street belonged to Phuong Hang Bac, Hoan Kiem District, but now it is part of Hoan Kiem Ward, Hanoi City. The street stretches approximately 0.5 kilometers from east to northeast. At its western end, it intersects with Hang Ngang, Hang Dao, and Hang Bo streets, while its eastern end meets Hang Mam Street. It is situated about 0.3 kilometers north of Hoan Kiem Lake.

According to historical records inscribed on a stele at the Dong Han Temple (number 42), Hang Bac Street was established during the Le Dynasty or slightly earlier. During this period, Hang Bac was part of Dong Cac ward, Tho Xuan county. Under the Nguyen Dynasty, the area belonged to Dong Tho village, Tho Xuan county, Hoai Duc prefecture, Hanoi province.

The traditional jewelry craft on Hang Bac Street has roots in the village of Chau Khe in Thuc Khang commune, Binh Giang district, Hai Duong province. In the 15th century, during the reign of King Le Thanh Tong, Shangshu Liu Xuan Tin, originally from Chau Khe village, was tasked by the court to establish a silver minting workshop in the capital city of Thang Long (now Hanoi). By the early 19th century, when the Nguyen dynasty moved to Hue, they took the silver minting workshop with them. However, most of the Chau Khe craftsmen remained in Thang Long and continued their traditional jewelry trade, establishing a guild in what is now Hang Bac Street. Additionally, Hang Bac attracted goldsmiths from Ding Cong and Dong Tam to settle there.

Throughout its development, the community of Hang Bac craftsmen, including those from Chau Khe, maintained strong bonds, supporting each other in their professions, businesses, and cultural and religious activities. Despite living in the city, they retained a sense of village life, returning annually on the 19th day of the first lunar month to participate in the village festival, offering prayers to the Village Guardian and honoring the Ancestral Craftsmen.

Today, Hang Bac Street still features several houses that bear witness to the history of the Chau Khe craftsmen. For instance, number 58 was once a silver minting workshop, number 50 houses the Upper Shrine, and number 42 houses the Lower Shrine, which were sites for collecting and processing silver ingots. The Dong Han Temple (number 42), built at the end of the 18th century during the 44th year of the Canh Hung era, is dedicated to Ling Lang Wang and also houses a shrine for a female deity. This temple is the largest in the old quarter of Hanoi.

Since the reign of Emperor Gia Long, Hang Bac Street had an official responsible for managing silver transactions, collecting scrap silver from various provinces, and delivering it to the minting workshops. After refining the silver into ingots, these would be returned to the provinces and then sent to the capital to be deposited into the treasury.

Using traditional handcraft techniques, the artisans of Hang Bac have produced exquisite jewelry such as rings, earrings, bracelets, and necklaces for women and children. They also specialize in engraved pieces inspired by motifs like the Four Spirits (lion, unicorn, tortoise, phoenix), Two Dragons Chasing the Moon, and the Eight Treasures. Situated in the bustling heart of Hanoi's historic district, Hang Bac Street stretches for a length of 330 meters, nestled within the Hoan Kiem District. This vibrant thoroughfare is conveniently located near the Hoan Kiem Lake, allowing visitors to reach the iconic Ngoc Son Temple in just 10 to 15 minutes by walking northward. The street is bordered by other notable streets such as Hang Mam, Hang Be, and Pho Phat Lieu, while also touching upon Hang Gai and Hang Dao to the west. It intersects with Ngang Street at Ma May and Dong Xuan Market at Tho Mo Lane, creating a lively network of commerce and culture.

The history of Hang Bac Street dates back to the late 19th century during French colonial rule when it was known as Rue des changeurs, meaning the street of money changers. After the August Revolution in 1945, the street was renamed Hang Bac, which translates to Silver Street. According to historical records, the Emperor Le Thanh Tong, in the 15th century, granted permission to the village of Chau Khe (or Trau Khe), located in Thuong Khanh Commune, Binh Giang District, Hai Duong Province, to produce silverware and coins. This village was then relocated to Hang Bac Street, where they established a workshop at number 58 Hang Bac. The historical marker at number 42 Hang Bac further corroborates this tradition, indicating that the street has been home to silver workshops since the time of the Le Dynasty or even earlier.

The craft of silver making on Hang Bac Street has a storied past, originating from the village of Chau Khe, which was renowned for its skilled artisans who produced exquisite silverware. During the reign of King Le Thanh Tong in the 15th century, the village was tasked with producing silverware and coins for the royal court in Thang Long, now modern-day Hanoi. When the Nguyen Dynasty moved their capital to Hue in the early 19th century, they brought along the tradition of silver making, ensuring its continuity. Today, descendants of the Chau Khe community continue to practice this ancient craft, contributing to the vibrant atmosphere of Hang Bac Street.

Throughout the centuries, the street has evolved into a hub of activity, not only for the original inhabitants but also for those who have settled there more recently. The residents of Hang Bac Street maintain strong ties with their ancestral roots, engaging in various aspects of life including business, social activities, and cultural practices. Despite the passage of time, the spirit of the village remains alive, with many families still participating in communal activities and festivals, fostering a sense of unity and shared heritage.

Visitors to Hang Bac Street can explore numerous historical sites and landmarks that reflect the rich cultural heritage of the area. Notable among these is the Trang Xuong Silver Workshop at number 58, which continues to produce fine silverware. The Thien Thang Pagoda at number 50 and the Dong Han Stele at number 42 are also significant, with the latter dating back to the late 18th century and featuring intricate carvings that tell the story of the street’s history. The Kim Ngan Pagoda, with its striking red lacquer finish, stands out as one of the most prominent structures in the area, adding to the visual appeal of the street.

Hang Bac Street is a living testament to the enduring legacy of traditional craftsmanship and cultural significance. The architecture of the buildings along the street reflects the historical layers of its development, with many retaining the traditional Vietnamese architectural style characterized by ornate facades and intricate wood carvings. The narrow lanes and closely packed houses create a cozy and intimate atmosphere, inviting visitors to immerse themselves in the daily life of the community. The street is a vibrant blend of old-world charm and contemporary energy, offering a unique glimpse into the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s cultural heritage.

As visitors stroll down Hang Bac Street, they are greeted by the sounds of hammering and the clinking of silverware being crafted, the aroma of freshly baked pastries wafting from local bakeries, and the sight of artisans meticulously working on their crafts. The street is a dynamic space where tradition meets modernity, providing a fascinating insight into the lives of the people who call Hang Bac Street home. Whether it’s the intricate silver jewelry, the bustling markets, or the warm hospitality of the locals, Hang Bac Street offers a memorable experience that captures the essence of Hanoi’s rich cultural heritage.

Hang Bac Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a historic thoroughfare that stretches for 280 meters and is 6.5 meters wide. The street runs from the end of Hang Mam Street at the intersection with Ma May Street, crossing through the junction with Ta Hien and Dinh Lieu streets, and terminates where it meets the boundary between Hang Ngang and Hang Dao streets. This narrow lane has been a significant part of Hanoi's rich history, dating back to the time of the Le Dynasty when it was known as Dong Cac ward, which served as the setting for the story "Mieu lua" in Vu trung tuy bieu by Pham Dinh Ho. During this period, Dong Cac was also the site of silver ingot exchange and trade, a practice that continued into the 19th century when the area was part of Dong Tho and Dung Han villages within the Huu Tuc district of Tho Xuan county.

Under French colonial rule, the street was referred to as Rue des Changeurs, reflecting its role as a center for silver exchange. The current name, Hang Bac, was officially adopted after the revolution. Today, Hang Bac Street falls under the jurisdiction of Hang Bac ward, Hoan Kiem district.

The street's history is deeply intertwined with three distinct trades: silver ingot casting, jewelry making, and money exchange. The craft of silver ingot casting was brought to Hang Bac by residents of Truong Khe village, now part of Binh Giang district in Hai Duong province. According to legend, during the reign of King Le Thanh Tong (1460-1497), a man named Luu Xuan Tin from Truong Khe village was appointed as the head of the Upper Treasury Office and received permission from the king to establish a silver ingot casting workshop in the capital. He then brought villagers from his home to work in this specialized trade. The village of Truong Khe had five clans, each represented by different generations who moved to Hang Bac to engage in the silver casting business. These clans established two communal houses to honor their ancestors and the profession: the upper communal house, or Truong communal house (number 50), and the lower communal house, or Kim Ngan communal house (number 42).

The communal houses were not only places of worship but also served as centers for processing silver ingots. The term "trang," meaning workshop, refers to the place where silver was melted and cast into ingots. The "ding," or communal house, was responsible for receiving raw materials and delivering finished products to the official office, known as the Ty quan, who acted on behalf of the royal court. The silver casting trade was exclusive to the people of Truong Khe-Hang Bac due to the need to maintain secrecy and prevent fraud, given that silver ingots were used as currency in ancient times. However, the communal houses did not honor Luu Xuan Tin but rather worshipped Hien Van, a mythical figure considered the ancestor of all crafts.

By the late 19th century, the population of Truong Khe residents in Hang Bac had grown significantly, necessitating the acquisition of additional space for communal activities. They purchased the Inner Temple (Nội Miếu) of the Hài Tượng shoemakers' community to create a memorial hall called Truong Khe Vong So, dedicated to the spirits of those who had returned to their ancestral homes.

In addition to silver casting, the residents of Truong Khe also engaged in money exchange, converting large sums of money from coins and small pieces of silver into more manageable forms. This service was essential before the advent of paper currency, as handling large amounts of metal coins or small silver pieces was cumbersome and inconvenient.

The silver casting industry ceased operations at the beginning of the 19th century when Emperor Gia Long moved the capital to Hue, compelling the silver casting workshops to relocate there. However, the money exchange business continued until the arrival of the French colonizers.

Hang Bac Street also hosted another important trade related to silver and gold: jewelry making. This craft encompassed three sub-disciplines: engraving, which involved carving designs onto gold and silver objects; drawing, which entailed pulling molten gold or silver into fine threads and weaving them into intricate patterns; and polishing, which focused on creating smooth, shiny surfaces without any embellishments.

Jewelry makers from Ding Cong Thượng, now part of Hoang Mai district in Hanoi, were known for their skills in these areas. Legend has it that during the Ly Nam De era (6th century), three brothers from Ding Cong Thượng—Tran Dian, Tran Dien, and Tran Hoa—learned the art of jewelry making and taught it to their fellow villagers. These artisans settled in Hang Bac but initially resided at the eastern end of Hang Bo street. They built a communal house in Hang Bo to honor their ancestors, with the altar later relocated to the communal house in Ding Cong Thượng.

Another group of jewelry makers came from Dong Sam village in Kien Xuong district, Thai Binh province. While both groups practiced engraving, drawing, and polishing, they often specialized in different types of jewelry. Dong Sam craftsmen were known for creating larger silver items such as incense burners, boxes, trays, and bowls, while Ding Cong artisans focused on smaller, ornamental pieces like earrings, necklaces, and rings.

Until the early 20th century, Hang Bac retained its status as a traditional street, characterized by its rows of "diem" houses, a type of Vietnamese architecture featuring high, narrow structures with overhanging second floors. The shops along the street were simple yet functional, equipped with basic tools such as molds, anvils, and polishing stones. 

The street also featured two communal houses representing the original inhabitants of Dong Cac, the former Dong Han and Dong Tho villages. These communal houses, located at number 54 and 24 respectively, served as centers for local traditions and rituals. As you slow your pace and take in the sights and sounds, you can't help but feel a deep sense of connection to this vibrant street, which has been a hub of activity for centuries. documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Be Street
documents.content:
Hang Be Street is one of the ancient streets in Hanoi, stretching from the intersection of Hang Mam and Hang Bac to the junction of Cau Go and Hang Thuong, connecting with Hang Dau Street. It belongs to Hang Bac ward, Hoan Kiem district, Hanoi. In the past, Hang Be was part of an old dike where wooden rafts and construction materials from the northern regions were brought to sell. Hence, this section of the dike was named Hang Be, and the market on the dike was called the Hang Be Market. During the French colonial period, the street was officially named Hang Be Street (Rues des Radeaux).

The area where Hang Be Street now stands was originally part of the Nam Hoa village, which belonged to the Huu Tuc commune, Tho Xuan county. By the mid-19th century, it became known as Nam Pho village, Dong Tho commune. Historically, this location was close to My Loc wharf by the Red River. Rafts made of bamboo and reeds were transported here for sale, forming a raft market within the Hang Be Market. Initially, these rafts were sold at Hang Tre Street, but later moved to Hang Be Street. The beginning of Hang Be Street was once called Hang Dua Street because it was a place to trade dried betel nuts. When rafts could no longer reach the foot of the dike due to sedimentation pushing the river further away, the street became a place to trade betel nuts, hence its alternative name, Hang Dua Street.

In the past, annually, bamboo rafts from the southern regions would bring goods such as sugar from Quang, fish nets, shrimp, dried fish, fish sauce, dried betel nuts from Qui Nhon and Binh Dinh, bowls, paper, silk, copper pots, and tin trays. Large boats carried goods like altar tablets, ancestral shrines, tea cabinets, and even kept chickens and dogs. Chinese merchants also participated in trading, bringing goods in large quantities to storehouses along Hang Be Street until the river shifted, a new dike was built farther away, and the bamboo rafts and wood were relocated elsewhere, while betel nuts continued to be sold here. The new dike had a section named Bè Thượng, which the French called Rue de la Digue (Street on the Dike) when they first arrived in Hanoi, corresponding to Nguyen Huu Huan Street today.

The narrow pathways are lined with small shops and stalls selling a variety of goods, from traditional handicrafts to fresh produce. The atmosphere is lively and bustling, with the sounds of vendors calling out to customers and the aroma of freshly cooked food wafting through the air. This vibrant scene is a reflection of the street’s role as a hub of commerce and social interaction, where locals and tourists alike come together to experience the unique flavor of Hanoi.

The street’s history is further enriched by the numerous legends and stories associated with it. One such tale involves a young woman from a wealthy family who lost her fortune and had to sell her property, a poignant reminder of the unpredictable nature of life and the importance of community support. Such narratives add layers of depth to the street’s identity, making it more than just a place of commerce but a repository of cultural memory and human experience.

As visitors wander through Hang Be Street, they are invited to engage with the local culture, whether through casual conversations with shopkeepers, sampling traditional dishes at street-side cafes, or simply observing the daily routines of the residents. Hang Be Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a charming and historically rich area that stretches for 172 meters and is 6 meters wide. The street runs from Hang Mam Street to the intersection of Hang Dao and Cau Go streets. Originally part of the Nam Hoa village, which was situated near the My Loc gate, this area was later renamed Nam Pho during the mid-19th century when the village's administrative division was changed to Dong Tho.

During the French colonial period, the street was known as "rue des Radeaux" or "Phố Hàng Bè," meaning "Raft Street." In 1920, it was renamed "rue Hulet" or "Phố Hu Lê," but in 1945, the original name "Hang Be" was restored. Today, Hang Be Street belongs to Hang Bac ward, Hoan Kiem district.

The origin of the street's name is rooted in its history as a marketplace for raft sellers and buyers. Due to its proximity to the Red River, the area became a hub for selling rafts made of bamboo and other materials. Initially, the market was held at the end of Hang Tre Street, where the Royal Hotel now stands, but it gradually moved to Hang Be Street. This transition led to the street's current name, reflecting its historical significance as a trading center for rafts.

Interestingly, the beginning of Hang Be Street was once called Hang Cau Street because it was home to many shops selling dried rattan. At number 29 on Hang Be Street, there is a temple dedicated to Ngũ Hầu, also known as Cao Tu, a legendary hero from the time of King An Duong Vuong. Inside the temple, there is a pair of poetic couplets that beautifully capture the spirit of the place:

"Sông Tô nổi sóng căm thù, một tấm lòng trung truyền sử Thục.
Thành Loa treo vầng nhật nguyện áo hoa phong tặng tự triều Đinh."

Translated, these lines mean: "The waves of the To River surge with anger, a loyal heart passing down the history of Shu. The Loa City hangs a sun and moon, flowers bloom in the wind, a gift from the reign of Emperor Dinh."

According to legend, Emperor Dinh Tien Hoang bestowed the title of king upon Cao Tu. The temple itself is not associated with the Nam Pho village but rather with the Ngũ Hầu village, which was originally located outside the ancient Thang Long Citadel, close to the Red River. To avoid flooding, the villagers eventually relocated to the land of Nam Pho.

Hang Be Street played a significant role during the early stages of the national resistance war, serving as a command post for the leadership of the First Regional Command and the 101st Regiment, a main force regiment of the region. This historical context adds a layer of importance to the street beyond its commercial origins.

Visitors to Hang Be Street can immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s past, exploring the narrow lanes lined with traditional houses and small shops. The atmosphere is one of tranquility and nostalgia, with the sounds of daily life blending seamlessly into the urban landscape. The street offers a glimpse into the city’s heritage, where old traditions coexist with modernity, creating a unique blend of history and contemporary life.

The cultural significance of Hang Be Street extends beyond its physical boundaries, embodying the resilience and adaptability of the local community. It serves as a testament to the enduring spirit of Hanoi, where each corner tells a story of the past while embracing the future.

description: Nestled amidst the intricate network of the Old Quarter, Hàng Bồ street emerges as a bustling highlight, bearing the strong imprint of trade of the thousand-year-old capital of civilization. Tracing back through history to centuries past, this street was a gathering place for weavers specializing in making and selling various types of large baskets, hampers, and rattan/bamboo trays for storing agricultural products. The rustic name Hàng Bồ was born from these simple items, sowing in the hearts of Tràng An people memories of a prosperous handicraft era intertwined with the bustling trade of the marketplace. The breath of life here today has completely transformed, becoming a vibrant paradise of garment accessories. Day after day, travelers and tailors bustle back and forth, engrossed in choosing each roll of lace, ribbon, or sparkling bead behind glass cabinets. Especially in the days leading up to Tết, the street suddenly bursts with the vibrant colors of spring from stalls of greeting cards and colorful artificial flowers. Lost amidst the maze of these charming little items, one's heart suddenly fills with a strange mix of excitement and nostalgia. The experience of gently touching each button or spool of colored thread brings an absolute sense of familiarity, helping us understand the resilient vitality and ingenious transformation of this imperial land through countless ups and downs of the eras.

Nestled within the labyrinthine network of Hanoi’s Old Quarter, Hang Bo Street stands out as a vibrant artery pulsating with the energy of commerce and tradition. Historically, this street was a hub for weavers who specialized in crafting and trading large baskets, hampers, and rattan trays used for storing agricultural produce. The rustic name “Hang Bo” emerged from these utilitarian items, evoking memories of a thriving handicraft era that once flourished alongside the bustling marketplaces of Thang Long, the ancient capital. 

Today, Hang Bo Street has undergone a remarkable transformation, now serving as a bustling haven for garment accessories. The narrow street, lined with tube houses featuring sloping tiled roofs, is a kaleidoscope of colors, with countless rolls of ribbon and lace displayed prominently in shop windows. The walls, adorned with their characteristic yellowish, moss-covered hues, add a layer of charm and historical depth to the scene. A defining feature of the street is the towering piles of beads and buttons, often spilling onto the sidewalks, creating a mesmerizing spectacle for visitors and locals alike.

The atmosphere is perpetually alive with the hum of activity, as travelers and tailors穿梭于街道上，忙于挑选每卷蕾丝、缎带或玻璃柜后的闪光珠子。特别是在接近春节的日子里，这条街突然充满了来自贺卡摊位和五彩缤纷的人造花的春天色彩。迷失在这些迷人的小物品中，人们的心中突然充满了兴奋与怀旧交织的情感。轻轻触摸每一个纽扣或彩色线轴带来的熟悉感，让人深刻体会到这片古老土地历经无数起伏后依然坚韧的生命力和巧妙的转变。

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Bo Street
documents.content:
Hang Bo Street is located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi. During the French colonial period at the end of the 19th century, it was known as Rue des Paniers. After 1945, the street officially adopted its current name, Hang Bo. Historically, this street was home to shops selling bamboo and rattan weaving tools such as baskets, crates, and winnows. During Tet (Lunar New Year), traditional goods would fill the street, bustling with buyers and sellers.

Previously, Hang Bo Street belonged to the Hang Bo ward in Hoan Kiem district, but now it is part of the Hoan Kiem ward in Hanoi city. The street stretches approximately 0.27 kilometers from east to west. At its eastern end, it intersects with Hang Dao, Hang Ngang, and Hang Bac streets. To the west, it meets Hang The, Thuoc Bac, and Bat Dan streets. It is situated 0.35 kilometers north of Hoan Kiem Lake and 0.5 kilometers south of Dong Xuan Market.

The area around Hang Bo Street originally comprised parts of the villages of Xuan Hoa (to the east) and Nhan Noi (to the west), both part of the former Tien Tuc district of Tho Xuan county. By mid-19th century, Xuan Hoa village merged with Yen Hoa village to form Xuan Yen village. The Tien Tuc district also changed its name to Thuong My district. Under French rule, Hang Bo Street was called "Rue des Paniers." After the revolution, Hanoi officially named it "Hang Bo." In the early 20th century, many Chinese immigrants from Quanzhou settled in this area, where they weighed rice and fruits, and some opened photography studios.

Traces of the old villages can still be found in the form of remaining temples and shrines: the Xuan Yen Temple (formerly of Xuan Hoa village) at number 44 Hang Can Street worships Princess Lan Ngoc, another Xuan Yen Temple (formerly of Yen Hoa village) at number 6 Lương Văn Can Street worships Nguyen Quan Phu’s wife, and the Nhan Noi Temple at number 84A Hang Bo Street also worships Princess Lan Ngoc. Additionally, the Nhan Noi Communal House at number 33 Bat Dan Street honors the White Horse God. Until the beginning of the French colonial era, the middle section of Hang Bo Street was where shops selling woven baskets and other items made of bamboo and rattan were concentrated. The eastern part of the street, near Hang Dao and Hang Ngang streets, was formerly known as Hang Dep Street, where shops sold wooden clogs and sandals.

documents.title: Thông tin Website - Hang Bo Street
documents.content:
Hang Bo Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a historic thoroughfare that stretches for 272 meters and is approximately 6 meters wide. It runs from the intersection of Hang Dao and Hang Ngang streets to the junction of Hang The, Thuoc Bac, and Bat Dan streets, intersecting with Hang Can and Luong Van Can streets. This street was originally part of the land belonging to the villages of Xuan Hoa (the eastern segment) and Nhan Noi (the western segment), which were both part of the former Tien Tuc district of Tho Xuan county. By the mid-19th century, the village of Xuan Hoa merged with the village of Yen Hoa to form the village of Xuan Yen, and the district of Tien Tuc was renamed Thuong My.

During the French colonial period, this street was known as "rue des Paniers," or "Basket Street." After the revolution, the official name was retained as Hang Bo Street. Today, it falls within the jurisdiction of Hang Dao and Hang Bo wards in Hoan Kiem District. 

The remnants of these ancient villages can still be seen today through the surviving temples and shrines scattered throughout the area. For instance, the Xuan Yen Temple at number 44 Hang Can Street honors Princess Lan Ngoc, while another Xuan Yen Temple at number 6 Luong Van Can Street venerates the original Princess Lan Ngoc. Additionally, the Nhan Noi Temple at number 84A Hang Bo Street also pays homage to Princess Lan Ngoc, and the Nhan Noi Communal House at number 33 Bat Dan Street is dedicated to the White Horse deity. The village of Nhan Noi was formerly known as Hang Nui, suggesting that the area once had a thriving pottery industry, producing clay pots and utensils.

The name "Hang Bo" itself is derived from the middle section of the street, where until the early French colonial era, shops selling various bamboo baskets and other woven goods were concentrated. At the eastern end of the street, near the intersections with Hang Dao and Hang Ngang, the area was historically known as Hang Dep, or "Shoe Street," where vendors sold a variety of wooden clogs and shoes. These included hand-carved wooden clogs, intricately carved wooden sandals with leather straps, and wooden-soled shoes with leather tips, catering to both men and women.

According to genealogies of prominent families, such as those from the Nguyen clan of Du Lam (now part of Dong Anh District), during the late Le dynasty and early Nguyen dynasty (late 18th to early 19th centuries), many officials resided in grand mansions along Hang Bo Street, leading contemporaries to nickname it "O Y Hang," meaning "Black Robe Alley," after a similar alley in the Tang Dynasty capital of China, where high-ranking officials wore black robes.

In the middle of the street, there used to be a communal house built by the Ding Cong silversmith guild to honor their ancestors and trade deities. However, when the guild relocated, the building was sold to a wealthy businessman named Pham Le Bay, who converted it into a three-story commercial building. Today, this structure houses the headquarters of the Labor newspaper.

Around the turn of the 20th century, Hang Bo Street became home to many Chinese immigrants from Chaozhou, who engaged in rice and fruit trading, as well as operating photography studios. The street's rich history and cultural significance continue to attract visitors interested in exploring its traditional crafts, architecture, and the vibrant local life that thrives there.

description: Stretching like a long silk ribbon connecting from Hàng Gai intersection all the way to Cửa Nam, Hàng Bông street emerges as one of the most elegant and charming touches in the heart of the Old Quarter. Tracing back through history to centuries ago, this street used to be home to many families engaged in the craft of bật bông, weaving fabric, and selling warm cotton blankets. The rhythmic sound of bật bông echoing day and night amidst the bustling kẻ chợ naturally gave birth to the rustic name Hàng Bông, encapsulating the memories of a time of diligent labor by the ancients. Nowadays, although the sound of bật bông has faded into the past, the street's breath of life has donned a vibrant and captivating garment of prosperity. Travelers from all directions and Hanoi residents often stroll leisurely through here, engrossed in admiring sparkling fashion showcases, choosing to buy elegant áo dài tơ tằm, or gathering cheerfully to enjoy famous street food. Standing silently, observing the intersecting flow of ancient charm and modernity, one's heart is suddenly filled with an inexpressible nostalgia intertwined with pride. The experience of touching soft silk folds in the heart of the time-honored Old Quarter brings a deep sense of peace, helping us understand the noble, elegant, and eternal beauty of Thăng Long, a land of a thousand years of civilization.
