Ngược dòng lịch sử về những thế kỷ trước, con phố này từng quy tụ rất nhiều gia đình làm nghề bật bông, dệt vải và bán những tấm mền bông ấm áp. Tiếng bật bông phành phạch vang vọng suốt đêm ngày giữa chốn kẻ chợ sầm uất đã tự nhiên khai sinh ra cái tên Hàng Bông mộc mạc, gói trọn cả ký ức về một thời lao động miệt mài của người xưa. Ngày nay, dẫu tiếng bật bông đã lùi xa vào dĩ vãng, hơi thở đời sống trên phố lại khoác lên mình tấm áo phồn hoa đầy cuốn hút. Lữ khách muôn phương và người dân thủ đô thường thong dong dạo bước qua đây, mải mê ngắm nhìn những lăng kính thời trang lấp lánh, chọn mua chiếc áo dài tơ tằm thướt tha hay tụ tập rôm rả thưởng thức các món ăn vỉa hè nức tiếng. Đứng lặng yên ngắm nhìn dòng chảy giao thoa giữa nét cổ kính và hiện đại ấy, lòng người bỗng dâng lên một sự hoài niệm đan xen niềm tự hào khôn tả. Trải nghiệm chạm tay vào nếp lụa mềm mại giữa lòng phố cổ nhuốm màu năm tháng mang lại cảm giác bình yên thẳm sâu, giúp ta thấu hiểu vẻ đẹp đài các, hào hoa vĩnh cửu của mảnh đất Thăng Long ngàn năm văn hiến.

Article Title: Hàng Bông Street

Hang Bong Street, known in Vietnamese as Phố Hàng Bông, was formerly named Rue du Coton during the French colonial era. This bustling thoroughfare is located within the historic district of Hanoi. Stretching approximately 932 meters, it begins at the intersection of Hàng Bông, Hàng Gai, Hàng Trong, and Hàng Hom, and extends towards the former city gate, Cửa Nam, also known as the South Gate. Historically, Hang Bong Street was dedicated to the production of cotton used for clothing and winter blankets. Today, however, it has transformed into one of Hanoi's most vibrant shopping destinations, featuring numerous art galleries, silk shops, and clothing stores.

documents.content:
Hang Bong Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a vibrant thoroughfare that stretches for 932 meters and spans a width of 9 meters. The street intersects with several other historic streets such as Hang Trong, Hang Hom, Hang Gai, Hang Manh, Ly Quoc Su, Duong Thanh, Phu Doan, Hang Da, and Quan Su, ultimately leading to Ngang Cua Nam. This bustling area was formerly known as "rue du Coton" during the French colonial period, and after the revolution, it retained its name as Hang Bong Street.

The history of Hang Bong Street is deeply rooted in the traditional crafts and trades of old Hanoi. Originally, the street was divided into several segments, each with its own distinct name and purpose. The initial section, from where it meets Hang Gai Street to the end of Hang Manh Street, was called Hang Hai, named after the production and sale of wooden clogs adorned with silk embroidery. These clogs were made with square wooden soles and embroidered silk tips, while imitation clogs were crafted from colorful paper and used for religious ceremonies. This part of the street belonged to the Kim Bat Thượng village, which was part of the Tien Tuc district.

Following Hang Hai, the next segment was known as Hang Bong Dem, extending from Hang Manh to Hang Da. This stretch was dedicated to the production and sale of cotton quilts and mattresses, reflecting the activities of the Kim Bat Ha village, also within the Tien Tuc district. Both these villages were part of the Thuong My district until the mid-19th century when they merged with the Co Vu Thượng village to form the Kim Co village.

Further along, the street continued with the Hang Bong Cua Quyen section, which featured a large banyan tree known as the Co Quyen tree. After a lightning strike destroyed the shrine near this tree, the banyan was felled, but the name persisted, becoming synonymous with the area. This segment belonged to the Thuong Mon Dong Ha village, part of the Tien Nghiem district, which later became the Vinh Xuong district.

The final stretch of Hang Bong Street, known as Hang Bong Lo, extended from the Hoa Vu alley to the Cua Nam junction. This area specialized in dyeing blue cloth, earning it the name Hang Lam. It was situated in the Yen Trung Ha village, also within the Tien Nghiem district.

Throughout Hang Bong Street, one can find numerous ancient temples and communal houses that reflect the rich cultural heritage of the area. Notable among these are the Phuc Hau Temple, Tam Thanh Communal House, Luong Ngoc Temple, Kim Hu Communal House, Vong Tien Shrine, Thien Tien Communal House, and Dong My Communal House. Each of these structures holds significant historical and spiritual importance.

For instance, the Phuc Hau Temple, now located on the second floor of number 2, honors the ancestor of the mirror-making trade and a guardian who helped locate lost children. The temple's history is intertwined with the legend of Tran Nhu Dinh, a figure associated with the Tran dynasty, who taught the craft of mirror-making to the people of Kim Bat and Co Vu villages. His dedication to helping lost children earned him the title of Phuc Hau, a revered protector of the community.

Another important site is the Luong Ngoc Temple at number 68A, built by residents from the Luong Ngoc village in Hai Hung province who migrated to Thang Long. This temple serves as a place of worship and remembrance for their ancestral homeland.

The Kim Hu Communal House at number 95 is dedicated to Tran Hung Dao, a national hero. The temple displays a pair of poetic couplets that celebrate his military prowess and heroic legacy. Similarly, the Vong Tien Shrine at number 120B commemorates the legendary encounter between King Le Thanh Tong and a fairy. According to folklore, the king met a beautiful maiden at the Jade Lake Pagoda and invited her to ride in his sedan chair. However, she vanished before reaching the Dai Hung Gate. In response, the king ordered the construction of a pavilion at the spot where she disappeared, naming it the Vong Tien Pavilion. Historical records indicate that this shrine was likely constructed after the rebuilding of the Thang Long Citadel in 1805.

The Thien Tien Communal House at number 120 may have been established to honor Ly Thuong Kiet, another significant historical figure. These temples and communal houses not only serve as places of worship but also preserve the cultural and historical essence of Hang Bong Street.

In addition to its religious and historical significance, Hang Bong Street has played a crucial role in the development of modern Hanoi. During the early years of French colonial rule, the first elementary school in the city was established here. The street also saw the emergence of the first Vietnamese-owned printing presses, such as Nghiem Ham Ink Shop, Trung Bac, and Mac Dinh Tu. Moreover, the renowned poet Tan Da operated a bookstore, Tan Da Bookstore, at number 58, contributing to the intellectual and cultural life of the city.

Hang Bong Street is also notable for its connection to the early days of the Communist Party of Vietnam. At number 177, the official establishment of the Hanoi Municipal Party Committee took place in June 1930, with Nguyen Ngoc Vu appointed as the Secretary of the City Committee. This event marked a pivotal moment in the political history of Hanoi and Vietnam.

Today, Hang Bong Street remains a testament to the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s past, blending traditional crafts, historical landmarks, and modern urban life. description: Lying across the heart of the bustling Old Quarter, Hàng Buồm street appears like a simple, nostalgic stroke in the heart of Hanoi capital. In the past, this place used to run along the peaceful Tô Lịch riverbank, famous throughout the kinh kỳ for its weaving and trading of rattan sails and fabric sails for boats traveling up and down. The name Hàng Buồm thus took root in the consciousness of Tràng An people, encapsulating memories of a bustling waterway trade era of the merchants of Thăng Long, a thousand years of civilization. Nowadays, even though the sails have receded deep into the past, the breath of life here still pulsates with intense vibrancy. During the day, tourists leisurely stroll past ancient architectural works or crowded eateries, enthusiastically enjoying the rustic culinary flavors. When night falls, especially on weekends, the entire street suddenly transforms into a bustling entertainment hub, filled with the lively sounds of laughter, the sizzling of hot pans, and the melodious tunes of street music. Immersing oneself in that bustling crowd, one's heart suddenly overflows with a sense of familiarity mixed with enchantment. The experience of tasting a bit of the sidewalk flavors amidst a moss-covered, ancient space brings a strange warmth, helping one fully understand the graceful interplay between a tumultuous past and the vibrant pulse of the contemporary.

Nestled within the heart of Hanoi’s bustling Old Quarter, Hang Buom Street, also known as Phố Hàng Buồm, stands as a testament to the city’s rich cultural heritage and dynamic present. Historically, this narrow thoroughfare ran alongside the tranquil banks of the Tô Lịch River, renowned for its traditional weaving and trading of rattan and fabric sails used by boats navigating the region’s waterways. The street’s name, “Hàng Buồm,” meaning “Sail Street,” was etched into the collective memory of the people of Thăng Long, reflecting the vibrant era of maritime commerce that thrived here for centuries. 

Today, despite the sails having long since disappeared, Hang Buom Street continues to pulse with life. Its winding path, flanked by closely packed *nhà ống*—tightly arranged Vietnamese townhouses—offers a glimpse into the city’s architectural past. The weathered, moss-covered brick walls of these houses, painted in a faded yellow, contrast beautifully with the vibrant hues of countless food stalls and shop signs. Among the myriad structures, the majestic facade of Bach Ma Temple and Quang Dong Assembly Hall stands out, their solemn *âm dương* tiled roofs stretching nearly to the roadside, adding a touch of grandeur to the otherwise modest surroundings.

The street’s layout, a labyrinth of narrow lanes and alleys, tightly embraces the sidewalk, which is perpetually teeming with pedestrians. During the day, visitors meander through the area, exploring the ancient architectural wonders and sampling the rustic culinary delights offered by the numerous eateries. The air is filled with the aromas of traditional Vietnamese dishes, enticing tourists and locals alike to partake in the rich flavors of the region.

As night falls, particularly on weekends, Hang Buom Street transforms into a lively entertainment hub. The sounds of laughter, the sizzle of cooking pans, and the melodic tunes of street musicians blend together, creating a symphony of urban nightlife. The street becomes a melting pot of cultures, where young and old gather to enjoy the vibrant atmosphere. This transformation underscores the street’s ability to seamlessly merge its tumultuous past with the vibrant pulse of contemporary life, offering visitors a unique experience that is both familiar and enchanting.

Hang Buom Street not only serves as a physical link to Hanoi’s storied past but also as a vibrant center of modern-day activity, embodying the city’s enduring spirit and cultural richness.

documents.content:
Hang Buom Street, also known as Xingfan in Chinese, is located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi. When the French arrived in Tonkin in 1872, the street was named Rue des Voiles. At that time, residents lived alongside the Nhị Hà River (now known as the Red River) and the To Lich River, engaging in various occupations related to waterways. The main products included baskets, woven mats, sails, and screens made from materials like bamboo and straw. From 1954 onwards, the street has been known by its Vietnamese name, Hang Buom.

Hang Buom Street stretches approximately 0.3 kilometers in an east-west direction and is situated in the Hoan Kiem district of Hanoi. Before 2025, it belonged to the Hang Buom ward, but now it falls under the Hoan Kiem ward. The eastern end of the street intersects with Dao Duy Tu and Ma May streets, while the western end meets Hang Ngang, Hang Duong, and Lan Ong streets. It is about 400 meters north of Hoan Kiem Lake and around 300 meters south of Dong Xuan Market.

Historically, Hang Buom Street was part of Ha Kou (also called Giang Kou), which was in the Huu Tuc prefecture of Tho Xuan county, at the confluence of the To Lich River and the Red River. In the 19th century, people from Guangdong in China expanded to this area from Hang Ngang Street, gradually taking control of the entire street. The Guangdong Association established a meeting hall here. Previously, there was a Bai Ma market near Bai Ma Temple, which later merged with the Cau Dong market into Dong Xuan Market.

During the French colonial period, the street was known as Rue des Voiles. Traditionally, the products made on Hang Buom Street included various types of baskets, bags, sail frames, and woven sails using bamboo and straw. Raw materials were transported directly to the street by boats, and the finished products were shipped out by the same means. After the Chinese community took over the street, these traditional goods gradually disappeared. Instead, many restaurants run by the Chinese community opened up along the street.

Today, Hang Buom Street features numerous shops selling candies, nuts, and various beverages such as wine, beer, and soft drinks. During festivals like Tet and Mid-Autumn Festival, the street becomes bustling with activity. Additionally, there are several well-known eateries offering dishes like roast pork, rice vermicelli, and salad.

The street is home to several historical sites including Bai Ma Temple at number 76, the Guangdong Association at number 22, and Tzu Yang Shrine at number 8. There is also the Quan Di Temple at number 28.

Situated within the heart of Hanoi's ancient quarter, Hang Buom Street stands as a testament to the city’s rich history and cultural heritage, seamlessly blending traditional charm with modern vibrancy. Formed in the 17th century, this street was once one of the bustling commercial centers of the imperial capital, serving as a hub for trade and cultural exchange between Vietnamese, Chinese, and Western influences. Today, Hang Buom Street retains many of its original architectural and social characteristics, contributing significantly to the unique identity of the old quarter.

The street is part of a larger urban fabric that includes narrow, elongated houses typical of old Hanoi, designed to facilitate both business activities and daily life. The architecture here is a harmonious blend of Eastern and Western styles, featuring curved roofs adorned with intricate carvings characteristic of Chinese influence, alongside French colonial elements such as iron balconies and arched windows. This architectural diversity reflects centuries of cultural interaction and provides a visually captivating backdrop for visitors.

Beyond its architectural allure, Hang Buom Street is also a vibrant community space where tangible and intangible cultural values converge. It hosts several religious sites like the Bai Ma Temple, Quan Diem Temple, and Hang Buom Communal House, which serve not only as spiritual sanctuaries but also as focal points for communal activities and traditional festivals. These sites offer a glimpse into the spiritual life of the local residents and attract tourists interested in experiencing the depth of Hanoi’s cultural heritage.

The street is also renowned for its culinary offerings, featuring numerous long-standing eateries and restaurants that serve authentic Hanoi cuisine. Visitors can indulge in traditional dishes while immersing themselves in the atmospheric setting of the old quarter, creating a unique dining experience that combines cultural exploration with gastronomic pleasure.

Traditional crafts form another integral part of Hang Buom Street’s identity. Passed down through generations, these crafts include making glutinous rice balls, incense sticks, seals, molds for cakes, and paper offerings. Each craft embodies a meticulous approach and dedication to quality, as exemplified by artisans like Mr. Pham Tinh, a seal engraver who emphasizes the importance of mastering one’s craft. These crafts not only preserve intangible cultural heritage but also provide distinctive souvenirs that draw domestic and international tourists seeking a deeper connection with Hanoi’s traditional culture.

Historically, Hang Buom Street was also known for its commercial activities and services, serving as an early trading center in the imperial capital. Even today, the street maintains a lively atmosphere with shops selling food ingredients, sweets, and household goods, catering to both local needs and tourist interests. This continuity helps recreate the traditional market ambiance, enhancing the appeal of experiential tourism.

In addition to its commercial and craft traditions, Hang Buom Street is home to various religious ceremonies and festivals. Festivals and rituals such as the prayer for peace and traditional worship activities are still organized, enriching the spiritual landscape of the area. These events foster community engagement with cultural heritage and enhance awareness of the historical and cultural significance of these spaces, providing a foundation for developing specialized cultural tourism products.

Despite its rich heritage, Hang Buom Street faces challenges in maintaining its cultural integrity amidst rapid urbanization and commercial pressures. The fast-paced development has altered the physical structure and landscape closely tied to the community’s collective memory. Additionally, the influx of new residents unfamiliar with traditional customs poses a risk to cultural continuity. Effective collaboration between local authorities, community members, creative businesses, and researchers is crucial to fully harness the potential of Hang Buom Street as a cultural hub within Hanoi’s evolving urban ecosystem.

In summary, Hang Buom Street remains a dynamic space where historical preservation and contemporary innovation coexist, offering visitors a multifaceted experience that encompasses architecture, culture, religion, and cuisine. Its enduring legacy as a site of cultural exchange and heritage conservation makes it a vital component of Hanoi’s ongoing transformation into a UNESCO Creative City.

Hang Buom Street, also known as Rue des Voiles in French, is a vibrant and historically significant thoroughfare located in the heart of Hanoi, Vietnam. Stretching approximately 300 meters in length, this street runs from east to west, connecting several important areas within the city. The eastern end of Hang Buom Street leads into Ma May Lane, while the western end connects to three other streets: Hang Ga, Hang Be, and Lan Ong. A cross-street, Hang Giay, intersects with Hang Buom, providing easy access to the bustling commercial district of Hanoi.

The street's location in the Giang Khuu ward, part of the Old Quarter, places it near the To Lich River, which flows into the Hong River. This strategic position has historically made Hang Buom Street a hub for activities related to river trade and commerce. The street is renowned for selling various types of sails, bags, and other maritime-related goods, crafted from materials such as cotton and rush. Due to its focus on sail-making and trading, the street earned its Vietnamese name "Hang Buom," which translates to "Sail Street" in English.

Hang Buom Street has been home to a large Chinese community since the late 19th century. Initially, the Chinese immigrants settled in the area around the Vietnamese Eastern Gate (now Hang Ngang Street), then gradually spread to nearby streets like Hang Be and Phuc Kien (now Lan Ong Street). The area became a center for Chinese merchants, who engaged in trade and commerce, making Hang Buom Street a focal point for their activities. The proximity to the riverside markets facilitated their business operations, leading to the concentration of Chinese traders in the area.

When the French colonizers arrived in Hanoi in 1872, they found Hang Buom Street populated by Chinese communities and established a Chinese Consulate there. During this period, many Chinese merchants operated under the laws of the Qing Dynasty, conducting business with French traders and sometimes acting as intermediaries. However, the years between 1873 and 1882 were marked by numerous conflicts and uprisings, resulting in the destruction of much of the city. Despite these challenges, the Chinese community in Hang Buom Street managed to survive and thrive, contributing significantly to the economic life of the area.

The street's architecture reflects its historical significance. It features traditional Vietnamese houses with intricate wooden carvings and ornate facades, some of which date back to the colonial era. The buildings along Hang Buom Street showcase a blend of Vietnamese and French architectural styles, with many structures having been restored or renovated over the years. The street's layout is characterized by narrow lanes and small shops, creating a dense and lively atmosphere that is typical of the Old Quarter.

Visitors to Hang Buom Street can experience the rich cultural heritage of the area through its traditional crafts and local cuisine. The street is known for its handcrafted sails and other maritime products, which are still produced using traditional methods passed down through generations. These items not only serve practical purposes but also hold cultural and historical value, reflecting the importance of river trade in the region's history.

In addition to its commercial activities, Hang Buom Street is also a place where visitors can immerse themselves in the daily life of the local community. The street is lined with small shops, cafes, and restaurants, offering a variety of goods and services. The atmosphere is lively and bustling, with vendors calling out to passersby and locals going about their daily routines. The street's vibrant energy is a testament to its enduring role as a center of commerce and cultural exchange.

Throughout the year, Hang Buom Street hosts various events and festivals that celebrate its cultural heritage. These include traditional boat races, dragon dances, and other festivities that attract both locals and tourists alike. The street's cultural significance extends beyond its commercial activities, serving as a living museum that preserves the history and traditions of the Chinese community in Hanoi.

Overall, Hang Buom Street offers a unique glimpse into the rich tapestry of Hanoi's history and culture. Its blend of traditional crafts, historical architecture, and vibrant community life makes it a must-visit destination for anyone interested in exploring the cultural heritage of Vietnam.

description: Nestled at the bustling intersection in the heart of the Old Quarter, Hàng Cân street is like a timeless measure preserving the delicate commercial pulse of the imperial capital. Tracing back through history, this place was once bustling with skilled artisans specializing in crafting and trading cân ta and cân tiểu ly to weigh gold, silver, or thuốc bắc. From these very meticulous balance beams, the rustic name Hàng Cân was born. Although the sight of copper scales has now faded into the past, the street's vibrant life continues to pulse with prosperity through the trade of packaging and various types of paper. Day by day, travelers and locals alike stroll busily, weaving through the crowds to choose colorful stacks of paper or leisurely sip iced tea on the sidewalk, watching the bustling street. Losing oneself in this interwoven space, one's heart is suddenly filled with an inexpressible sense of tranquility and nostalgia. The experience of gazing at the moss-covered old houses brings a profound sense of balance, helping each person fully understand the integrity and standards in the enduring business culture of the Tràng An people.
description_vi: Nằm nép mình nơi giao điểm nhộn nhịp giữa lòng phố cổ, con phố Hàng Cân tựa như một thước đo thời gian lưu giữ nhịp đập giao thương tinh tế của chốn kinh kỳ. Trở ngược dòng lịch sử, nơi đây từng tấp nập những người thợ tài hoa chuyên chế tác và buôn bán cân ta, cân tiểu ly để đong đếm vàng bạc hay thuốc bắc. Từ chính những chiếc cán cân đòi hỏi sự tỉ mỉ ấy, cái tên Hàng Cân mộc mạc đã ra đời. Dẫu bóng dáng những chiếc cân đồng nay đã lùi vào dĩ vãng, hơi thở đời sống trên con phố vẫn cuồn cuộn nhịp đập phồn vinh với nghề buôn bán bao bì và các loại giấy. Ngày ngày, lữ khách cùng người dân tấp nập dạo bước, len lỏi giữa dòng người để chọn mua các tệp giấy sặc sỡ hay thong dong nhâm nhi tách trà đá vỉa hè ngắm nhìn phố phường hối hả. Lạc bước giữa không gian giao thoa ấy, lòng ta bỗng dâng lên sự tĩnh tại và hoài niệm khó tả. Trải nghiệm ngắm nhìn những nếp nhà rêu phong mang lại cảm giác cân bằng thẳm sâu, giúp mỗi người thấu hiểu trọn vẹn sự ngay thẳng, chuẩn mực trong văn hóa kinh doanh trường tồn của người Tràng An.

Historically, this bustling thoroughfare was home to skilled artisans who crafted and traded cân ta and cân tiểu ly, traditional balance beams used to weigh precious metals such as gold and silver, as well as药材北，从这些精细的平衡杆中诞生了这条街道朴实无华的名字——Hang Can。尽管铜制天平的身影已逐渐淡出历史舞台，这条街的生命力依然旺盛，通过包装和各种类型的纸张贸易继续繁荣着。日复一日，游客和当地居民熙熙攘攘地穿梭于人群之中，挑选色彩斑斓的纸张堆或悠闲地在人行道上品尝冰茶，欣赏繁忙的街道景象。在这交织的空间中漫步，人们的心灵会突然被一种难以言喻的宁静与怀旧之情所充满。凝视那些覆盖着青苔的老房子，体验到一种深邃的平衡感，帮助每个人深刻理解Tràng An人民商业文化中的正直与标准。

翻译后的英文内容如下：

Nestled in the heart of Hanoi’s Old Quarter, Hang Can Street, known locally as Phố Hàng Cân, stands as a testament to the enduring commercial heritage of Vietnam’s imperial capital. Historically, this bustling thoroughfare was home to skilled artisans who crafted and traded cân ta and cân tiểu ly, traditional balance beams used to weigh precious metals such as gold and silver, as well as medicinal herbs. From these meticulously crafted balance beams, the rustic name Hang Can was born. Although the sight of copper scales has now faded into the past, the street's vibrant life continues to pulse with prosperity through the trade of packaging and various types of paper. Day by day, travelers and locals alike stroll busily, weaving through the crowds to choose colorful stacks of paper or leisurely sip iced tea on the sidewalk, watching the bustling street. Losing oneself in this interwoven space, one's heart is suddenly filled with an inexpressible sense of tranquility and nostalgia. The experience of gazing at the moss-covered old houses brings a profound sense of balance, helping each person fully understand the integrity and standards in the enduring business culture of the Tràng An people.

The short, straight street segment is sandwiched between two rows of tightly packed "nhà ống," traditional Vietnamese townhouses. The rustic brown hue of cardboard, blended with patches of yellowed, moss-covered walls, immediately catches the eye. A unique identifying feature is the multitude of paper files and stacks of cardboard boxes piled precariously high, completely obscuring the facades. This bustling scene is dwarfed by a tangled network of electrical wires, adjacent to a narrow intersection always teeming with a constant flow of people and vehicles moving back and forth. The architectural style of these townhouses reflects the traditional Vietnamese design, characterized by their narrow width and deep depth, built primarily with wood and brick, and often featuring ornate wooden doors and windows. 

Hang Can Street’s cultural significance extends beyond its commercial activities. It serves as a living museum, where visitors can immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of Vietnamese history and culture. The street’s vibrant atmosphere, combined with its historical legacy, makes it a popular destination for tourists seeking a glimpse into the traditional way of life in Hanoi. As one wanders through the narrow lanes, the sounds of vendors calling out their wares and the chatter of passersby create a symphony of urban life that resonates with the city’s past and present.

Hang Can Street is located within the Old Quarter of Hanoi, specifically in Hang Dao ward, Hoan Kiem district, stretching from Lan Ong Street to Hang Bo Street, with a length of 104 meters. Historically, this area was part of the Huu Dong Mon and Xuan Hoa villages, which belonged to the Thien Tuc prefecture of the former Tho Xuan county. In the mid-19th century, the prefecture was renamed Thuong My, and the village of Xuan Hoa merged with the village of Yen Hoa to form Xuan Yen.

The street is home to two temples: the Xuan Yen Temple of the old Xuan Hoa village at number 44, and the Xuan Yen Temple of the old Yen Hoa village at number 6A on Luong Van Can Street. The old village of Huu Dong Mon now has its communal house, the Dong Mon Communal House, at number 8 on Hang Can Street.

The name "Hang Can" originates from the historical production and sale of various types of traditional scales known as "can ta," which are horizontal scales with weights made of bronze or iron. During the French colonial period, the street was called "rue des Balances," which translates to "Hang Can Street" in Vietnamese.

Bus routes 31 and 146 terminate at the end of Hang Can Street.

Nestled within the heart of Hanoi's ancient quarter lies Hang Can Street, a place where time seems to stand still amidst the bustling modernity that surrounds it. At number 42 on this historic street, one can find a remarkable testament to the city’s rich heritage – a house that has stood the test of time for over a century. This ancient abode, owned by Mrs. Le Thi Thanh Tam, is a living museum, preserving the essence of old Hanoi through its unique architecture and storied past.

The house at 42 Hang Can Street was constructed towards the end of the 19th century and the beginning of the 20th century, serving as a residence and business hub for generations. It was once known as "Ich-An," a name imbued with positive connotations, symbolizing a life of purpose and tranquility. The original owners, the Tran Huu Lap family, were well-known for their successful trading business, which operated from this very location. The name "Ich-An" reflects the aspirations of the family, embodying a desire for a life filled with meaningful pursuits and serene happiness.

The structure itself is a masterpiece of traditional Vietnamese architecture, characterized by its elongated shape and intricate design. From the outside, the house appears as a slender box, typical of many homes in old Hanoi. Its dimensions are impressive, covering more than 100 square meters and stretching over 40 meters in length, making it a grand yet intimate space. The house's layout is divided into two floors, each serving distinct purposes. The ground floor houses a living room, two skylights that allow natural light to permeate the interior, a kitchen, and a bathroom. The upper level is dedicated to ancestral worship, a practice deeply rooted in Vietnamese culture.

One of the most striking features of the house is its preservation of original design elements. The entire structure, including the ceiling, wooden columns, windows, doors, and staircase, is crafted from lim wood, a material renowned for its durability and aesthetic appeal. These components have endured for over 130 years, standing as silent witnesses to the passage of time. The roof, adorned with moss-covered tiles, adds to the house's timeless charm, while the wooden doors and windows, with their intricate carvings, reflect the skilled craftsmanship of earlier generations.

Despite the surrounding neighborhood undergoing renovations and adopting modern aesthetics, this house remains steadfast in its traditional appearance. The only modifications made were to replace some of the floor tiles with smoother ceramic ones to prevent accidents among the grandchildren. This decision did not detract from the house's allure; rather, it enhanced its appeal to visitors who come to admire its unique architecture and historical significance.

The house's cultural importance extends beyond its physical attributes. It serves as a tangible link to the past, embodying the spirit of preserving cultural traditions and historical continuity. For the residents and visitors alike, it stands as a reminder of the values and lifestyles of previous generations. The house is not merely a relic but a living archive, telling stories of the family's history and the broader context of Hanoi's evolution.

Visitors to Hang Can Street often pause to gaze upon this architectural gem, capturing its image as a memento of their journey through the old quarter. The house's presence amidst the contemporary urban landscape underscores the enduring legacy of traditional Vietnamese architecture and the resilience of cultural heritage in the face of rapid modernization. As one wanders through the narrow streets lined with ancient trees and traditional houses, the house at 42 Hang Can Street emerges as a beacon of the past, inviting all who pass by to step back in time and experience the charm of old Hanoi.

Hang Can Street, also known as Rue des Balances, is a charming and historic thoroughfare located in the bustling district of Hoan Kiem, Hanoi, Vietnam. The street's name, which translates to "Scale Street," reflects its historical significance as a center for the production and sale of scales, particularly those used for weighing precious metals like gold and silver, as well as dry goods. This unique moniker was adopted towards the end of the 19th century when the area began to specialize in the crafting and selling of these essential tools.

The origins of Hang Can Street trace back to the 19th century when it was initially named Hang Son, or Rue de la Laque, due to its proximity to the To Lich River. During this time, boats laden with lacquer from Phu Tho Province would dock at this stretch of the river, where merchants would sell their wares. However, as the river was eventually filled in, the trade shifted to other locations such as the Lò Sũ wharf, and the lacquer business moved to streets like Cau Go, Hang Be, and Hang Dau. 

It was around this period that the craft of making and selling scales emerged in Hang Can Street. The small shops along the street began producing and selling various types of scales, including the traditional Vietnamese scale known as "can ta." These scales were used for weighing precious metals and herbs, as well as dry goods, and became a significant part of the local economy. As more shops opened and the scale-making industry expanded, the street's name was officially changed to Hang Can, reflecting its new identity as a hub for scale production and trade.

Today, Hang Can Street retains much of its old-world charm, with many of the buildings dating back to the colonial era. The narrow lanes and small houses are reminiscent of a bygone era, offering visitors a glimpse into the rich history and cultural heritage of Hanoi. The architecture of the houses is characterized by their modest size and simple design, often featuring wooden doors and windows adorned with intricate carvings. These structures not only serve as a testament to the city’s architectural evolution but also provide a serene backdrop against the vibrant urban landscape.

Visitors to Hang Can Street can explore the quaint shops that line the street, each one a repository of traditional craftsmanship and local culture. The atmosphere is imbued with a sense of nostalgia, as the sounds of hammering and the clinking of metal resonate through the air, echoing the industrious spirit of the past. The street is a living museum, where one can witness the meticulous process of scale-making, from the shaping of metal rods to the precise calibration of the scales. This hands-on approach to craftsmanship is a rare sight in today’s fast-paced world, making Hang Can Street a must-visit destination for those interested in preserving traditional arts and crafts.

In addition to its historical and cultural significance, Hang Can Street is also a place where one can experience the warm hospitality and friendly demeanor of the locals. The narrow streets are lined with small stalls and shops, each offering a unique array of products, from handcrafted scales to traditional Vietnamese snacks. The community here is closely knit, and the street remains a vital part of the neighborhood’s social fabric, hosting various cultural events and festivals throughout the year.

As visitors wander through Hang Can Street, they are transported back in time, surrounded by the sights, sounds, and smells of a bygone era. The street serves as a microcosm of Hanoi’s rich cultural tapestry, blending the old with the new, and offering a window into the city’s enduring traditions and heritage.

description: Stepping through the lens of time of the old quarter's rhythm of life, Hàng Chiếu appears like a bustling piece connecting from the moss-covered Quan Chưởng Gate, extending deep into the heart of the thirty-six streets and guilds area. Tracing back history, this place was originally located next to the Eastern gateway of the ancient Thăng Long imperial city. The name Hàng Chiếu came into being simply because the street was once a bustling stop for merchants carrying sedge mats from distant craft villages, making their way upstream on the Hồng Hà to trade. The breath of life in this place today still surges with the hurried pulse of commerce. During the day, locals and travelers bustle back and forth, eagerly shopping for rolls of packaging and closely packed blinds. When night falls, the street suddenly takes on a new look, with a lively stream of people gathering around bowls of steaming mì vằn thắn or famous warm chè sắn from the sidewalk. Standing silently watching the traffic pass by under the dim yellow lights, an indescribable nostalgia suddenly rises in one's heart. The experience of inhaling the pungent smell of sedge mats mixed with the flavors of late-night cuisine brings a familiar feeling, helping each person understand the enduring vitality and the everlasting prosperity of this thousand-year-old marketplace.

A defining feature of Hang Chieu Street is the moss-covered gray brick arch gate of Ô Quan Chưởng, which stands majestically at the end of the street, serving as a silent sentinel over the passage of time. documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Chieu Street
documents.content:
Hang Chieu Street is a small street located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi, situated in the Hoan Kiem district of Hanoi city. The street stretches for 275 meters within Dong Xuan ward, Hoan Kiem district, Hanoi city. It connects from the Quan Chau gate to the intersection of Hang Duong and Dong Xuan streets. Three streets branch off from the Quan Chau gate towards Hang Chieu Street: Quan Chau, Thanh Ha, and Dao Duy Tu. At the opposite end, it intersects with Hang Duong, Dong Xuan, and Hang Ma streets. Additionally, Hang Chieu Street runs through Nguyen Thien Thuat and Hang Day streets, and there is an alley that leads to Dong Xuan, connecting to Cau Dong street. The street has a width of 11 meters and is bustling with various goods.

Historically, Hang Chieu Street was built upon the old Thanh Ha village of Tho Xuong county. In the past, this area sold many mats made of rush and also included bowls, hence another name for the street was Hang Bat (Street of Bowls). The Thanh Ha communal house, which once stood near the Quan Chau gate, was moved to number 77 Hang Chieu Street in 1817 due to the expansion of the gate, but its main entrance faces number 10 Gach alley. This communal house honors Tran Luu, a general from the Tran dynasty.

During the French colonial period, the street was known as Rue Jean Dupuis and was primarily used for selling weapons and ammunition to the French army at the beginning of the street. It was here that Francis Garnier advanced into the lower city of Hanoi under General Hoang Duy. Hang Chieu Street was the first street the colonizers planned to expand after capturing Hanoi in 1883. In 1888, the colonists set fire to the entire row of houses on the street. Afterward, they seized land to open shops, forcing residents to buy Western-style bricks if they lacked funds, purchasing them at low prices otherwise. The street featured sidewalks, trees, and streetlights similar to those in France, making it the first street in Hanoi with Western architecture, hence earning the nickname New Street. During the anti-French resistance war, Hang Chieu Street served as a battleground for the troops. It remained steadfast until February 17, 1947, when the Capital Regiment withdrew from the city.

Today, Hang Chieu Street mainly sells bedding items such as quilts, mats, and pillows.

Hang Chieu Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a historic thoroughfare that stretches for 276 meters and spans a width of 8 meters. The street's origins trace back to the land of Thanh Ha village, which was part of the Hau Tuc district (later renamed Dong Xuan) within the old Tho Xuan county. This area has been a significant part of Hanoi’s urban landscape since ancient times, with its history deeply intertwined with the city’s development and cultural heritage.

The street's name, Hang Chieu, reflects its historical significance as a trading hub for bamboo mats and other similar goods. It is believed that the street's original name was Dong Ha, derived from the nearby Dong Ha ward, which was one of the 36 wards of Thang Long during the time when the city was divided into these administrative units. The name Hang Chieu itself likely evolved from the trade of bamboo mats, known as "chieu" in Vietnamese, which were a staple product in the region. Additionally, the street was also known as Hang Bat, indicating that it once traded not only bamboo mats but also ceramic wares, particularly those from Bat Trang, a renowned pottery village near Hanoi.

The street's historical importance is further highlighted by its proximity to the Quan Chauong gate, an ancient city gate that may have existed as early as the Le dynasty. According to historical records, the gate was part of the defensive walls built around the capital city of Thang Long in 1749 during the reign of King Le Duc Tong. The gate's name, Quan Chauong, is shrouded in legend, with various theories suggesting its origin. One theory posits that the name comes from a retired official who settled near the gate, while another suggests it was named after a guard who oversaw the gate during the Nguyen dynasty. Yet another theory claims the name honors a soldier who died defending the gate against French invaders in 1873. Despite these legends, the most accurate historical reference to the gate is found in Chinese characters inscribed above its arch, which read "Dong Ha Men," meaning "Eastern Ha Gate."

The street's architecture and layout reflect its historical evolution. Originally, the Thanh Ha communal house stood near the Quan Chauong gate until 1817 when the gate was expanded, necessitating the relocation of the communal house to its current site at number 77 Hang Chieu Street. The communal house faces the Ngoc Gach alley, where it stands as a testament to the area's rich cultural heritage. Inside, the communal house venerates Tran Luu, a legendary figure credited with heroic deeds during the resistance against Mongol invaders.

Hang Chieu Street's cultural significance extends beyond its historical landmarks. It was once the site of important rituals, such as the annual "spring ox" ceremony, which was held in the Dong Ha ward, now part of Hang Chieu. This ceremony, documented in historical texts like the Dai Nam Nhat Thong Chi, involved the presentation of a clay ox to the local community, symbolizing agricultural prosperity and fertility. The ox was then paraded through the streets before being ceremonially presented to the royal court, reflecting the deep-rooted traditions and agricultural practices of the region.

In modern times, Hang Chieu Street has continued to play a vital role in Hanoi's cultural and political life. During the early days of the national resistance war against the French, the street served as the headquarters for the First Regional Command, a strategic location that underscored its importance as a center of resistance. In January 1947, amidst intense fighting, a New Year's Eve dinner was hosted at number 87b Hang Chieu Street, organized by the command to gather foreign guests and explain the just cause of the Vietnamese resistance. This event showcased the resilience and unity of the local population, countering French propaganda that suggested the resistance movement was weakening.

Today, Hang Chieu Street remains a vibrant part of Hanoi's urban fabric, offering visitors a glimpse into the city's rich history and cultural traditions. Its narrow lanes lined with traditional shops and homes evoke a sense of continuity with the past, while the sounds and sights of daily life provide a vivid backdrop to the street's enduring charm. Tourists can explore the area's historical sites, including the Thanh Ha communal house, and experience the unique atmosphere of this historic thoroughfare, where the echoes of centuries-old traditions blend seamlessly with the rhythms of contemporary life.

Hang Chieu Street, a vibrant artery of Hanoi's ancient quarter, stretches for 280 meters from the Quan Chau Gate to the intersection of Dong Xuan, Hang Ma, and Hang Duong streets. This historic thoroughfare, nestled within the heart of the city, carries a rich tapestry of history, culture, and commerce that has evolved over centuries. The street's origins trace back to the time when it was part of Thanh Ha village, located in the old Hau Tuc district, which later became Dong Xuan district. The name "Hang Chieu" is derived from the tradition of selling smooth mats or "chiếu," which were imported by waterways from nearby villages and sold at the nearby To River port.

In the late 19th century, during the colonial era, Hang Chieu Street played a significant role in the French occupation of Hanoi. In 1873, Francis Garnier led an expedition into Hang Chieu, where he encountered fierce resistance at the Dong Ha gate, now known as the Quan Chau gate. A valiant officer named Chau Co, along with approximately 100 soldiers, fought bravely but ultimately perished in this battle. This event marked a turning point in the history of the street, leading to its renaming as the Quan Chau gate in honor of the fallen hero.

The French colonial period brought substantial changes to Hang Chieu Street. In 1888, after the French had secured control of Hanoi, they razed the entire street and rebuilt it according to their urban planning ideals. The new design included wide sidewalks, trees, and streetlights, earning it the nickname "New Street." During the early 1900s, the French renamed the street Jean Dupuis, after a famous French explorer, while the section near the Quan Chau gate was called Nattes en Joncs, or Reed Mats Street. By 1945, these two sections were merged back into a single street known as Hang Chieu, and in 1949, it was officially divided into Hang Chieu Street and Quan Chau Street as we know them today.

Throughout its history, Hang Chieu Street has been home to various businesses and activities. In the colonial era, the street was known for its arms dealers who supplied weapons and ammunition to the French army, making the area heavily guarded by the colonial authorities. After the August Revolution of 1945, Hang Chieu Street became a strategic location during the national resistance war. It served as the command center for the First Military Region until February 17, 1947, when the Capital Division withdrew to the outskirts of the city.

Today, Hang Chieu Street is bustling with activity, serving as one of the most vibrant commercial areas in the Old Quarter. The primary goods sold here are various types of mats, reflecting the enduring tradition of mat-making that has been passed down through generations. While traditional reed mats remain popular, modern varieties such as plastic mats, bamboo mats, and wooden grain mats have also found their place among the offerings. Alongside mats, visitors can find a range of handmade crafts made from reeds and bamboo, including baskets, hats, and decorative items.

In addition to mats, Hang Chieu Street is also known for its array of other products like banners, nylon bags, ropes, quilts, and floor coverings. The street's culinary scene adds another layer of charm, particularly with its reputation as a hub for "văn thắn" noodles, a type of wonton noodle soup that is a beloved local delicacy. Numerous noodle shops line the street, offering visitors a taste of authentic Hanoi cuisine.

Visiting Hang Chieu Street provides a unique glimpse into the rich cultural heritage of Hanoi. The atmosphere is lively and filled with the sounds of vendors calling out their wares, the sight of colorful mats displayed in shop windows, and the aroma of freshly cooked noodles wafting from the many eateries. For tourists, exploring Hang Chieu Street means immersing oneself in the traditional crafts and daily life of the Old Quarter, experiencing firsthand the blend of historical significance and contemporary vibrancy that defines this storied street.

description: Nestled embracing the western edge of the Old Quarter, Hàng Da street appears as a fascinating intersection between ancient Thăng Long and modern commercial life. Tracing back history, this place was originally a gathering spot for talented buffalo and cow leather tanners, who day and night crafted saddles or drumheads. The rustic name Hàng Da was born from those bustling tanning workshops of that era, etched deep into the memory of market-goers. documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Da Street
documents.content:
Hang Da Street is located in the Old Quarter of Hanoi, specifically within Hoan Kiem District, stretching from Duong Than Street to Hang Bong Street, with a length of 240 meters. Historically, this street was part of the village of Yen Noi, which belonged to the former Tho Xuan district's Tien Tuc commune (later renamed Thuan My). Today, it falls under the Cua Dong ward of Hoan Kiem District.

In the past, Hang Da Street was known for selling various types of cow and buffalo leather. The production of these leathers took place in the area between Tam Thuong alley and Yen Thai Street due to the availability of spacious areas suitable for drying and processing. At the beginning of Hang Da Street, there was a market by the same name, which was a small village-style market primarily selling fresh cow and buffalo hides that had been dried. The market consisted of only a few temporary shelters, making it a convenient venue for performances such as puppet shows and circus acts during the evenings. It wasn't until around 1937-1938 that a bridge was built at the market, giving it a more defined structure. In 1943, when Japanese forces were stationed in Hanoi and American planes began bombing the city, a raid hit the Hang Da Market, resulting in numerous casualties.

Midway along Hang Da Street stands a communal house called the Vu Du communal house, now numbered 42, dedicated to Le Cong Hanh, the founding father of embroidery craftsmanship. During the French colonial period, Hang Da Street was known as Rue des Cuirs. 

The only bus route mentioned that passes through Hang Da Street is Route 01, which terminates at the end of the street.

Nestled within the northern fringe of Hanoi's historic Old Quarter, Hang Dau Street stands as a testament to the city’s enduring charm, seamlessly blending the vestiges of its storied past with the vibrant energy of the present. Spanning the length of a curving asphalt road, the street is lined with a dense array of narrow tube houses, their moss-covered yellow facades contrasting vividly against the bright hues of modern signage. These structures, typical of traditional Vietnamese architecture, are characterized by their slender profiles and intricate wooden shutters that offer both ventilation and privacy.

The historical roots of Hang Dau Street trace back to the 19th century when it served as a bustling dock for merchants trading in agricultural goods such as seeds, mung beans, and soybeans. The cacophony of voices from vendors selling these commodities gave rise to the street’s name, “Hang Dau,” which translates to “Bean Street.” Over time, the original agricultural stalls have been replaced by a myriad of shops, each adorned with colorful displays and modern signage, yet the essence of the street’s vitality remains undiminished.

Today, Hang Dau Street is a vibrant commercial hub, where tourists and locals alike meander through the crowded sidewalks, exploring the diverse range of shops that line the thoroughfare. The street is particularly known for its numerous shoe stores, with long rows of shoe racks displayed prominently along the sidewalks, creating a distinctive visual identity. Additionally, the presence of countless shimmering glass aquariums filled with ornamental fish adds a unique touch to the street’s ambiance, reflecting the cultural fascination with aquatic life.

Adjacent to the bustling scene, the wide-spreading canopies of bàng trees provide welcome shade, enhancing the pedestrian experience and contributing to the street’s serene atmosphere. The constant flow of people and vehicles along Hang Dau Street underscores its role as a vital artery within the Old Quarter, connecting various neighborhoods and landmarks such as the nearby Hoàn Kiếm Lake and Ba Dinh Square.

Culturally, Hang Dau Street holds significant importance as a microcosm of Hanoi’s continuous evolution. It serves as a living museum, where visitors can immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of Vietnamese commerce and daily life. The street’s enduring appeal lies not only in its historical significance but also in its ability to adapt and thrive amidst the ever-changing urban landscape. As one wanders through the narrow lanes, the rhythmic sounds of chatter, the aroma of freshly brewed iced tea, and the sight of locals engaging in lively conversations create a deeply evocative experience that bridges the gap between nostalgia and contemporary life.

In summary, Hang Dau Street is more than just a commercial thoroughfare; it is a dynamic reflection of Hanoi’s thousand-year-old heritage, embodying the city’s resilience and adaptability. Its unique combination of historical charm and modern vibrancy makes it a must-visit destination for anyone seeking to understand the soul of Vietnam’s capital.

documents.content:
Hang Dau Street is a street that stretches over 270 meters from Tran Nhut Duat Street to Hang Than Street. This street was once part of the old National Route 1, leading directly to the Long Bien Bridge. 

Located in the Nguyen Trung Truc ward of Ba Dinh district and Dong Xuan ward of Hoan Kiem district, Hang Dau Street runs parallel to and intersects with several other streets including Tran Nhut Duat, Nguyen Thep, Hong Phuc, Hang Giay, and Hang Than. 

Historically, Hang Dau Street was named for its former trade in various types of beans. At one time, this area belonged to the villages of Phuc Lam in the Tả Túc district and Nghia Lap in the Hoi Tuc district of the old Tho Xuan county. Today, it falls within the Dong Xuan ward of Hoan Kiem district. During the French colonial period, the street retained its name as Hang Dau (rue des Graines), and the section from Phung Hung Street to the road leading up to the Long Bien Bridge was part of the old National Route 1.

Several bus routes run through Hang Dau Street, including routes 01, 14, 18, 22, 23, and 36, which terminate at the end of the street.

Hang Dau Street, a historic artery in Hanoi, carries within its cobblestones the echoes of centuries past, where the traditions of commerce and culture intertwine seamlessly. The name "Hang Dau" itself is a testament to the street's historical significance, derived from the tradition of naming streets after the goods sold there. In days gone by, during market days, villagers from the outskirts would carry various types of beans—such as green beans, black beans, and soybeans—to sell at this bustling thoroughfare. This practice gave rise to the street's original name, reflecting the agricultural heritage of the region.

During the French colonial era, Hang Dau Street was known as Rue des Graines, meaning "Street of Seeds," and served as a boundary marker between the Cua Bac and Cua Dong districts. After the August Revolution in 1945, the street reclaimed its traditional name, Hang Dau, symbolizing continuity and resilience in the face of change.

Today, Hang Dau Street is not merely a relic of the past but a vibrant hub that has evolved over time. Following World War I, the development of transportation led to an increase in automobiles, transforming the street into a center for automobile repair shops and parts suppliers. The strategic location of Hang Dau Street made it a gateway to Hanoi, attracting numerous businesses that catered to the growing number of vehicles. Many families prospered through these ventures, alongside others who thrived in woodworking and pharmaceuticals.

The street still retains vestiges of its ancient past, with notable landmarks such as the Nghia Lap communal house at number 32, which stands as a testament to the community's spiritual life. Additionally, two private elementary schools, one named Cuc Hien, founded by the patriotic scholar Le Dinh Duyen in 1878, continue to educate generations of students. These institutions, along with other structures like the Thang Long Water Tower, contribute to the rich tapestry of Hang Dau Street's history.

The Thang Long Water Tower, one of Hanoi's iconic architectural marvels, once supplied water to the inner city. Constructed in the early 20th century, it stood as a symbol of modernity and progress. However, after 1954, the tower fell into disuse and was repurposed for various functions until 2003 when it underwent restoration to restore its original grandeur. Today, it remains a significant landmark, drawing visitors interested in the city's architectural heritage.

Beyond the immediate vicinity of Hang Dau Street, there are several sites that bear its name, such as the Hoa Dau Garden (formerly known as Van Xuan Garden) and the Hoa Dau Guard Post. These locations, while not directly on the street, are integral to the area's identity and cultural landscape.

The cultural significance of Hang Dau Street extends beyond its commercial activities. It is a place where history and modernity converge, offering visitors a glimpse into the layered narrative of Hanoi's evolution. The atmosphere of the street is imbued with a sense of continuity, where old traditions blend with contemporary life. Visitors can explore the quaint shops, admire the architecture, and experience the vibrant energy of the local community.

In addition to its commercial and historical importance, Hang Dau Street also hosts cultural events and festivals that celebrate the city's heritage. These events provide a platform for artists and performers to showcase their talents, enriching the cultural scene and fostering a deeper appreciation for Hanoi's diverse traditions. The street's role as a living museum allows visitors to immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of Vietnamese culture, from its culinary delights to its artistic expressions.

Overall, Hang Dau Street is more than just a street—it is a microcosm of Hanoi's complex history, a place where the past meets the present, and where the spirit of the city lives on in every corner.

The historic Bốt Hàng Đậu, located at the bustling intersection of several streets including Hàng Than, Hàng Lược, Hàng Giấy, Hàng Đậu, Quán Thánh, and Phan Đình Phùng in the Ba Đình district of Hanoi, has officially opened its doors to visitors from November 17th to December 31st, 2023. This iconic structure, also known as the Tháp Nước Hàng Đậu, was constructed in 1894 during the colonial era by the French, making it one of the oldest water towers in Hanoi. The tower stands as a testament to the city's rich architectural heritage, blending elements of French colonial design with local traditions.

The Bốt Hàng Đậu is a cylindrical structure with a diameter of 19 meters and rises three stories high, topped by a conical roof that resembles a pointed hat. At the center of this distinctive roof is a lightning rod, ensuring the safety of the building and its visitors. The tower houses a large steel reservoir with a capacity of 1,250 cubic meters, which sits atop eight stone walls, providing a significant water storage capacity for the surrounding area. Despite the passage of time, the Bốt Hàng Đậu retains much of its original appearance, showcasing the enduring quality of its construction.

Inside the tower, visitors can explore a unique artistic space that combines modern installations with the historical significance of the site. The interior features a series of sound and light installations designed to highlight the importance of water in daily life and the impact of urbanization on natural environments. These installations include a sound arrangement that recreates the sounds of water in nature, and a lighting system that emphasizes the effects of urban development on the natural world. The aim is to educate visitors about the role of water in sustaining life and to foster a deeper connection between people and their natural surroundings.

The artistic displays within the Bốt Hàng Đậu are not only visually striking but also thought-provoking. Visitors can walk through a wooden path lined with sound-emitting jars, each producing different tones when touched, creating an immersive auditory experience. Additionally, there are exhibits made from recycled materials, demonstrating the theme of sustainability and environmental conservation. These interactive elements provide a unique and engaging experience for tourists visiting Hanoi, offering them a glimpse into the city’s past while reflecting on contemporary issues.

The opening of the Bốt Hàng Đậu to the public marks a significant milestone in the preservation and promotion of Hanoi’s cultural heritage. It serves as a bridge between the old and new, inviting visitors to appreciate the historical value of the structure while experiencing innovative artistic expressions. For those interested in exploring the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s history and culture, the Bốt Hàng Đậu offers a fascinating destination that seamlessly blends architectural grandeur with modern artistic interpretation.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Dau Water Tower
documents.content:
The Hang Dau Water Tower, originally named the Head Reservoir and also known as the Hang Dau Post Office or Round Water Plant, is located at Hang Dao Street in Ba Dinh District, Hanoi. The tower was constructed in 1894 along with the Tranquil Fort Water Tower, serving as a water supply facility for the city during the French colonial period and later becoming a historical relic of the capital.

In the context of its construction, on July 19, 1888, President of France Sadi Carnot issued an edict to establish Hanoi as a city, and from 1898, Hanoi became a French protectorate. Prior to the construction of the water tower, residents of Hanoi primarily relied on dug wells or water from numerous ponds scattered throughout the city. In the years 1894, several large outbreaks of diseases linked to water contamination occurred in the city, affecting many inhabitants, including twelve thousand French soldiers. The death of Paul Bert from dysentery shortly after his appointment as governor of Annam and Tonkin in 1896 prompted the French to urgently implement a European-style clean water system rather than relying on old water sources.

In 1896, the French established a special committee to survey local water sources as a priority in planning Hanoi. The decision to build the water plant (Yen Phu Water Plant) was mainly due to the unsanitary drinking water. The water project, along with the Hang Dau Water Tower and other urban water and electricity facilities, were primarily intended to serve the French colonists and soldiers, while the local population was restricted and only allowed access to excess water. Consequently, the Hang Dau Water Tower, part of the major water distribution system within the city, marked the first significant change in the face of Hanoi, predating prominent contemporary constructions such as the Long Bien Bridge and the Hanoi Opera House.

Construction of the Yen Phu Water Plant began in 1894, coinciding with the demolition of Hanoi's city walls by the French. Stones from the dismantled walls were purchased by businessman Tu Hong and sold for the construction of both the water plant and two water towers: one called the Head Reservoir built in 1894, situated at the northeast corner of the old city wall near where French troops were stationed, and another less famous tower called the Tail Reservoir (Tranquil Fort Water Tower) located in the Tranquil Fort concession area southeast of the city, close to the military hospital of that time (now part of the Central Military Hospital No. 108). The location of the Hang Dau Water Tower was deemed ideal for water distribution without requiring additional pumping, allowing water to flow directly into the Cua Bac Gate. The height of the Hang Dau Water Tower created sufficient pressure to deliver water to the French quarters and public faucets cast in iron placed at the ends of streets, supplying various government offices, villas, and private residences in the inner city.

Designed like a sturdy fortress, the Hang Dau Water Tower stands three stories high, featuring a cylindrical body and a conical roof, with a diameter of 19 meters and a height of 21 meters (25 meters including the roof). The interior space measures approximately 250 square meters, housing a steel reservoir on the top floor with a capacity of 1,250 cubic meters. Surrounding the tower are fifty-four narrow and tall windows resembling gun ports, complemented by arches and ornamental ironwork to avoid a heavy appearance. The entrance to the tower features two doors in the style of French architectural designs of the time, and atop the tower is a lightning rod.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Dieu street
documents.content:
Hang Dieu street is located in the Old Quarter of Hanoi, specifically within Hoan Kiem district, stretching from Hang Ga street to Duong Than street, with a length of 276 meters. Historically, this area was part of the Yen Noi village in the former Tien Tuc commune, which later became the Thuong My commune of the old Tho Xuan county. Today, it falls under the Cua Dong ward of Hoan Kiem district.

In the past, Hang Dieu street was known for selling various types of pipes used for smoking opium, such as silver-tipped, gold-tipped pipes, bowl-shaped pipes, and clay pipes. However, by the early 20th century, only a few shops remained that sold these pipes, while most shops shifted to producing and selling leather goods. Unlike Hang Trung street, which specialized in making horse saddles, schoolbags, and gun holsters using Western leather, Hang Dieu focused on crafting shoes and sandals using local leather, initially producing simple sandals and suede shoes before moving on to European-style footwear made from Western leather.

Midway along the street, at number 30, stands the Fire God Temple, also known as the House Fire Temple. This temple venerates the Five Manifestations of Firelight Great Emperor, a deity believed to have the power to prevent fires. The temple was built in 1838 and houses a large bell that would ring during fires to both pray for divine assistance and serve as an alarm. Since its establishment in the 19th year of the Minh Mang era (1838), the Fire God Temple has become a significant religious center for worship and seeking blessings to avoid disasters, not only for residents of Hanoi but also for people across the country. In 1996, the temple was recognized as a historical and cultural relic. To commemorate the millennium anniversary of Thang Long-Hanoi, the Hoan Kiem District People's Committee initiated a major renovation project for 26 ancient relics in the district, including the Fire God Temple.

During the French colonial period, the street was called Rue des Pipes, and it reverted to its original Vietnamese name, Hang Dieu street, in 1945. Traditionally, in addition to betel chewing, smoking opium was also a social custom where pipes were offered to guests. As folk songs and oral traditions suggest:

"My body is like a pipe of opium,
You bury one pipe down and dig another up."

Or,

"Men smoke their pipes, women get dizzy,
A child lights a pipe and rolls out of the house,
An old man passes by,
Sniffs the smoke and gets dizzy for three or four days,..."

The bus routes that run through Hang Dieu street include lines 01 and 36, terminating at the end of the street.

Nestled gracefully within the heart of Hanoi’s Old Quarter, Hang Dong Street stands as a testament to the enduring legacy of Vietnam’s rich cultural heritage. This narrow thoroughfare, known locally as Phố Hàng Đồng, is a vibrant tapestry woven with the intricate threads of history, craftsmanship, and community. Centuries ago, during the imperial era, artisans from the renowned Dai Bai bronze casting village ventured to Thang Long, now modern-day Hanoi, to establish their livelihoods. These skilled craftsmen brought with them their bellows and furnaces, setting up shop along this street, which became a hub for the production of exquisite bronze goods such as trays, incense burners, and religious artifacts. The rhythmic clang of hammers and the glow of furnaces gave birth to the street’s name, Hang Dong, symbolizing the golden age of Vietnamese craftsmanship.

Today, Hang Dong Street remains a living museum, where the ancient traditions of bronze casting continue to thrive. The street’s architecture is characterized by the iconic nhà ống, or tube houses, which line its narrow path, their walls sometimes adorned with patches of moss that add a touch of natural charm. The predominant visual cue is the dazzling array of bronze items displayed prominently along the storefronts—sparkling đỉnh đồng and lư hương, or incense burners, that catch the eye with their gleaming surfaces. These ornate pieces, often featuring intricate dragon and phoenix motifs, not only serve as functional objects but also carry deep cultural and spiritual significance.

The cultural significance of Hang Dong Street extends beyond its physical appearance. It is a place where visitors and locals alike can immerse themselves in the artistry of bronze casting, watching as elderly artisans meticulously hammer and solder their creations right before their eyes. The atmosphere is one of reverence and tranquility, with the slow pace of daily life allowing for moments of reflection and appreciation. During the festive period leading up to Tet, the Lunar New Year, the street transforms into a hive of activity. People throng the area, eager to purchase new sets of incense burners, imbuing the air with the warm, aromatic scent of incense that permeates the entire neighborhood.

Despite the modernization of Hanoi, Hang Dong Street retains its traditional charm, standing as a bridge between the past and present. The narrow lanes are often crowded with a hurried flow of people and vehicles, creating a dynamic interplay of old and new. Overhead, a tangle of electrical wires adds a contemporary twist to the otherwise timeless scene. documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Dong Street
documents.content:
Hang Dong Street, also known as 行銅, is located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi. During the French colonial period at the end of the 19th century, Hang Dong Street and Bat Su Street were part of a single street named Rue des Tasses, or Street of Bowls. Since ancient times, the residents of Hang Dong Street have specialized in producing and trading goods made from copper materials.

Currently, Hang Dong Street is situated in Hang Bo ward, Hoan Kiem district, Hanoi city. The street stretches approximately 0.13 kilometers in an east-northeast to west-southwest direction. At its eastern-northeastern end, it intersects with Hang Ruoi and Hang Ma streets, while at its western-southwestern end, it meets Hang Vai, Bat Su, and Lan Ong streets. It is positioned about 0.7 kilometers southwest of Hoan Kiem Lake and 0.3 kilometers northwest of Dong Xuan Market.

Historically, Hang Dong Street was part of the village of Yen Phu, which belonged to the Thien Tuc district of Tho Xuong county.

The traditional craft of Hang Dong Street involves manufacturing and selling copper utensils such as trays, pots, pans, and woks. From these common items, craftsmen have developed antique replicas, decorative spheres, and artistic bronze dishes. Additionally, the residents trade in cast bronze items like cranes, incense burners, and flower vases, which they purchase from villages such as He Nom in Hung Yen province and Ngua Xa in Hanoi.

For more information, one can refer to the ancient streets of Hanoi.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Duong Street
documents.content:
Hang Duong Street, also known as Phố Hàng Đường, is a historic street located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi, running from north to south. It connects at its southern end to Hang Ngang Street and at its northern end to Dong Xuan Street. The street intersects with Hang Ca Street and Ngoc Gach Alley. The name "Hang Duong" originates from the traditional goods sold there, which include sweets, candies, and products made from sugar and honey.

The history of Hang Duong Street dates back to before the 15th century when it was part of the dike system in the villages of Dong Hoa Noi, Hau Dong Hoa Mon (later renamed Duc Mon), and Vinh Thai (later changed to Vinh Hanh), all within the Hau Tuc district of Tho Xuan city, then known as Thang Long. Today, the street falls under the jurisdiction of Hang Dao ward, Hoan Kiem district. In the past, the To Lich River flowed through this area, featuring a stone bridge called Dong Bridge. Although the bridge no longer exists, its name lives on in the nearby Chua Cau Dong temple. There was once a market near the bridge called Chua Dong Market, which later moved to Hang Duong Street and became known as Dong Xuan Market.

During the French colonial period, the street was named Rue du Sucre, and a tram line ran along the route between Ho Tay and Dong Xuan streets. Currently, Hang Duong Street operates as a one-way street from Hang Ngang to Dong Xuan. It is part of the pedestrian zone that opens during weekend evenings.

Historically, the main products sold on Hang Duong Street included various types of sweets, candies, and goods made from honey and sugarcane. Sugarcane syrup from Quang Ngai and honey from different regions were brought by traders to sell in small quantities or to produce sweets and candies. The busiest months were those leading up to Tet and the Mid-Autumn Festival.

Today, many shops still sell candied fruits and sweets on Hang Duong Street, particularly famous for its delicious pickled fruits. 

Among the notable landmarks on Hang Duong Street are Chua Cau Dong, formerly known as Chua Duc Mon, located at number 38. Inside the temple, besides Buddha statues, there are also statues of Tran Thu Do and Tran Thi Dung. Adjacent to the temple is the Duc Mon communal house, dedicated to Ngo Van Long, a general from the Hung Vuong era. Another significant site is the Vinh Hanh communal house at number 19B, where the ground floor used to serve as a marketplace while the upper level was reserved for worship. However, this communal house no longer functions in its original capacity.

Hang Gai Street, also known as Phố Hàng Gai, is a captivating thoroughfare nestled beside the picturesque Hoan Kiem Lake, its winding path weaving through the heart of the Old Quarter. This historic street has been a hub of commerce since the ancient imperial capital era, when it was renowned for its skilled artisans who wove ropes and hammocks from the prized gai fibers. The name Hang Gai has been etched in history, as the street gradually transformed, donning a new persona as the capital's most celebrated silk street. Today, it is a haven of elegance and prosperity, where tourists from around the world stroll leisurely, admiring the vibrant silk and brocade displays through glass windows, and trying on traditional áo dài garments.

As one meanders along the narrow, winding street, sandwiched between two rows of closely packed nhà ống, the shimmering colors of the silk and the dazzling yellow light from the glass windows immediately catch the eye. The unique identifying feature of the street is the mannequins wearing traditional áo dài, one after another, lining the entire facade, creating a visually stunning spectacle. This vibrant scene is nestled amidst the bustling traffic, leading directly to a tree-lined fountain square, where the sounds of laughter and chatter fill the air.

Hang Gai Street is a testament to the enduring aristocratic character of the land and people of Tràng An, where the past and present converge. The experience of caressing each cool silk thread brings a sense of tranquility, as one fully understands the elegant beauty and cultural significance of this iconic street. During Tết holidays, the street bursts with vibrant colors, as young women in their festive attire head to festivals, filling the air with joy and celebration. As one gets lost in this space imbued with the soul of the Orient, the heart is suddenly filled with a strange sense of wistfulness, a feeling that lingers long after the visit.
