documents.content:
Nestled proudly alongside the windswept shores of Hoan Kiem Lake, Hang Gai Street unfurls like a delicate silk ribbon, seamlessly connecting the bustling heart of Hanoi’s Old Quarter. Historically, this vibrant thoroughfare traces its roots back to the ancient imperial capital era when it served as a bustling trading hub, specializing in the sale of ropes and hammocks crafted from gai fibers. The name Hang Gai, meaning “Street of Gai Fibers,” thus became firmly etched into the annals of Vietnamese history. Over time, the street underwent a transformation, shedding its former identity to embrace a new role as the city’s premier silk market, renowned for its exquisite textiles.

Today, Hang Gai Street stands as a testament to the enduring elegance and prosperity of Hanoi. Its narrow, winding path, flanked by closely packed nhà ống (tube houses), invites visitors to meander through a labyrinth of vibrant hues and textures. The shimmering colors of silk and brocade, displayed prominently in the shop windows, catch the eye with their dazzling array of yellows, reds, and greens. Mannequins adorned in traditional áo dài line the facades, adding a touch of cultural charm to the streetscape. Tourists from around the globe frequently stroll along the street, captivated by the allure of the áo dài, which they eagerly try on, immersing themselves in the rich cultural heritage of Vietnam.

During the Tết holiday season, Hang Gai Street transforms into a kaleidoscope of colors and sounds. Young women dressed in festive attire parade through the streets, en route to local festivals, infusing the area with a festive spirit. The vibrant atmosphere is further enhanced by the sight of tube houses adorned with colorful decorations and the sound of traditional music wafting through the air.

The architectural style of the houses along Hang Gai Street reflects the traditional Vietnamese design, characterized by their narrow width and deep length, allowing them to maximize living space within the confines of the city’s narrow streets. These structures, often made of wood and brick, stand as a testament to the ingenuity and craftsmanship of past generations. The street’s proximity to Hoan Kiem Lake and its connection to Ba Dinh Square adds to its cultural significance, making it a focal point for both locals and tourists alike.

Hang Gai Street not only serves as a commercial hub but also as a cultural landmark, embodying the essence of Vietnamese tradition and modernity. It is a place where one can experience the tranquil beauty of silk, the vibrant energy of Tết celebrations, and the timeless elegance of the áo dài. Each visit to Hang Gai Street offers a glimpse into the soul of Hanoi, a city where the past and present coexist harmoniously, creating a unique tapestry of life and culture.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Gai Street
documents.content:
Hang Gai Street is a historic street located in the Old Quarter of Hanoi, stretching from Dong Kinh Nghia Thuc Square to Hang Bong Street. The street is 252 meters long. Prior to 2025, Hang Gai Street was part of Hang Gai Ward in Hoan Kiem District, but now it belongs to Hoan Kiem Ward, Hanoi City.

Historically, Hang Gai Street was originally part of Dong Ha (the eastern half) and Cau Vu (the western half), both of which were under the former Tien Tuc Commune (later renamed Thuong My Commune) in the old Tho Xuan district. The street houses two ancient communal houses: the Dong Ha communal house at number 46, dedicated to Quy Minh, a son of Mountain God who fought against Water God; and the Cau Vu communal house at number 85, dedicated to Bai Ma and Ling Lang. However, these communal houses have been converted into private residences and kindergartens.

In the past, Hang Gai Street specialized in selling various types of rattan products such as ropes, hammocks, and cords. However, since the 19th century, printing became an important industry in the area. Many shops specializing in engraving blocks, printing books, and selling books opened up, pushing the sellers of rattan products to move to Dong Thanh and Bat Dan streets. During the French colonial period, the street was known as rue de Chanvre and was home to two significant administrative buildings: the Governor-General's Residence at numbers 79-83 and the French Consul's Residence across the street at number 80. According to Nguyen Huu Ngoc, the former chief editor of the World Publishing House, who was born and raised in Hang Gai Street since 1918, number 83 was the residence of the Office of the Governor-General Nguyen Trong Hop. In his memoirs, musician Pham Duy mentions that the cafe Thien Thai, established in 1946 at number 83, belonged to the businessman Dang Tran Van, who moved to France after 1954.

Previously, bus routes 09 and 14 used to run through Hang Gai Street, but since 2011, these routes no longer pass through the area. Currently, only bus route 31 runs through the initial segment from Luong Van Can Street to Hang Trong Street.

Hang Gai Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a historic thoroughfare that stretches for 273 meters and is 11 meters wide. It begins at the intersection near Dong Kinh Nghia Thuc Square, adjacent to Hang Dao Street, and extends to the junction of Hang Hom and Hang Trong streets, where it connects with Hang Bong Street and intersects with Luong Van Can Street. This street has a rich history dating back to before the French colonial era, when it was known as "rue du Chanvre" by the French, and later reclaimed its original Vietnamese name, Hang Gai, in 1945. The alternative local name for this street is Hang Thung, reflecting its historical significance in selling hemp products such as ropes, nets, and other related goods.

The origins of Hang Gai Street can be traced back to two ancient neighborhoods: Dong Ha and Co Vu, both part of the former Tho Xuong district. These areas were home to two ancient communal houses, the Dong Ha Temple at number 46 and the Co Vu Temple at number 85, which are now sadly converted into private residences and a kindergarten respectively. The Dong Ha Temple honors Quy Minh, a brother of Son Tinh who helped fend off the floodwaters sent by Thuy Tinh, while the Co Vu Temple venerates Bai Ma and Ling Lang, figures associated with the nearby Hang Buom and Cau Giay districts.

Historically, Hang Gai Street was a hub for the production and sale of hemp-related goods, but from the 19th century onwards, the printing industry began to flourish here. Printers and book sellers established numerous shops along the street, gradually pushing the hemp traders to move to Dong Thanh and Bat Dan streets. During the lead-up to the Mid-Autumn Festival each year, Hang Gai Street transforms into a bustling market for traditional children's toys, lanterns, and paper-cutting displays.

The northern end of Hang Gai Street, from its junction with Hang Dao Street to To Tich Street, was formerly known as Hang Tien, a neighborhood where skilled craftsmen from Nhi Khê village sold intricately carved wooden items like trays, wine stands, incense tubes, window frames, round tables, and small wooden toys. Further down the street, the area became renowned for its printing presses and bookstores. Notable among these were the Quan Van Duong and Tu Van Duong establishments, which were significant publishers of books during the late 19th century. These publishers produced a wide range of literature, including Confucian classics, romantic novels, and historical texts, using the traditional method of woodblock printing.

During the French colonial period, Hang Gai Street saw the emergence of modern printing presses that used the Latin script, alongside traditional woodblock printing. Prominent among these were the Dong Kinh Press at number 82 and the Ngo Tu Ha Press at number 104. Additionally, the first French-run general store opened on the site of the former governor's residence, marking the beginning of a new era of commercial activity. Over time, various other shops selling miscellaneous goods, hat stores, and optical shops sprouted up, contributing to the vibrant commercial atmosphere of the street.

In the early days of the national resistance war against the French, Hang Gai Street served as the southern boundary of the First Liberation Zone. During this period, the street was a frontline battleground, with the odd-numbered side controlled by the enemy and the even-numbered side serving as the guerrilla line. Historical accounts, such as those detailed in "Hanoi 60 Days of Smoke and Fire" by Vuong Thu Vu and "The Capital Division" by Duy Duc, highlight the bravery of local residents like Luong Vy, a high school student who led the self-defense team of Hang Gai Street. For 15 consecutive days, he infiltrated enemy lines to carry out ambushes, earning him one of the earliest awards of the War Medal from the First Liberation Zone.

Today, Hang Gai Street retains much of its historical charm, offering visitors a glimpse into the rich cultural heritage of Hanoi. The street's architecture, though influenced by colonial-era buildings, still preserves elements of traditional Vietnamese design, blending seamlessly with the modern urban landscape. Visitors can explore the narrow lanes lined with old houses, many of which have been converted into cafes, boutiques, and art galleries, providing a unique blend of past and present. The atmosphere is lively, with the sounds of street vendors, the chatter of tourists, and the occasional clatter of bicycles creating a dynamic scene that reflects the city's enduring spirit.

Hang Gai Street, nestled in the heart of Hanoi's Old Quarter, is a vibrant tapestry woven with threads of history, culture, and commerce. Stretching for approximately 250 meters, this bustling thoroughfare connects seamlessly to other historic streets such as Hang Dao, Le Thai To, and Hang Hoam, creating a network that encapsulates the essence of Hanoi’s ancient charm. The street’s eastern end meets the bustling intersection of Hang Dao and Le Thai To, while its western side leads to Hang Hoam and Hang Trong, eventually connecting to Hang Bong Street. In between, it intersects with Luan Van Can and To Tich Streets, forming a complex yet harmonious urban layout.

Historically, Hang Gai Street was known for selling rope and rattan products, hence its original name derived from the Vietnamese term "gai," meaning rattan. During the French colonial era, the street was referred to as "rue de Chanvre" or "rue de Gai," reflecting the same trade in French. Over time, the street evolved into a hub for silk and brocade, particularly after the 19th century when the printing industry began to flourish here. This shift marked a significant transformation, as silk merchants gradually replaced the earlier vendors of rope and rattan goods. Today, Hang Gai Street is renowned as one of the premier centers for silk trading in Hanoi, with over a hundred shops dedicated to the sale and production of silk products.

The architecture of Hang Gai Street is a blend of old and new, reflecting the city’s dynamic evolution. Traditional houses with their characteristic wooden doors and lattice windows still stand alongside modern structures, each contributing to the street’s unique aesthetic. Many of these traditional homes feature small gardens and courtyards, offering a glimpse into the past. Some houses retain their original design, with rear entrances leading to narrow alleys that connect to other streets, preserving the intricate web of pathways that define the Old Quarter. These alleys, often no wider than a few dozen centimeters, are reminiscent of the tunnels found in Cu Chi, evoking a sense of nostalgia and historical depth.

The cultural significance of Hang Gai Street extends beyond its commercial activities. It is home to several historical sites, including the ancient Cau Vu Temple at number 85, which honors the White Horse and Ling Lang, accompanied by a centuries-old banyan tree. This temple serves as a testament to the area’s rich heritage and spiritual traditions. Additionally, the street is dotted with remnants of its past, such as the former photography studio Tam Anh, the Nui Dien café, and the Hien Thuc Cooperative for engraving seals, all of which contribute to the street’s storied identity.

Visitors to Hang Gai Street can immerse themselves in a world where tradition and modernity coexist harmoniously. The street is lined with shops selling silk and brocade, many of which source their materials from the famous Vạn Phúc Silk Village. The atmosphere is lively and vibrant, with a constant stream of tourists and locals browsing through the colorful displays of silk fabrics, scarves, and garments. The shops not only sell finished products but also offer workshops where visitors can watch artisans at work, learning about the meticulous processes involved in weaving and dyeing silk. This hands-on experience allows visitors to appreciate the skill and artistry behind each piece of fabric.

During the warmer months, especially autumn, Hang Gai Street takes on a special allure. The mild weather and the scent of frangipani flowers create a serene ambiance, enhanced by the sight of vendors selling fresh young rice cakes and the golden leaves falling from the trees. The street becomes a picturesque setting, perfect for leisurely strolls and photo opportunities. Visitors can explore the narrow lanes and hidden corners, discovering hidden gems and experiencing the authentic charm of Hanoi’s Old Quarter.

Travelers can reach Hang Gai Street via various means of transportation, including bus, taxi, or motorbike. Walking through the streets provides a more intimate experience, allowing one to fully absorb the unique character of the area. From the bustling intersections to the quiet alleyways, every step reveals a story of Hanoi’s rich history and enduring cultural legacy. Whether visiting during the day or evening, Hang Gai Street offers a captivating journey through time, where the past and present converge in a symphony of colors, sounds, and scents.

description: Nestled gracefully at the bustling intersection crossing Ngo Gach, Pho Hang Giay emerges as a captivating culinary highlight amidst the Thirty-Six Old Quarter streets. Tracing back through history, this area was once the domain of talented artisans from Hai Duong who journeyed to the imperial capital to establish their livelihoods, diligently crafting traditional shoes, wooden clogs, and leather shoes for the nobility. It was the rhythmic clatter of shoe soles back then that gave birth to the simple name Hang Giay, preserving the complete memory of a glorious handicraft era. Gradually, as time passed, the shoe workshops faded, giving way to a vibrant culinary scene. Wandering through this fragrant space, one's heart is suddenly filled with a blend of nostalgia and a strange warmth. The experience of inhaling the simple kitchen smoke amidst the moss-covered street corner brings a profound sense of peace, helping everyone understand the culinary essence and eternal vitality of the thousand-year-old Thang Long.

Nestled gracefully at the bustling intersection of Ngo Gach Street, Hang Giay Street emerges as a captivating culinary highlight within the historic Thirty-Six Old Quarter of Hanoi. Historically, this vibrant thoroughfare was home to skilled artisans from Hai Duong province, who migrated to the imperial capital to establish their livelihoods. These talented craftsmen dedicated themselves to creating traditional footwear such as sandals, wooden clogs, and leather shoes for the nobility, a craft that earned the street its name, Hang Giay, which translates to "Shoe Street." The rhythmic clatter of shoe soles against cobblestones preserved the memory of a glorious era of craftsmanship, reflecting the cultural richness and economic importance of the area during the Nguyen dynasty.

Over time, the shoe workshops gradually faded away, making way for a thriving culinary scene. Today, Hang Giay Street is renowned for its array of street food stalls and restaurants, attracting both tourists and locals. Visitors can be seen cheerfully gathering around plastic chairs by the roadside, savoring refined dishes like bun thang, a delicate noodle soup, or enjoying warm banh troi tau, sweet rice flour balls, especially during the winter months. The narrow street stretches long, flanked by rows of tube houses leaning closely together, their walls often covered in patches of yellow moss. The visual cues include a series of food display cabinets and bubbling broth pots placed tightly together, spilling out onto the sidewalk, creating a lively and bustling atmosphere.

The architectural style of the buildings along Hang Giay Street reflects the traditional Vietnamese design, characterized by tube houses with narrow facades and deep interiors. These structures are typically made of brick and wood, with tiled roofs, contributing to the street’s distinctive charm. The white hue from kitchen smoke blends seamlessly with the moss-covered walls, adding to the nostalgic ambiance. The street is also adorned with a tangled mess of electrical wires, which adds to its urban character, while the constant flow of people and vehicles moving back and forth keeps the atmosphere lively and dynamic.

Hang Giay Street holds significant cultural and historical value, serving as a testament to the enduring culinary traditions of Hanoi. Its transformation from a center of traditional shoemaking to a vibrant culinary hub exemplifies the adaptive nature of the city’s heritage. The street’s culinary offerings not only satisfy the taste buds but also provide a glimpse into the rich cultural tapestry of Vietnam, making it a must-visit destination for those interested in experiencing the authentic flavors and atmosphere of Hanoi.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Giay Street
documents.content:
Hang Giay Street is located within the Old Quarter of Hanoi, specifically in Hoan Kiem District, stretching from Hang Chieu Street to Luong Ngoc Quyen Street (formerly known as Hang Man Street). The street is 228 meters long.

Historically, Hang Giay Street was part of the ancient village of Co Luong, which belonged to Dong Xuan Commune in the former Tho Xuong district. This village was situated on the northern bank of the To Lich River. Crossing the To River at Ngoc Gach Alley would lead to Ha Khau ward. From there, moving towards Hai Tuong village marked the beginning of Hang Giay Street. Today, it falls under Hang Boom ward in Hoan Kiem District.

Originally, Hang Giay Street was home to shoemakers who were originally from Cham Village (Truc Lam, Van Lam, Phong Lam) in Gia Loc district, Hai Duong province. They established a temple dedicated to their leather craft guild at what is now number 16 Hai Tuong Alley. Until the late 19th century, around the mid-point of Hang Giay Street, there was a temple at number 30, which was initially the Inner Temple of Hai Tuong village. In 1895, residents of Hang Bac Street, whose origins were from Trau Khe village, purchased this temple, renovated it, and turned it into a place to honor the guardian deity of Trau Khe village. Consequently, the temple became associated with Hang Bac Street rather than Hang Giay Street.

During the French colonial period, the northern section of the street (formerly Hang Man Street) was called Rue Lataste. The southern section (Hang Giay Street) was named after Nguyen Duy Han, the governor of Thai Binh province, who was killed by Pham Van Trang, a member of the Vietnam Restoration Society, with a grenade in Thai Binh city on April 12, 1913. After the liberation of the capital, the official name of the street was restored to Hang Giay Street.

Hang Giay Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a vibrant thoroughfare that stretches for 267 meters and spans a width of 7 meters. This street connects from Hang Chieu Street to Luong Ngoc Quyen Street, intersecting at the corner of Ngoc Gach, Nguyen Sieu, and Hang Bun streets, near the Bạch Mã Temple and Hang Buom Street. The street's history is rich and layered, reflecting its significance in the urban tapestry of Hanoi.

Originally, Hang Giay Street was formed by merging two separate streets: the northern segment, known as Hang Man, extended from Hang Chieu to Ngoc Gach, while the southern part, called Hang Giay, continued from Ngoc Gach to Hai Tượng. These segments were part of the ancient administrative divisions of the area, with the northern section belonging to the village of Co Luong in the Hau Tuc ward, and the southern part to the village of Hai Tuong in the Huu Tuc ward. Both villages were situated on the northern bank of the To Lich River, with the southern side of the river falling under the jurisdiction of Ha Khau ward.

During the French colonial period, this area was designated as Route Number 23 (voie No23). In 1928, the northern part of the street, formerly known as Hang Man, was renamed Rue Lataste, while the southern part, Hang Giay, bore the name of Nguyen Duy Han, a traitor who served as the prefect of Thai Binh province. He was assassinated by Pham Van Trang, a member of the Vietnam Revolutionary League, in Thai Binh city on April 12, 1913. In 1945, the street was renamed Tan Thuat, and in 1949, it finally adopted its current name, Hang Giay. Since then, the street has retained its name through various changes.

Today, Hang Giay Street is part of the Hang Buom ward, maintaining its historical and cultural significance. The street is home to artisans who specialize in shoemaking, a tradition that traces back to the craftsmen from the village of Cham (Truc Lam, Van Lam, Phong Lam) in Tu Ky district of Hai Duong province. These skilled workers established the village of Hai Tuong, where they built a temple dedicated to their craft, located at number 16 in Hai Tuong alley. This temple, originally the Inner Shrine of the Hai Tuong village, now serves as a place of worship for the spirits of the village of Trau Khe, whose residents purchased and renovated the shrine in 1895.

In the heart of Hang Giay Street, at number 30, stands a small temple that was once the Inner Shrine of the Hai Tuong village. The temple's roof still bears the inscription "Trau Khe Inner Shrine," indicating its original purpose. Despite being located on Hang Giay Street, the temple now belongs to the residents of Hang Bac Street, a testament to the complex interweaving of historical and cultural identities in Hanoi.

The street itself is a living museum of traditional craftsmanship, where visitors can witness the intricate process of shoemaking. The atmosphere is filled with the sounds of hammering and the smell of leather, creating a sensory experience that transports one back in time. Alongside the shoemakers, the street also houses a variety of shops selling shoes and other leather goods, offering a glimpse into the rich heritage of Vietnamese shoemaking.

Visitors to Hang Giay Street can explore the narrow alleys lined with old houses and traditional shops, each telling a story of the past. The street's architecture reflects a blend of old and new, with traditional wooden houses standing alongside modern structures. The visual elements of the street include ornate doorways, colorful storefronts, and the occasional glimpse of a temple or pagoda, adding to the cultural richness of the area.

For those interested in the cultural significance of Hang Giay Street, there are numerous opportunities to engage with local traditions and crafts. The street is not just a place of commerce but also a site of spiritual and communal activities, where the community comes together to honor their ancestors and celebrate their heritage. The shoemaking tradition continues to thrive, with artisans using traditional methods passed down through generations, ensuring that the legacy of Hang Giay Street remains alive and vibrant.

Visiting Hang Giay Street offers a unique opportunity to immerse oneself in the rich cultural tapestry of Hanoi. The street's historical significance, combined with its ongoing role as a center for traditional shoemaking, makes it a must-see destination for tourists and locals alike. As one wanders through the narrow lanes, the sights, sounds, and smells of the street create a vivid picture of life in Hanoi, blending the past with the present in a seamless and captivating way.

Hang Giay Street, a charming and historically significant location in the bustling heart of Hanoi, is often mistaken for its nearby counterpart, Hang Giay (Paper) Street, due to their similar names and proximity. However, these two streets have distinct identities and histories that set them apart. Hang Giay Street, located in the Hoan Kiem district, specifically within the former Hau Tuc ward, is a place steeped in tradition and history, offering visitors a glimpse into the rich tapestry of Vietnamese culture.

The street's name, Hang Giay, translates to "Shoe Street," reflecting its historical significance as a hub for shoe-making and trading. However, today, the street no longer specializes in footwear but instead hosts a variety of small shops selling sweets, snacks, and other miscellaneous goods. This transformation from a specialized market to a more general retail area reflects the dynamic nature of urban development and the changing needs of the community over time.

Historically, Hang Giay Street was part of a larger area known as Dong Xuan, which included the famous Dong Xuan Market. The street itself stretches from Hang Chieu Street, connecting to Nguyen Thien Thuat Street, and terminates at Luong Ngoc Quyen Street, intersecting with Ngo Gach-Nguyen Sieu and Hang Buom streets. This strategic location places it in close proximity to other historic sites and bustling commercial areas, making it a vibrant part of Hanoi’s urban landscape.

The origins of Hang Giay Street can be traced back to the pre-colonial era when it was known as Pho Nguyen Duy Han, named after Nguyen Duy Han, a former governor of Thai Binh province. After 1945, the street underwent several name changes, first becoming Pho Tan Thuat, and then finally settling on its current name, Hang Giay, in 1947. This evolution in naming reflects the complex layers of history and governance that have shaped the city over the decades.

One notable feature of Hang Giay Street is the presence of a historic temple, the Inner Shrine of Hoi Tuong Village, located at number 30 on the street. This temple, originally a local shrine, was later sold to residents of Hang Bac ward and converted into a place of worship dedicated to Trau Khe in 1895. The temple stands as a testament to the spiritual and cultural heritage of the area, providing insight into the religious practices and beliefs of the local community.

The architecture of Hang Giay Street is characterized by narrow, winding lanes typical of old Hanoi, lined with traditional Vietnamese houses and small shops. These structures, often made of wood and brick, reflect the architectural styles prevalent during different periods of Vietnam’s history. The layout of the street, with its tight-knit community and closely spaced buildings, creates a cozy and intimate atmosphere, inviting visitors to explore and immerse themselves in the local way of life.

Visitors to Hang Giay Street will find themselves surrounded by a lively and vibrant atmosphere, where the sounds of vendors calling out their wares blend seamlessly with the chatter of locals going about their daily business. The street is a microcosm of Hanoi’s rich cultural heritage, where one can experience the unique flavors of Vietnamese cuisine, the intricate designs of traditional crafts, and the warm hospitality of the people. Despite its transformation from a specialized market to a general retail area, Hang Giay Street retains a strong sense of community and cultural identity, making it a must-visit destination for those interested in exploring the authentic side of Hanoi.

These artisans, renowned for their exquisite craftsmanship, brought with them a tradition that would forever shape the identity of Hang Hom Street.

These items were not only essential for daily life but also played a crucial role in religious ceremonies and rituals, symbolizing the prosperity and cultural richness of the bustling marketplace. documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Hom Street
documents.content:
Hang Hom Street is located in the Old Quarter of Hanoi, specifically within Hoan Kiem District, stretching from the end of Hangquat Street to the end of Hanggai Street. The street is 120 meters long.

Historically, Hang Hom Street was part of the ancient village of Cau Vu Thuong, which belonged to the former district of Tho Xuan, later known as Thuong My. Today, it falls under the jurisdiction of Hanggai Ward, Hoan Kiem District.

Around the mid-19th century, residents from Ha Vi Village, known for its woodworking and lacquerware crafts in Thuan Tien District, moved to this area to open shops making coffins and trunks. Initially, they produced black-lacquered boxes for clothing and documents. Over time, they began crafting modern wooden coffins similar to those seen today. 

The settlers from Ha Vi Village established a communal house called Ha Vi Communal House at number 11 on the street, dedicated to their founding ancestor, Tran Lu, who taught lacquer techniques to his village. According to the "Toan Viet Thi Luc," Tran Lu was born in 1470 and died in 1540. He was a native of Binh Vong Village and passed the imperial examinations in 1502. His teachings spread the craft to neighboring villages.

During the French colonial period, Hang Hom Street was known as Rue des Caisse.

Hang Hom Street, a narrow and charming lane nestled within the historic heart of Hanoi, stands as a testament to the city's rich cultural heritage and enduring charm. Known for its quaint beauty and storied past, this street is one of the 36 ancient streets that form the nucleus of the Old Quarter, each bearing the name of a traditional craft or trade practiced there. The term "Hanoi - 36 streets" is widely recognized among locals, encapsulating the essence of the bustling commercial district that has thrived since the Tran Dynasty, when the area was home to 61 administrative units. By the time of the Le Dynasty, this number had been reduced to 36, a configuration that remained unchanged for nearly three centuries.

Hang Hom Street, with its length of just 120 meters and width of only 6 meters, is one of the smallest yet most significant streets in the Old Quarter. Its compactness makes it easy to traverse, allowing visitors to quickly move from Hang Quat Street to Hang Ga Street, passing through Hang Hom Street in mere steps. Despite its diminutive size, the street is a vital part of the Old Quarter’s intricate network of lanes and alleys, each contributing to the vibrant tapestry of Hanoi’s history and culture.

The street’s origins trace back to the early 19th century when residents from Ha Vi village, located in what is now Thanh Oai District, moved to the area known as Cau Vu Thang, part of the former Tien Tu ward. These settlers brought with them their traditional craft of making wooden boxes coated with lacquer, a skill they had inherited from generations past. Over time, the street became renowned for producing various types of lacquered wooden boxes, including those used for storing clothes and stationery, as well as more ornate pieces adorned with intricate designs and vibrant colors. This legacy continues today, with artisans still crafting these exquisite items, albeit with modern techniques and materials that make the products lighter and more appealing to contemporary tastes.

The street’s name, Hang Hom, reflects its primary function as a marketplace for these lacquered boxes, which were essential household items in old Hanoi. The lacquer boxes, or hom, were not only practical but also beautifully crafted, often featuring elaborate designs and vibrant colors. The production process involved meticulous work, from selecting the wood to applying layers of lacquer and allowing it to dry before polishing it to a glossy finish. This labor-intensive process required skilled craftsmen who could handle every step of the creation, from design to completion.

In addition to the lacquered boxes, Hang Hom Street is also known for its production of lacquerware, including small decorative items such as flower pots, incense burners, and even ceremonial chairs. The lacquer used in these items can be either black or colored, with intricate patterns and designs that reflect the artistic traditions of Vietnam. The artisans here have preserved the traditional methods of lacquer application, which involve multiple layers of lacquer being applied and dried over time, creating a durable and beautiful finish.

The architecture of Hang Hom Street is a blend of old and new, with many of the buildings dating back several decades, some even older. The houses are typically two-story structures with narrow facades, built close together along both sides of the street. The walls of these buildings often show signs of age, with cracks and wear visible, testifying to the passage of time. Many of the houses feature traditional Vietnamese architectural elements, such as ornate wooden doors and windows, and tiled roofs that add to the street’s charm. The atmosphere of the street is one of quiet dignity, with the sounds of footsteps and the occasional chatter of passersby blending harmoniously with the gentle hum of daily life.

Visitors to Hang Hom Street are drawn not only by the historical significance of the place but also by the opportunity to witness the traditional crafts being practiced there. The street retains much of its original character, with many of the shops still operating as family businesses that have been passed down through generations. The artisans continue to produce lacquered boxes and other lacquerware items, often working right within their homes, where the smell of lacquer and the sound of tools can be heard. Visitors can watch as the craftsmen apply layer upon layer of lacquer, carefully smoothing it out until it achieves a perfect shine, a process that requires patience and skill.

For tourists, Hang Hom Street offers a unique glimpse into the traditional crafts of Hanoi, providing a tangible connection to the city’s past. The street is a living museum, where the sights, sounds, and smells of old Hanoi are still very much present. Walking through the narrow lanes, one can almost feel transported back in time, surrounded by the echoes of generations past who lived and worked here. The experience is enhanced by the friendly locals who are often willing to share stories about the street’s history and the traditional crafts practiced there, making each visit a memorable encounter with the soul of Hanoi.

Hang Hom Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a historic thoroughfare that stretches for 127 meters and is 6 meters wide. The street runs from the end of Hang Quat Street to the end of Hang Gai Street, connecting two vibrant areas of the Old Quarter. This narrow lane has a rich history dating back to before the French colonial era, when it was known as Rue des Cerceuils. On January 22, 1891, a devastating fire broke out in this area, consuming not only Hang Hom but also several other nearby streets such as Rue des Bambous (Hang Tre), Rue des Radeaux (Hang Manh), Rue des Sceaux (Hang Thung), Rue de la Saumure (Hang Mam), Rue des Changeurs (Hang Bac), Rue du Pont en Bois (Cau Go), and Rue de la Chaux (Hang Voi). The conflagration destroyed 208 houses, including four temples, and caused significant damage to the local community. One notable victim was a Chinese cart owner who lost 60 carts in the blaze. After the fire, the street was renamed Rue des Caisses by the French, and in 1945, it reclaimed its original Vietnamese name, Hang Hom. Further name changes occurred in 1949 and 1951, but the street retained its original title.

The origins of Hang Hom Street can be traced back to the mid-19th century when residents from Ha Vi Village, known for their woodworking skills, moved to this area to establish shops making coffins and chests. Initially, they produced simple wooden boxes and trunks used for storing clothes and documents. Over time, they began crafting more elaborate wooden furniture, which can still be seen today. The craftsmen from Ha Vi Village established a communal temple, called the Ha Vi Temple, at number 11 on the street, dedicated to Tran Lu, a revered ancestor of the craft. Tran Lu, born in 1470 and a native of the village of Binh Vuong in Thuan Thanh district, was a prominent figure who taught the art of lacquer work to his fellow villagers. His teachings spread to neighboring villages like Duyen Truong, Ha Thai, and Ha Vi, fostering a thriving community of artisans.

Today, Hang Hom Street remains an integral part of the bustling Old Quarter, situated within Hang Gai Ward. The street's cultural significance extends beyond its physical presence, embodying the rich heritage of Hanoi's traditional crafts. Visitors can explore the quaint shops along the street, where skilled artisans continue to practice the ancient craft of lacquering wood, creating beautiful coffins, chests, and other wooden items. The atmosphere is one of quiet reverence, punctuated by the soft tapping of brushes against lacquer-coated surfaces and the subtle scent of drying lacquer.

Visitors to Hang Hom Street will find themselves immersed in a world where tradition meets modernity. The narrow lanes are lined with small workshops and stores, each preserving the legacy of generations past. The architecture of the buildings reflects the colonial influence, with many structures featuring French-style facades adorned with intricate ironwork and ornamental details. Despite the passage of time, the essence of Hang Hom Street remains unchanged, offering a glimpse into the enduring spirit of Hanoi's artisanal traditions.

documents.content:
Hang Khoai street is located in the Old Quarter of Hanoi, specifically within Hoan Kiem district, stretching from Tran Nhat Duat street to Hang Loc street, with a length of 360 meters. Historically, this area was part of the Huyen Thien village in the Hau Tuc district (later renamed Dong Xuan district) of the former Tho Xuan county. Today, Hang Khoai street falls under the jurisdiction of Dong Xuan and Hang Ma wards in Hoan Kiem district.

The name "Hang Khoai" originated from the various types of sweet potatoes sold by merchants in the past. Midway along the street, at number 54, stands the ancient Huyen Thien temple, also known as the Huyen Thien shrine, which venerates Huyen Thien Tran Vu, commonly referred to as "the saint," originally worshipped at the Quan Than temple. This temple is dedicated to Daoist worship and still houses a stele erected in the sixth year of the Canh Tri era (1668). Earlier, Trang Nguyen Dan had composed a poem praising this place:

"Ascending to heaven in broad daylight,
Seeking out Yao and Shun is difficult.
In the secular world for sixty years,
How can one face the golden-robed guests with shame?"

During the French colonial period, the street was known as rue des Tubercules, or Street of Tubers.

Nestled within the bustling heart of Hanoi's historic district, Hang Khoai street stands as a testament to the city’s rich agricultural heritage and vibrant market culture. This narrow thoroughfare, stretching for approximately 350 meters, is located in the Dong Xuan ward of Hoan Kiem district, just a kilometer north of Hoan Kiem Lake. The street runs parallel to Tran Nhat Duat Street, intersecting with Nguyen Thieu and Nguyen Thien Thuat streets, and Ha Giay and Dong Xuan streets, creating a lively network of commerce and community interaction.

The origins of Hang Khoai street date back to a time when it served as a central hub for farmers from nearby rural areas to sell their produce, particularly various types of potatoes and other agricultural products. The name "Hang Khoai" itself is derived from the word "khoai," meaning potato, reflecting the primary goods traded here. During the French colonial period, the street was known as Rue des Tubercules, or "Street of Potatoes," highlighting its continued importance as a marketplace for these root vegetables.

Today, Hang Khoai street remains a vital part of Hanoi’s economic landscape, where vendors gather early in the morning to sell fresh produce sourced from surrounding villages. The street is a bustling scene of activity, with carts laden with vegetables, fruits, and grains arriving from distant regions to supply the city’s markets and households. This daily ritual not only supports local agriculture but also enriches the urban food supply chain, ensuring that fresh produce reaches consumers throughout the city.

One of the notable landmarks along Hang Khoai street is the ancient Huyen Thien Temple, which sits prominently amidst the commercial bustle. Constructed in the 17th century, this temple originally served as a Quan Huyen Thien, a place of worship for Lao Buddhist monks and a significant spiritual center for the Huyen Thien Tran Vuong clan. Over time, the temple underwent several transformations, eventually becoming a Buddhist pagoda with the addition of statues of Buddha and bodhisattvas. Today, visitors can still see the original temple name inscribed on the main gate, a testament to its enduring cultural significance.

The history of Hang Khoai street is deeply intertwined with the broader narrative of Hanoi’s development. In the late 14th century, during the reign of Emperor Tran Nguyen Danh, the area around Hang Khoai was already recognized as a key trading zone. The emperor himself visited the Huyen Thien Quan and left behind a poem praising the site, marking it as a culturally significant location. As the centuries passed, the temple evolved, adapting to changing religious practices and societal needs, yet retaining its core identity as a place of spiritual and communal importance.

The architecture of Hang Khoai street reflects a blend of traditional Vietnamese and colonial influences. The narrow lanes are lined with old houses, many of which have been preserved over the years, offering a glimpse into the city’s past. These structures, often made of brick and wood, feature intricate carvings and ornamental details that speak to the skilled craftsmanship of local artisans. The street’s layout, with its winding paths and small alleyways, creates a sense of intimacy and connection, drawing visitors into the heart of the community.

Visitors to Hang Khoai street are greeted by a vibrant atmosphere that combines the sights, sounds, and smells of a traditional market. The air is filled with the aroma of freshly harvested produce, while the chatter of vendors and customers adds to the lively ambiance. Alongside the bustling market stalls, one can find small shops selling local handicrafts and traditional foods, providing a taste of Hanoi’s culinary heritage. The street’s proximity to Dong Xuan Market further enhances its role as a hub of commerce, making it a must-visit destination for those interested in experiencing the authentic flavors and traditions of northern Vietnam.

In summary, Hang Khoai street is more than just a street; it is a living museum of Hanoi’s agricultural and cultural heritage. From its historical roots as a potato market to its current status as a vibrant commercial and spiritual center, the street continues to play a crucial role in the life of the city. Visitors can immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of local life, exploring the market stalls, visiting the historic temple, and enjoying the warm hospitality of the community. Each visit to Hang Khoai street offers a unique window into the soul of Hanoi, a place where tradition and modernity coexist in perfect harmony.

documents.content:
Nestled within the heart of Hanoi’s historic Old Quarter, Hang Luoc Street (Phố Hàng Lược) meanders gracefully, serving as a living testament to the city’s rich cultural heritage. Originally constructed upon the ancient bed of the Sông Tô Lịch river, this street has been a bustling hub since the early days of the imperial capital, Tràng An. Historically, it was home to artisan guilds specializing in the crafting and selling of exquisite wooden and horn combs, giving rise to its name, “Hàng Lược,” which translates to “Comb Street.” Over time, this moniker became deeply ingrained in the collective memory of the local populace, symbolizing a vibrant era of trade and craftsmanship.

Today, although the sight of comb stalls is a relic of the past, Hang Luoc Street remains a vibrant thoroughfare, teeming with life and activity. During quieter moments, visitors can leisurely stroll along its moss-covered, yellow-tinted tube houses, each structure leaning slightly towards the center, creating a cozy, intimate atmosphere. The faded hues of these buildings, combined with the lush greenery of moss, provide a serene backdrop against which the street’s modern bustle unfolds.

However, the true magic of Hang Luoc Street is revealed during the spring season, when it transforms into one of the oldest traditional flower markets in the capital. As the gentle spring breeze sweeps through, the street becomes a riot of color and fragrance, with thousands of vibrant đào bích trees lining the pathways. These cherry blossoms, interspersed with pots of quất (kumquat), create a breathtaking spectacle that draws crowds of locals and tourists alike. The sight of these flowering trees, coupled with the sweet scent of blooming kumquats, evokes a profound sense of tranquility and joy, making Hang Luoc Street a cherished destination during the Tết holiday season.

The architectural character of Hang Luoc Street is defined by its unique, winding layout, which contrasts sharply with the rigid grid pattern of most urban streets. This distinctive design not only adds aesthetic appeal but also enhances the pedestrian experience, allowing visitors to immerse themselves fully in the vibrant atmosphere. The street is flanked by a dense canopy of trees, providing shade and a natural buffer against the city’s hustle and bustle. Despite its narrow width, Hang Luoc Street is always alive with the sounds and sights of daily life, from the steady flow of motorbikes to the cheerful chatter of passersby.

Hang Luoc Street’s cultural significance extends beyond its historical roots and seasonal festivities. It serves as a microcosm of Hanoi’s enduring spirit, blending traditional crafts with contemporary urban life. For tourists and residents alike, a visit to Hang Luoc Street offers a glimpse into the warm, festive traditions of Tết, as well as a deeper appreciation for the city’s architectural heritage and natural beauty. Whether strolling through the quiet lanes or joining the throngs at the flower market, visitors are enveloped in a sense of community and shared joy, reinforcing the street’s role as a vital cultural artery in the heart of Hanoi.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Luoc Street
documents.content:
Hang Luoc Street is located in the Old Quarter of Hanoi within Hoan Kiem District. The street stretches for 264 meters, starting from Hang Cot Street and ending at the intersection of Hang Ma, Cha Ca, and Thuoc Bac streets. Historically known as Song To Lich Street due to its proximity to the old To Lich River, it was renamed Hang Luoc because of the many shops that sold combs. Today, Hang Luoc Street is where city residents come to handle funeral and celebratory matters. 

In the past, when the river no longer served as a port, the inhabitants relied on Dong Xuan Market for their livelihoods. They engaged in small-scale trading and craftsmanship. Some families were civil servants or employees of private enterprises, with husbands working in government offices while wives sold goods at the market. 

The street is served by bus routes 31 and 146, which terminate at its end. Notable landmarks along Hang Luoc Street include the Quynh House and the Dinh House.

documents.title: Thông tin Website - Hang Luoc Street
documents.content:
Hang Luoc Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a charming thoroughfare that stretches for 264 meters and is 8 meters wide. It connects the bustling streets of Hang Cot and Hang Ma, offering visitors a glimpse into the rich history and vibrant culture of the city. Originally part of the ancient villages of Phu Tu and Vinh Tru, which were once part of Dong Xuan Commune within the old Tho Xuong County, Hang Luoc Street has undergone several name changes over the years, reflecting its evolving identity and significance.

Before 1901, the street was known as Hang Luoc, named after the production and trade of combs, a craft that thrived during the Le and early Nguyen dynasties. However, by the 20th century, this tradition had faded, and the street became known as Cong Cheo - Hang Luoc, a name that reflects the presence of a diagonal bridge that once spanned the To Lich River. This river, which used to flow through the area, played a significant role in the naming of the street, as the city council decided in 1901 to rename it "To Lich River Street" due to its historical importance. The name change aimed to preserve the memory of the river, which was a crucial element in local folklore and songs. In 1945, the street reverted to its original name, Hang Luoc, only to be renamed again in 1949 as To Lich River Street, before finally returning to its historic name in 1951.

The street retains vestiges of its past, notably two ancient communal houses: the Phu Tu communal house at number 19 and the Vinh Tru communal house at number 59. Both structures honor the Four Holy Ladies, a revered group of women associated with a tragic tale from the Tran Dynasty. Legend has it that during the Tran period, fishermen near the Can Hai Gate (now known as the Con Gate in Quynh Luu district of Nghe An province) found the bodies of four women who had drowned themselves in the sea to escape capture by Mongol invaders. These women were believed to be the queen mother of the Song dynasty and her attendants. The locals built shrines to honor these women, known colloquially as the Con Shrine, and later, sailors from the coastal regions of Nghe An and Ha Tinh would carry small altars dedicated to the Four Holy Ladies aboard their boats as a form of protection against storms and rough seas. Over time, these shrines spread throughout Vietnam, particularly along the Red River and the former course of the To Lich River, where numerous shrines dedicated to the Four Holy Ladies can still be found.

Despite its historical association with comb-making, Hang Luoc Street today is perhaps best known for its annual flower market, which takes place during the Tet holiday season, typically from the 23rd day of the twelfth lunar month until New Year's Eve. This tradition began when the nearby Dong Xuan Market replaced the old Cau Dong Market, which had been situated along the banks of the To Lich River. As the flower trade expanded, vendors found that the Dong Xuan Market could not accommodate the growing number of flower sellers, leading them to seek out new locations. By the early 20th century, Hang Luoc Street emerged as a popular spot for flower vendors, especially during the Tet holiday, when the street transforms into a vibrant marketplace filled with an array of flowers such as peach blossoms, apricot blossoms, and various other blooms from nearby areas like Quang Ba and Nhat Tan.

The flower market on Hang Luoc Street has become an integral part of the city’s cultural landscape, drawing visitors from all over Hanoi to admire the colorful displays and purchase fresh flowers for their homes and temples. Even during times of conflict, such as the war against the French colonialists and the American War, the flower market continued to thrive, albeit sometimes in different locations. During the American War, the market briefly moved to Duong Thanh Street but always returned to Hang Luoc Street, where it remains a beloved tradition. Notably, during the Tết holiday in 1947, when Hanoi was under siege, the flower market did not operate, yet the spirit of the festival persisted. Flowers from Nhat Tan and Quang Ba were sent to the front lines, symbolizing the unity between the front and the rear, and serving as a morale booster for the soldiers.

Today, Hang Luoc Street continues to be a hub of activity, especially during the Tet holiday season, when the air is filled with the scent of blooming flowers and the sounds of festive celebrations. Visitors can explore the narrow lanes lined with traditional Vietnamese architecture, visit the ancient communal houses, and immerse themselves in the lively atmosphere of the flower market. The street offers a unique blend of historical charm and contemporary vibrancy, making it a must-visit destination for anyone interested in experiencing the rich cultural heritage of Hanoi.

Article Title: Hàng Mã Street

Hang Ma Street, located in Hanoi, is renowned for its diverse array of goods, particularly toys, paper products, and paper votive offerings. With a history spanning over five centuries, this street has been a hub for trading paper goods, contributing significantly to the local economy and cultural heritage. Among the various items sold here, paper votive offerings stand out as a specialty, reflecting both traditional and contemporary Vietnamese beliefs and practices.

These votive offerings include an extensive range of joss paper goods designed to be burned as gifts for the deceased. Modern versions feature replicas of everyday items such as cars, villas, mopeds, and even electronic gadgets like iPads, alongside more traditional offerings like paper servants and horses. These items symbolize the desire to provide comfort and necessities to loved ones who have passed away.

Additionally, the street sells "hell banknotes," which are imitation currencies and credit cards, often referred to as ghost money. These items serve as symbolic representations of wealth and financial resources intended for the afterlife. Historically, during periods of suppression prior to Vietnam's economic reforms, the production and sale of these offerings were restricted. However, Hang Ma Street continues to thrive, embodying the resilience and adaptability of its merchants and the enduring traditions it represents. The term "đồ hàng mã," or "Hàng Mã things," has become synonymous with paper votive offerings, further cementing the street's significance in Vietnamese culture.

Hang Ma Street, nestled within the bustling heart of Hanoi's Hoan Kiem District, is a charming and historically significant thoroughfare that has captivated visitors for generations. Spanning a length of 339 meters, this ancient street runs from the intersection of Hang Duong to Phung Hung Street, offering a unique blend of traditional charm and modern vibrancy. Its strategic location, just one kilometer south of Dong Xuan Market and half a kilometer north of Hoan Kiem Lake, places it at the epicenter of Hanoi’s cultural and commercial life.

The origins of Hang Ma Street trace back to a time when it was part of two separate villages, Vinh Hanh and Yen Phu, which were divided by the To Lich River. This river once connected to the Red River but was later filled in, leading to the amalgamation of these two villages into what is now known as Hang Ma Street. The area became renowned for its traditional craft of making paper products and gold paper goods used in religious ceremonies and decorations. Over time, skilled artisans from Tan Khai village migrated here, establishing businesses that catered to the local demand for these items.

Today, Hang Ma Street continues to thrive as a hub for traditional crafts and modern retail, reflecting the dynamic evolution of Hanoi’s urban landscape. While it remains famous for its handcrafted paper goods and gold paper offerings, the street now also hosts a diverse array of shops selling office supplies, wedding invitations, and contemporary toys. These additions have not only diversified the market but also enriched the shopping experience for both locals and tourists alike.

The architectural beauty of Hang Ma Street is a testament to the ingenuity and craftsmanship of its inhabitants. Characterized by narrow, elongated houses known as "house-shaped tubes," these structures stretch along the street with minimal width but considerable depth, providing ample space for living, production, and commerce. Additionally, the distinctive "stilted" houses, or two-story buildings with false doors or small windows facing the street, feature sloping roofs that extend over the sidewalks, offering shade and protection from the elements while enhancing the street’s aesthetic appeal. These architectural elements not only serve functional purposes but also contribute significantly to the street’s unique charm and cultural identity.

Visitors to Hang Ma Street can immerse themselves in a world where tradition meets modernity, creating a vibrant tapestry of sights, sounds, and scents. During festive occasions such as Tet (Vietnamese New Year), Mid-Autumn Festival, and Christmas, the street transforms into a kaleidoscope of colors and activities. For instance, during the Mid-Autumn Festival, Hang Ma Street becomes a magical wonderland adorned with colorful lanterns and festive decorations, drawing families and children who come to enjoy traditional games and festivities. Similarly, during Christmas, the street is festooned with twinkling lights and holiday-themed decorations, inviting visitors to explore a whimsical winter wonderland filled with delightful surprises.

Beyond its commercial allure, Hang Ma Street holds a special place in the hearts of Hanoians as a repository of cherished childhood memories. The street is home to numerous vendors selling traditional folk toys and handicrafts, allowing visitors to relive their youth and connect with the cultural heritage of Vietnam. From simple bamboo wind chimes to intricately crafted paper flowers, each item carries a story and a sense of nostalgia that resonates deeply with those who visit.

For travelers seeking an authentic glimpse into Hanoi’s rich cultural tapestry, Hang Ma Street offers a wealth of experiences. Whether strolling through the narrow lanes, browsing through the myriad of shops, or participating in local festivals, the street provides a window into the daily lives and traditions of the people of Hanoi. It is a place where history, culture, and community converge, creating a unique and unforgettable destination for anyone exploring the vibrant city of Hanoi.

documents.content:
Hang Muoi Street is a historic street located within the Old Quarter of Hanoi, stretching for 190 meters from Hang Mam Street to where it intersects with Hang Bac Street at Ma May junction, and then continuing to the intersection with Tran Nhat Duat Street, where it meets Nguyen Huu Huan Street.

Historically, Hang Muoi Street was part of Thanh Yen village, situated near the U Nghia gate of Phuc Lam ward, which is now part of Ly Thai To ward in Hoan Kiem district. In the past, the beginning of this street was also known as Hang Trung (different from the current Dong Thai street, formerly called Hang Trung). During the colonial period, it was referred to as Hang Mam Street (rue de la Saumure).

Despite its name, Hang Muoi Street does not have any shops selling salt; only a few families engaged in trading salt. The salt was sold wholesale to traders from various provinces and retailed at local markets. At the end of the 19th century, Hang Muoi Street, along with the riverside area, was still part of an old village by the dike. When it became a street, many houses on the eastern side of the street, with odd-numbered addresses, were connected to both Hang Muoi Street and the riverside (now Tran Nhat Duat Street).

Several bus routes run through Hang Muoi Street, including routes 08A, 08B, 11, 23, 31, 34, 86, 146, E02, and E07, terminating at the end of the street.

Hang Muoi Street, nestled within the historic district of Hanoi, is a charming and narrow thoroughfare stretching approximately 190 meters from Hang Man street to Hang Bac street, intersecting Tran Nhat Duat street at its midpoint. The street runs parallel to the bustling Tran Quang Khai street on one side and Nguyen Hue street on the other, forming a picturesque urban landscape that reflects the rich history and culture of Vietnam's capital city. 

Historically, Hang Muoi Street was part of the ancient Thanh Nien ward, which bordered the old French Quarter, now known as Ly Thai To ward in Hoan Kiem district. The street’s name, though translated as "Salt Street," does not indicate that it was a place for selling salt but rather a hub for merchants involved in the salt trade. This unique designation stems from the fact that while the street itself did not have shops selling salt, several families residing there were engaged in the business of trading salt, which was then transported to various provinces and sold locally. 

The origins of Hang Muoi Street date back to the late 19th century when it was still a riverside village, part of the larger Thanh Nien community. As the city expanded and modernized, the area transformed into a bustling commercial district, with many houses built along both sides of the street and Tran Nhat Duat street, creating a vibrant urban scene. The street’s architecture is characterized by traditional Vietnamese homes, often connected to each other, reflecting the close-knit community that once thrived here. 

In the early 20th century, the street underwent significant changes as new buildings were constructed, replacing older structures that had been used for storing goods and salt. These new constructions featured a mix of traditional and colonial architectural styles, blending seamlessly into the existing urban fabric. The houses on Hang Muoi Street were typically two-story structures, with the ground floor often serving as storage space for goods and the upper floors as living quarters. This layout allowed for efficient use of space and facilitated the movement of goods between different levels of the building.

Despite its name, Hang Muoi Street did not have shops selling salt, but rather served as a residential and commercial hub for salt traders. The salt was stored in nearby warehouses and distributed to various markets and provinces. The street’s location near the river made it an ideal spot for traders to transport their goods via waterways, enhancing its importance as a trading center. Over time, the street became known for its association with salt traders, even though the actual sale of salt was conducted elsewhere.

The cultural significance of Hang Muoi Street extends beyond its commercial activities. Hang Muoi Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a historic thoroughfare that stretches for 104 meters and is 7 meters wide. The street runs from Tran Nhat Duct Street to Hang Mam Street, connecting two significant areas within the bustling city. Its origins trace back to ancient times when it was part of Trung Thanh, one of the ten original villages in the old district of Tho Xuong, which later became known as Phuc Lam. 

The name "Hang Muoi" (Salt Street) predates the French colonial era, but during their rule, the street was referred to as "rue de Sel." After the August Revolution in 1945, the street reclaimed its original Vietnamese name, Hang Muoi, which it has retained ever since. Today, it falls under the jurisdiction of Ly Thai To ward, Hoan Kiem district, maintaining its historical significance and cultural heritage.

In the past, Hang Muoi Street was renowned for its salt trade, a crucial commodity in Vietnam's economy. The street's proximity to the Red River, which once flowed close to the current embankment, facilitated easy access to maritime trade routes. This strategic location allowed merchants to store and distribute large quantities of salt to traders from various provinces. However, the street did not cater to retail sales of salt; instead, it focused on wholesale transactions. For smaller-scale retail sales, residents would visit Hang Chinh and Hang Mam streets.

The architecture of Hang Muoi Street reflects the traditional Vietnamese urban design, characterized by narrow lanes lined with small shops and residences. The buildings are typically constructed with brick and wood, featuring intricate wooden doors and windows adorned with delicate carvings. These structures not only serve as commercial spaces but also house the daily lives of the local community, blending commerce and residential life seamlessly.

Visitors to Hang Muoi Street can immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s history and culture. Walking along the street, one can imagine the bustling activity of centuries past, where merchants and traders exchanged goods, contributing to the economic vitality of the region. The atmosphere is imbued with a sense of continuity, where modern life intersects with historical traditions, creating a unique blend of old and new.

While the street no longer serves as a major hub for salt trading, it remains an integral part of Hanoi’s cultural landscape. The area around Hang Muoi Street continues to thrive with a vibrant mix of traditional crafts, cuisine, and modern amenities. Nearby attractions such as the Temple of Literature and the Old Quarter offer visitors a deeper understanding of Hanoi’s rich cultural heritage. The street itself, though modest in size, holds a significant place in the city’s history, serving as a testament to the enduring legacy of Hanoi’s commercial and cultural evolution.

Exploring Hang Muoi Street provides a glimpse into the heart of Hanoi’s historical and cultural identity. The street’s narrow lanes and traditional architecture offer a serene contrast to the bustling energy of the surrounding areas, making it a must-visit destination for those interested in the city’s storied past and vibrant present.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Ngang Street
documents.content:
Hang Ngang Street, also known as 行昂, is a street located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi. It runs from Hang Dao Street to Hang Duong Street and is one-way traffic.

The origin of its name remains unclear and uncertain. Historically, Hang Ngang Street was part of the Dien Hung ward, in the Tien Tuc district of Tho Xuan city during the time of Thang Long. In the early 18th century, the upper part of the street was adjacent to Hang Dao Street and was called Hang Lam Street, where goods such as blue silk were sold. By the 19th century, it was renamed Viet Dong Street, which was a bustling trading area for Chinese immigrants from Guangdong. The prosperity of this Chinese community might have given rise to the name "Hang Ngang," possibly due to the practice of closing two gates at both ends of the street each evening. Today, Hang Ngang Street belongs to the Hang Dao ward in Hoan Kiem district.

During the French colonial period, the street was named Rue des Cantonais (Street of Guangdong people) and had a tramway running through its center. Currently, Hang Ngang Street, connecting with Hang Dao Street, is a vibrant commercial area characteristic of Hanoi. It operates as a one-way street and becomes pedestrian-only on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays.

In the time of the Le dynasty, Chinese immigrants concentrated on selling tea, medicine, and luxurious fabrics like silk and brocade. Later, Indian merchants added shops selling high-quality textiles. Nowadays, Hang Ngang Street is known for selling fashionable clothing and luxury consumer goods. There are also several portrait painting shops along the street.

Among the notable landmarks on Hang Ngang Street is number 48, where President Ho Chi Minh wrote the Declaration of Independence in 1945, establishing the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. At that time, the house belonged to Mr. Trinh Phuc Loi, who allowed the government to use it for work purposes. Today, the house has been converted into a museum.

Hang Ngang Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a historic thoroughfare that stretches for 152 meters and is 8 meters wide. It connects the streets of Hang Duong and Hang Dong, forming part of the vibrant network of ancient streets in the heart of the city. Originally, this area was known as the Diem Hung ward, which belonged to the Huu Tuc district, later renamed Dong Tho, within the old Tho Xuan county. The street's origins trace back to before the French colonial era, when it was referred to by the French as "rue des Cantonais," meaning "Street of the Guangdong People." After the August Revolution in 1945, the street reclaimed its original Vietnamese name, Hang Ngang, which the local populace had always affectionately used.

The history of Hang Ngang Street is deeply intertwined with the presence of Chinese immigrants who were allowed to reside in Thang Long (the ancient name for Hanoi) during the Le dynasty. These immigrants settled in specific neighborhoods according to their respective provinces, with those from Guangdong residing in Hang Ngang Street and parts of Hang Buom Street. The residents of Hang Ngang were predominantly Chinese immigrants, particularly those from Guangdong, whose ancestral province was also known as Viet, leading some historical texts to refer to the street as Viet Dong, or Eastern Viet Street.

One theory suggests that the name Hang Ngang, which translates to "Cross Street," derived from the practice of setting up two gates at each end of the street that would be closed at night, guarded by watchmen. This practice likely gave rise to the street's name. However, historical records from the book "Vu Trung Tuy But" by Pham Dinh Ho indicate that prior to the arrival of Chinese immigrants, Hang Ngang and the beginning of Hang Dao Street were bustling markets for clothing and silk products. The area was known as Hang Ao, or Clothing Street, where various textiles and garments were sold, including yem, a traditional Vietnamese undergarment.

Throughout the early 20th century, Hang Ngang Street was home to numerous large silk and textile shops owned by Chinese immigrants, many of whom were related to one another. Notable among these were the Phan family businesses such as Phan Duc Thanh, Phan Thai Thanh, Phan Hung Thanh, Phan Van Thanh, Phan Du Thanh, and Phan Hoa Thanh. Additionally, there were significant Vietnamese merchants like Trinh Phuc Loi and Loi Quyen who dealt in silk and textiles. One of the descendants of Trinh Phuc Loi, Trinh Van Bo, operated his business at number 48 on Hang Ngang Street.

In addition to silk and textile shops, Hang Ngang Street was also known for its tea shops run by Chinese immigrants. Stores like Sinh Thai, Chinh Thai, and Ninh Thai specialized in selling tea, often packaged in ceramic jars, tin containers, or paper wrappers adorned with Chinese characters. Interestingly, much of the tea sold here was actually sourced from Phu Tho and processed locally, bearing labels such as Vu Di Son and Phuc Kien.

Today, Hang Ngang Street holds a special place in Vietnamese history due to its connection with the country's struggle for independence. Number 48 on the street is particularly significant as it was here that Ho Chi Minh wrote the Declaration of Independence, marking the birth of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. On August 19, 1945, after the successful uprising against the colonial regime in Hanoi, Truong Chinh and other members of the Central Committee met at number 48 to discuss further actions and preparations for Ho Chi Minh's return to the city. 

Ho Chi Minh arrived in Hanoi on August 24, staying briefly in Phu Xa and then moving to Phu Gia, both now part of Phu Thuong commune in Tu Liem district. On August 25, he returned to the city center and stayed at number 48, the residence of Trinh Van Bo and his wife, Hoang Minh Ho, who were active members of the Viet Minh. Here, Ho Chi Minh chaired the first meeting of the Central Committee in Hanoi, deciding on key issues such as organizing a mass rally to introduce the new government and drafting the Declaration of Independence, a document of immense importance in Vietnam's history of nation-building and defense.

Visitors to Hang Ngang Street today can explore a blend of historical and modern elements. The street retains its traditional charm with narrow lanes lined with old buildings, many of which still house small shops and workshops. The atmosphere is a mix of quiet nostalgia and bustling commerce, offering a glimpse into the rich tapestry of Hanoi's past and present. Tourists can wander through the streets, admiring the intricate architecture and learning about the significant role this area played in shaping Vietnam's modern history. The experience is enriched by the stories of the people who lived and worked here, contributing to the cultural heritage of Hanoi.

Hang Ngang Street, a historic thoroughfare nestled within the heart of Hanoi's ancient quarter, is a testament to the city’s rich tapestry of history, culture, and commerce. Originally known as Phố Hàng Lam, this street was once dedicated to the vibrant trade of indigo dyeing, a crucial industry during the feudal era when specific colors were reserved for different social classes. The artisans who specialized in dyeing fabrics with shades of blue and green resided here, contributing to the bustling economic activity that characterized the area. Over time, due to shifts in economic conditions and societal changes, the primary focus of trade shifted, leading to a renaming of the street to reflect these new dynamics.

In the late 17th and early 18th centuries, Hang Ngang Street underwent significant transformations. As the demand for indigo dyeing declined, the artisans moved to other areas, such as Phố Hàng Bông and Phố Thợ Nhuộm, leaving behind a legacy of craftsmanship and tradition. However, the street continued to evolve, becoming a hub for Chinese immigrants from Guangdong province, who brought with them their own unique cultural influences and commercial practices. This influx of newcomers transformed Hang Ngang into a melting pot of cultures, where Vietnamese and Chinese traditions intertwined, creating a dynamic and prosperous community.

The strategic location of Hang Ngang Street near the riverfront made it an ideal spot for traders and merchants. Its proximity to waterways facilitated the transportation of goods, leading to the establishment of numerous shops and markets. The street became renowned for its bustling trade, attracting not only local residents but also visitors from afar. To ensure safety and security, the inhabitants constructed two gates at either end of the street, which were closed at night, giving rise to the name "Hang Ngang," meaning "Cross Street" in Vietnamese, reflecting the physical barrier created by these gates.

During the French colonial period, the street was referred to as Rue des Cantonais, highlighting its connection to the Chinese community. After the August Revolution in 1945, the street officially adopted its current name, Hang Ngang Street. This period marked a significant chapter in the street’s history, as it transitioned from a predominantly Chinese settlement to a more integrated community, blending Vietnamese and Chinese cultures seamlessly.

The cultural significance of Hang Ngang Street extends beyond its commercial activities. It is home to several important historical sites, including the đình Đồng Lạc, a traditional communal house that serves as a symbol of the area’s rich heritage. This structure, along with other historical landmarks, provides a glimpse into the past, offering visitors a tangible link to Vietnam’s storied history. Notably, the house at number 48 Hang Ngang Street played a pivotal role in the nation’s independence movement. Here, President Ho Chi Minh drafted the Declaration of Independence, a document that would shape the future of Vietnam. The house, originally owned by the wealthy merchants Trịnh Văn Bô and Hoàng Minh Hộ, now stands as a national monument, a testament to the critical decisions made during the country’s struggle for freedom.

Today, Hang Ngang Street continues to thrive as a center of commerce and culture. The street is lined with shops selling high-end clothing, luxury watches, cosmetics, and exquisite jewelry, catering to both locals and tourists. Despite the modernization of the city, Hang Ngang retains its timeless charm, with many of the original houses still standing, their facades adorned with intricate wood carvings and ornate decorations. These structures, though no longer dedicated to a single trade, attract visitors with their architectural beauty and historical significance.

Visitors to Hang Ngang Street can immerse themselves in the vibrant atmosphere of the nearby Chợ Châu Long, a traditional market that offers a glimpse into the daily life of Hanoi’s residents. The market, filled with stalls selling fresh produce and traditional delicacies, is a living testament to the enduring traditions of Vietnamese culture. Additionally, the Chợ Hôm - Đức Viên, located in the same vicinity, is another must-visit destination, known for its wide variety of textiles and traditional crafts. With roots dating back to the 19th century, this market remains a vital part of the local economy and a popular spot for tourists seeking authentic souvenirs and local flavors.

For those interested in the textile industry, a visit to Phố Lụa Hàng Gai, just a short distance away, provides insight into the traditional silk weaving techniques that have been practiced in Vietnam for centuries. This street, known for its high-quality silk products, showcases the elegance and sophistication of Vietnamese craftsmanship. Nearby, Phố Hàng Mã, with its colorful array of decorative items and festival paraphernalia, adds a festive touch to the urban landscape, making it a favorite among tourists and locals alike.

In summary, Hang Ngang Street is a microcosm of Hanoi’s rich cultural heritage, where the past and present coexist harmoniously. From its origins as a center for indigo dyeing to its current status as a hub for luxury goods and cultural exploration, the street continues to captivate visitors with its blend of historical significance and contemporary vibrancy.

Đứng lặng yên giữa dòng chảy giao thoa ấy, lòng người bỗng dâng lên một sự hoài niệm xen lẫn niềm háo hức thẳm sâu.
