Hang Non Street is a small street located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi, running through the districts of Hang Gai and Cua Dong in Hoan Kiem district. The name "Hang Non" (Hat Street) originates from its historical role as a marketplace for various types of hats. Today, the main products sold on this street include bedding, quilts, pillows, and mattresses, particularly near its intersection with Hang Dieu Street.

The street has existed since the time of the Middle Le Dynasty. During the French colonial period, the French renamed it Rue des Chapeaux, which translates to Hat Street. In 1945, Mayor Tran Van Lai restored the original name, Hang Non, which has remained unchanged since then.

Hang Non Street stretches for 216 meters, starting at the junction of Hangquat and Hanghom streets, passing through Hangmanh, Hangthiep, and Hangdieu streets, ending at Duongthanh Street. Historically, the upper part of the street was known as Ma Vi Street because it produced costumes, headdresses, flags, and props used in theatrical performances, all of which required horsehair. The lower part specialized in making and selling hats, hence the name Hang Non.

The street's origins date back to the Middle Le Dynasty, situated on the land of the former Dong Thanh ward, which was part of the old Tho Xuong district. Long before the French colonized Vietnam, this area was already home to many shops selling different types of hats, including the "tu lo" hats worn by monks in temples.

During the French colonial era, the French renamed the street Rue des Chapeaux, literally meaning Hat Street. In 1945, Mayor Tran Van Lai reinstated the original name, Hang Non. Until the late 19th century, both men and women in Vietnam commonly wore hats. Men wore conical hats with silver or brass tips, while women had a variety of options, such as the thung quai thao hat for the more affluent, and the ba tam or chao hat made from soft gourd leaves for laborers. The thung quai thao hat was a type of hat worn by northern Vietnamese women, made from palm or gourd leaves, with a diameter of 70-80 cm and a brim width of 10-12 cm. It resembled a mushroom cap with a handle and a flat top.

By the end of the 1910s, except for those in Hanoi, men no longer wore hats, opting instead for headscarves or umbrellas. Wealthy women carried parasols, while only hardworking laborers continued to wear straw hats outdoors. Consequently, the number of hat shops on Hang Non Street gradually decreased, eventually selling their products mainly in markets. On July 28, 1929, the founding meeting of the Red Trade Union of Northern Vietnam was held at No. 15 Hang Non Street. Shop owners shifted their focus to other goods, such as selling wooden clogs painted with lacquer, like the businesses My Sinh and My Thinh, owned by people from Ha Vy village, a traditional lacquer craft village. They moved from Hanghom Street to Hang Non Street, where they bought pre-carved wooden clogs, painted them, and sold them.

In the late 20th century, the hat-making trade was revived, primarily catering to tourists in hotels. Nowadays, Hang Non Street no longer sells traditional products but offers a wide range of goods. Hang Non Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a vibrant thoroughfare that stretches for 216 meters and spans a width of 6 meters. This historic street connects from Hang Quat Street to Duong Thanh Street, intersecting with Hang Dieu Street. The origins of Hang Non Street date back to the time before French colonial rule, when it was known as the land of the village of Yen Noi, part of the former Tien Tuc district, which later became Thuong My district. The street's name translates to "Hat Street" due to its historical significance as a center for hat-making and selling various types of hats.

The street's history is deeply rooted in the traditional crafts of Hanoi, with its name "Hang Non" derived from the Vietnamese term for "hat." During the French colonial period, the street was referred to as "rue des Chapeaux," meaning "Hat Street" in French. After the August Revolution in 1945, the street reclaimed its original Vietnamese name, Hang Non, which it has retained ever since.

Today, Hang Non Street is situated within the Hang Gai ward, a bustling area known for its rich cultural heritage and traditional crafts. The street's historical importance extends beyond just its current name, as it was once part of the larger Yen Noi village, which included two distinct areas: Yen Noi Dong Thanh and Yen Noi Co Vu. These areas were named based on their proximity to other neighborhoods such as Dong Thanh and Co Vu, now known as Hang Da.

The eastern segment of what was once Yen Noi Dong Thanh is now known as Ma Vi Street, where artisans produce and sell ceremonial and theatrical accessories used by officials, performers, and worshippers. These include costumes, hats, crowns, flags, fans, and other ritualistic items. The western portion, Hang Non Street, specializes in the production and sale of various types of hats, reflecting the diverse needs of different social classes and professions.

Visitors to Hang Non Street can witness the intricate process of hat-making, which involves meticulous craftsmanship using materials like bamboo, palm leaves, horsehair, and feathers. The hats produced here range from simple straw hats to elaborate ceremonial hats adorned with precious metals and fine embroidery. For instance, the Nón Nghệ, resembling a large wheel with a diameter close to one meter and a height of 10 centimeters, is a unique creation designed for ceremonial purposes. Similarly, the Nón Ba Tầm, a deeper and more complex design, often features ornamental quivers made of silver or gold threads.

The street's historical significance is further highlighted by its role in the early stages of labor movements in Hanoi during the late 1920s. In 1929, the First National Congress of Red Labor Unions was held at number 15 Hang Non Street. This event marked a pivotal moment in the labor movement, bringing together representatives from various regions including Haiphong, Nam Dinh, and the coal mines of Dong Trieu and Mao Ke. The congress adopted a program and charter for the Red Labor Unions, electing Tran Van Lan, a worker from the Nam Dinh textile mill, as the first chairman.

Today, Hang Non Street continues to preserve its rich cultural heritage while also adapting to modern times. Visitors can explore the narrow lanes lined with traditional shops and workshops, each dedicated to the art of hat-making. The atmosphere is filled with the sounds of craftsmen working diligently, the smell of freshly woven materials, and the sight of beautifully crafted hats displayed in windows and stalls. This blend of tradition and contemporary life makes Hang Non Street a fascinating destination for tourists interested in experiencing the authentic culture and craftsmanship of Hanoi.

Hang Non Street, also known as Rue des Chapeaux, has a history that traces back to the French colonial era. Even after the revolution, the street retained its original name, preserving a legacy that resonates through time. The street's origins are rooted in two distinct sections that were later merged into one. The eastern part was originally named Phố Mã Vĩ, dedicated to crafting and selling accessories for officials, performers, and religious ceremonies. This included items such as ceremonial robes, hats, banners, fans, and other paraphernalia used in theater performances and rituals. The name "Mã Vĩ" likely derived from the materials used in making theatrical props, particularly horsehair, which was integral to creating certain types of hats and stage decorations.

The western segment, now known as Hang Non Street, specialized in producing various types of hats. These ranged from sturdy straw hats suitable for farmers to more elaborate military-style helmets. Each hat was meticulously crafted using traditional techniques, with some hats featuring decorative elements like metal tips or ornamental bindings. For instance, the nón lính, resembling a large dish-shaped helmet, was made from woven bamboo strips and featured a pointed metal tip at the center, often secured tightly under the chin with a strap.

Today, Hang Non Street is not solely dedicated to hat-making but retains its historical charm and cultural significance. The street's transformation over the years reflects the dynamic nature of urban development in Hanoi. Despite no longer being a hub for hat production, it remains a vibrant area filled with shops offering a variety of goods. At the end of the street, visitors can find numerous stores selling wooden clogs in various styles, catering to different tastes and needs. Additionally, there are shops that sell traditional paper lanterns and other decorative items, blending seamlessly with the historical ambiance of the area.

One notable landmark on Hang Non Street is the ancient temple of Yên Nội-Đồng Thành, located at number 42. This temple serves as a testament to the historical importance of the area, connecting the present-day neighborhood to its past. The street's historical significance extends beyond its commercial activities, as evidenced by the fact that it was once the site of significant political gatherings. In the summer of 1920, the first National Red Trade Union Congress was held at number 15 Hang Non Street, hosted by Nguyen Duc Canh. This event marked a pivotal moment in Vietnamese labor history, where delegates disguised as traders from various provinces convened to discuss and establish the program and charter of the Red Trade Union. The congress elected Tran Van Lan as the first chairman, a worker from the Nam Dinh textile mill.

Throughout the early 20th century, Hang Non Street experienced periods of economic hardship, particularly during the Great Depression and the onset of World War II. Many merchants faced financial difficulties and had to relocate their businesses, while others transitioned into selling Japanese silk and other imported textiles. Despite these challenges, the street managed to maintain its identity and resilience, adapting to changing times while preserving its unique character.

During the First Indochina War, Hang Non Street, situated within the central region of Hanoi, remained relatively unscathed compared to other areas. Its strategic location between key administrative zones helped shield it from extensive damage, allowing it to retain much of its pre-war appearance and functionality.

Today, while Hang Non Street no longer specializes exclusively in hat-making, it continues to embody the spirit of traditional craftsmanship and commerce. The street's architecture and layout reflect the historical continuity of Hanoi's old quarter, with narrow lanes lined with small shops and bustling markets. Visitors can immerse themselves in the lively atmosphere, exploring the diverse range of products available, from wooden clogs to intricately designed furniture pieces. The street's cultural significance is further highlighted by its role in local traditions and community life, where residents and visitors alike can experience the rich tapestry of Vietnamese culture and heritage.

In summary, Hang Non Street stands as a living museum of Hanoi's past, where the echoes of historical events and the rhythms of daily life blend harmoniously. It offers a unique glimpse into the city's evolution, showcasing the enduring legacy of traditional crafts alongside modern adaptations, making it a must-visit destination for those interested in the cultural and historical richness of Vietnam.

description: Nestled deep within the intricate maze of alleys and lanes of the Old Quarter, the modest Hàng Phèn street emerges like a soft, lingering melody, reminiscent of the old Thăng Long way of life. Tracing back history, this place was once bustling with vendors selling phèn chua, an essential item helping the townspeople to clarify and filter domestic water drawn from sông Hồng or deep wells. The rustic name Hàng Phèn was born from that very bustling scene of trade, imbued with a strong sense of survival. Although time has washed away the sparkling phèn chua crystals, the breath of life on this small street still fully retains its simple and warm charm. Every day, tourists and capital residents alike often stroll slowly through here, eagerly enjoying the flavors of rustic street food or leisurely sipping hot tea by the old house verandas. Especially on chilly mornings, the calls of vendors mixed with lively chatter and laughter make the space burst with an indescribable rustic vitality. Standing in the narrow street corner, one's heart is suddenly filled with a boundless nostalgia. The experience of breathing in that time-tinged atmosphere brings a profound tranquility, helping us fully understand the resilient vitality and ancient hidden charm of this land of a thousand years of civilization.

Ngược dòng lịch sử, nơi đây từng tấp nập những gánh hàng buôn bán phèn chua, một vật dụng thiết yếu giúp người dân kẻ chợ đánh phèn lọc nước sinh hoạt lấy từ sông Hồng hay các giếng khơi. Cái tên Hàng Phèn mộc mạc đã ra đời từ chính cảnh tượng giao thương tấp nập mang đậm tính sinh tồn ấy. Dẫu thời gian đã cuốn trôi đi những tinh thể phèn chua lấp lánh, hơi thở đời sống nơi con phố nhỏ này vẫn giữ trọn vẹn nét bình dị và ấm áp. Ngày ngày, du khách cùng người dân thủ đô thường thả bộ thật chậm qua đây, say sưa thưởng thức hương vị ẩm thực vỉa hè dân dã hay thong dong nhâm nhi chén trà nóng bên những hiên nhà cũ kỹ. Đặc biệt vào những sớm mai se lạnh, tiếng rao hàng xen lẫn tiếng nói cười rôm rả khiến không gian bừng lên một sức sống mộc mạc khó tả. Đứng giữa góc phố hẹp, lòng người bỗng trào dâng một niềm hoài niệm miên man. Trải nghiệm hít thở bầu không khí nhuốm màu thời gian ấy mang lại sự tĩnh tại thẳm sâu, giúp ta thấu hiểu trọn vẹn sức sống dẻo dai và nét duyên ngầm cổ kính của mảnh đất ngàn năm văn hiến.

Nestled within the labyrinthine network of narrow alleys and lanes of Hanoi’s Old Quarter, Hang Phen Street (Phố Hàng Phèn) emerges as a quaint and charming thoroughfare, evoking the essence of traditional Thang Long life. Historically, this street was a bustling hub for vendors selling phèn chua, a crucial commodity used by local inhabitants to clarify and filter their drinking water drawn from the Red River (Sông Hồng) or deep wells. The name “Hang Phen” (Hàng Phèn) was coined from the vibrant trading scene that characterized the area, reflecting the resilience and ingenuity of its people. Over time, despite the disappearance of the sparkling phèn chua crystals, the street has retained its simple and warm charm, becoming a beloved destination for both tourists and locals.

Today, Hang Phen Street stands as a testament to the enduring spirit of Hanoi’s past, where visitors can meander through its narrow lanes lined with closely packed nhà ống (tube houses), their faded yellow and moss-covered lime-washed walls contrasting with the gray, askew tiled roofs. The street’s unique identifier is a small intersection shaded by lush, ancient bàng trees, creating a serene and tranquil atmosphere. This picturesque setting is further enhanced by the tangled network of electrical wires overhead, which add to the street’s character, while the cramped sidewalks are perpetually alive with the hustle and bustle of street vendors.

The architectural style of the tube houses along Hang Phen Street is typical of the Old Quarter, featuring narrow facades and deep interiors designed to maximize living space in a densely populated urban environment. These structures are built primarily with brick and wood, adorned with ornate wooden doors and windows, and often display intricate carvings and decorative motifs that reflect the cultural heritage of the region.

Culturally, Hang Phen Street holds significant importance as a microcosm of Hanoi’s rich history and traditions. It serves as a living museum, where one can experience the authentic flavors of Vietnamese street food, savoring dishes such as phở, bánh mì, and various regional delicacies. The street is also known for its vibrant morning markets, where vendors call out their wares amidst the lively chatter and laughter of shoppers, creating a dynamic and engaging atmosphere. Additionally, the street’s historic houses provide a glimpse into the daily lives of Hanoians, offering a window into the city’s past and present.

For tourists, Hang Phen Street offers a unique blend of historical exploration and cultural immersion. Visitors can wander through the narrow streets, immersing themselves in the sights, sounds, and smells of traditional Hanoi life. On chilly mornings, the street comes alive with the warmth of hot tea served at roadside stalls, adding to the nostalgic ambiance. The experience of walking through Hang Phen Street is not just about seeing but feeling the timeless charm of a city steeped in a thousand years of civilization, where the past and present coexist harmoniously.

Hang Phen Street is a historic street located within the Old Quarter of Hanoi, stretching approximately 100 meters from Thuoc Bac Street to Hang Ga Street. Originally part of Dong Thanh Thoi village in the former district of Tho Xuan, it is now situated in Hang Bo ward, Hoan Kiem district. During the French colonial period, the street was known as Rue du Vieille Marche, or Old Market Street. In 1945, it officially received its current name, Hang Phen Street.

One of the smaller ancient streets in Hanoi, Hang Phen Street features old one-story houses. Like many other streets in the Old Quarter, the name "Hang Phen" reflects the specific goods that were historically produced and traded there. Previously, this street specialized in selling various types of alum, including black alum, green alum, and sour alum, particularly used for water purification by residents of Hanoi and neighboring provinces. 

Today, while some families still engage in the traditional trade of alum, others have diversified their businesses to include food services, grocery stores, and fashion clothing, catering to the needs of the local community in the Old Quarter.

description: Nestled in the heart of the thirty-six streets and guilds area, Hàng Quạt appears like a miniature museum, preserving the spiritual and religious essence of the capital's people. Tracing back in time, this street was once home to artisans from Đào Xá village, bringing with them the renowned traditional fan-making craft of the imperial capital. From rustic paper fans to elegant silk fans, all contributed to the poetic name Hàng Quạt. Through many ups and downs, though the fans gradually faded into the past, the cultural pulse here brilliantly transformed into wood carving, making hoành phi, câu đối, and hand-carved seals. Daily, travelers and locals bustle back and forth, engrossed in admiring altars adorned with red lacquer and gold leaf or eagerly awaiting a meticulously carved ấn triện. Especially around Tet, the space seems to light up, with the faint scent of incense and the lively clinking sounds of carving. Wandering amidst those vibrant colors, one's heart is suddenly filled with reverence intertwined with boundless tranquility. The experience of touching the fragrant, freshly painted wood grain brings a profound sense of peace, helping to fully comprehend the artistry and rich spiritual life of this land of a thousand years of civilization.
description_vi: Nằm nép mình giữa trung tâm khu ba mươi sáu phố phường, Hàng Quạt hiện lên như một bảo tàng thu nhỏ lưu giữ vẹn nguyên nét tín ngưỡng tâm linh của người thủ đô. Ngược dòng thời gian, con phố này từng là nơi quần tụ của thợ thủ công làng Đào Xá, mang theo nghề làm quạt truyền thống lừng danh chốn kinh kỳ. Từ những chiếc quạt giấy mộc mạc đến quạt lụa đài các, tất cả đã dệt nên cái tên Hàng Quạt đầy thơ mộng. Trải qua bao thăng trầm, dẫu những cánh quạt dần lùi vào dĩ vãng, nhịp đập văn hóa nơi đây lại chuyển mình rực rỡ sang nghề chạm khắc gỗ, làm hoành phi, câu đối và khắc dấu thủ công. Ngày ngày, lữ khách và người dân tấp nập ngược xuôi, say sưa chiêm ngưỡng những ban thờ sơn son thiếp vàng hay mải mê chờ đợi một chiếc ấn triện được đục đẽo tỉ mỉ. Đặc biệt vào dịp giáp Tết, không gian như bừng sáng, thoang thoảng mùi hương trầm và rộn rã âm thanh lách cách đục chạm. Lạc bước giữa sắc màu rực rỡ ấy, lòng ta bỗng dâng lên niềm tôn kính xen lẫn sự tĩnh tại vô ngần. Trải nghiệm chạm tay vào những thớ gỗ thơm mùi sơn mới mang lại cảm giác bình yên thẳm sâu, giúp thấu hiểu trọn vẹn sự tài hoa và đời sống tâm linh phong phú của mảnh đất ngàn năm văn hiến.

This vibrant scene is nestled within the narrow roadway, always bustling with a hurried flow of people and vehicles moving back and forth.

The street's history dates back to the time when artisans from Đào Xá village brought their renowned craft to the area, transforming the cultural pulse of the district. Over time, the fans gradually faded into the past, but the artisans' skills were adapted to create intricate wood carvings, including hoành phi, câu đối, and hand-carved seals. Today, visitors can still marvel at the beautifully crafted wooden altars, adorned with red lacquer and gold leaf, and witness the artisans at work, meticulously carving ấn triện.

As the Lunar New Year approaches, the street comes alive with the faint scent of incense and the lively clinking sounds of carving. The air is filled with the vibrant colors of the wooden carvings, and the atmosphere is one of reverence and tranquility. Visitors can't help but feel a sense of awe and respect for the rich cultural heritage of this land, which has been shaped by the hands of artisans and craftsmen over the centuries.

Hang Quat Street is a must-visit destination for anyone interested in exploring the cultural and spiritual essence of Hanoi. The experience of wandering through this charming street, surrounded by the sights, sounds, and smells of traditional Vietnamese craftsmanship, is a truly unforgettable one.

Nestled in the heart of Hanoi’s historic district, Hang Quat Street stands as a testament to the city’s rich cultural heritage, a living museum that preserves the spiritual essence of Vietnam’s capital. Historically, this narrow thoroughfare was home to artisans from the village of Dao Xa, known for their exquisite craftsmanship in fan-making, a tradition that dates back centuries. The street’s name, “Hang Quat,” translates to “Fan Street,” reflecting its original purpose as a hub for fan makers who produced both rustic paper fans and elegant silk fans, contributing to the poetic charm of the area.

Over time, the fan-making industry gradually declined, but the cultural vibrancy of Hang Quat Street continued to thrive through the transformation of its crafts. Today, the street is renowned for its woodcarving traditions, where skilled artisans create intricate hoành phi (wooden plaques), câu đối (couplets), and hand-carved seals. These delicate works of art adorn the facades of houses and shops, creating a visually stunning tableau that captivates visitors and locals alike.

The architectural landscape of Hang Quat Street is characterized by the typical Vietnamese nhà ống, or tube houses, which line the narrow, winding path. These structures, often painted in brilliant red and adorned with golden details, reflect the traditional sơn son thiếp vàng (lacquered red and gold) style. The juxtaposition of these vibrant colors against the backdrop of the old, weathered buildings creates a striking visual contrast that is uniquely Vietnamese.

During the busy days leading up to Tet, the Lunar New Year festival, Hang Quat Street comes alive with activity. The air is filled with the faint scent of incense and the rhythmic sound of wood being carved, as artisans work diligently to complete their orders. Tourists and locals alike wander through the bustling streets, admiring the intricate carvings and the beautifully crafted altars. The atmosphere is one of reverence and tranquility, as the sounds of hammering and chiseling blend harmoniously with the soft whispers of conversation.

Visitors can explore the various workshops and stores along the street, where they can witness firsthand the meticulous process of creating these traditional wooden artworks. Each piece, whether it be a hoành phi, câu đối, or seal, is imbued with a deep sense of cultural significance and artistic skill. The experience of touching the freshly painted wood grains, still warm from the craftsmen’s hands, provides a profound sense of connection to the rich spiritual life and artistic traditions of Vietnam.

Hang Quat Street not only serves as a center for traditional crafts but also as a vital part of Hanoi’s cultural tapestry. Its location in the historic district, surrounded by other significant sites such as the Old Quarter and Hoàn Kiếm Lake, makes it a key destination for tourists seeking to immerse themselves in the city’s heritage. As one wanders through the narrow lanes, the vibrant colors, the rhythmic sounds of carving, and the serene ambiance combine to offer a deeply enriching experience that encapsulates the essence of Hanoi’s thousand-year-old civilization.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Quat Street
documents.content:
Hang Quat Street is located within the ancient quarter of Hanoi, stretching approximately 200 meters and intersecting only with To Tich Street. It begins at Luan Van Can Street and ends at the junction of Hang Nom and Hang Hom Streets.

Originally, Hang Quat Street was part of the land belonging to the villages of To Tich and Thuong My, in the former district of Tien Tuc, Tho Xuong county. Later, it became part of Hang Gai ward, Hoan Kiem district, which was later merged into the Hoan Kiem ward. The street consists of three small streets combined: the eastern half is the old Hang Quat Street and Hang Dan Street, while the western half is Ma Vi Street. After 1945, the official name of the street was established as Hang Quat Street. Today, it belongs to the Hoan Kiem ward.

The eastern section of the street, known as Hang Quat, was formerly home to shops that sold fans made both by local production and transported from other places. The craft of fan-making was brought by people originally from Dao Xa village, also known as Dong Quat village in Hung Yen province. These settlers lived there, produced fans, and established a communal house to honor their ancestor, Mr. Dao.

The middle part of Hang Quat Street was previously called Hang Dan because many households made and sold various types of musical instruments such as moon lutes, zithers, monochords, and flutes. At that time, there were no large stores, only families engaged in woodworking crafts.

After the French colonizers arrived in Hanoi, the street was named "rue des Eventails." In the early 20th century, most shops specialized in making and selling intricately carved wooden items like dragon pavilions, sedan chairs, and lattice doors. Later, they shifted to producing ordinary furniture like tables, chairs, cabinets, and cupboards.

Today, the western end of Hang Quat Street, from the Dau Temple to the beginning of Hang Nom Street, was formerly known as Ma Vi Street. This area specialized in making and selling traditional costumes, theatrical attire, festival clothing, flags, banners, and stage props made from horsehair, hence the name Ma Vi (horse tail).

Currently, Hang Quat Street no longer sells fans or musical instruments. The shops now deal in various goods such as large and small altars, embroidered paintings, and calligraphy used for mourning, celebrations, longevity wishes, and commendations. Besides the Nguyen Van To Continuous Education School, the street also houses Nguyen Du Middle School and Nguyen Ba Ngoc School.

Hang Quat Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a vibrant and historically rich area that stretches for 200 meters and is 8 meters wide. The street runs from Pho Luong Van Can to the intersection with Hang Non and Hang Hom streets. Originally part of the ancient villages of Toc Tich and Thuong My, which were later combined into the Thuong My village within the old Tho Xuan district, Hang Quat Street has a storied past that dates back to the time of the Le Dynasty. During this period, it was known by its Vietnamese name, but after the French colonial era, it was briefly renamed "rue des Eventails" before reverting to its original Vietnamese name in 1945. Today, it belongs to Hang Gai Ward, Hoan Kiem District.

The street's name reflects its historical significance as a center for quill production and trade. The craft of making fans here was brought by residents from Dao Xa Village, also known colloquially as Dong Quat, in An Thi District of Hung Yen Province. These settlers established themselves in Hang Quat Street, where they not only produced fans but also worshipped their patron saint, a Mr. Dao, at a local temple now located at number 4 on the street, known as the Spring Fair Temple or "cho quat mua xuan." This temple served as a marketplace for various types of fans during the spring season, attracting buyers from different provinces.

Fans made in Hang Quat Street are diverse and include several varieties. Quat Lu, crafted in Kim Lu Village of Thanh Tri District, are made from paper or thin silk-like material. Quat Hoi, originating from Hai Yen Village in Tien Lu District of Hung Yen Province, feature bamboo ribs. Quat Vac, from Canh Hao Village in Thanh Oai District of Hanoi, are distinguished by their intricate bamboo joints that shimmer when held up to light, resembling silk fans. Additionally, there are fans from Vo Village in Nong Vu Commune of Gia Lam District, featuring trellis designs like leaf-shaped or trapezoidal patterns, and quail feather fans from Dong Ding Village in Ha Dong District.

The tradition of fan-making in Hanoi is deeply rooted in history, as noted by Nguyen Trai in his work "Du Dia Chi," where he mentions that the left ward of Thang Jing, now known as Hanoi, had a fan-making industry. Although the exact location of this ward is no longer certain, it is known that until the late 19th century, there was still a fan-making industry in the area around the current Huu Street. However, Hang Quat Street remains the most renowned for its fan-making, particularly in Thuong My Village, which still retains its temple and shrine at numbers 64 and 74 respectively.

Visitors to Hang Quat Street can immerse themselves in the rich cultural heritage of fan-making, witnessing the intricate craftsmanship and the variety of materials used in creating these traditional fans. The atmosphere is one of nostalgia and tradition, with the sounds of bamboo being cut and shaped, and the sight of artisans meticulously assembling each fan. The street itself is lined with shops that not only produce fans but also sell them, offering a range of styles and designs that reflect the skill and creativity of the local artisans. The experience of walking through Hang Quat Street is a journey back in time, allowing visitors to appreciate the enduring legacy of this traditional craft and the cultural significance it holds in the heart of Hanoi.

Hang Quat Street, a historic thoroughfare nestled within the heart of old Thang Long, now known as modern-day Hanoi, is a testament to the rich tapestry of Vietnamese craftsmanship and cultural heritage. The street was originally built upon the ancient lands of two villages, Toc Tich and Thuong My, which were part of the former district of Tien Tuc, later renamed Thuong My, in the old county of Tho Xuan. This area has been a hub for artisans and craftsmen since its inception, with the establishment of a distinct community dedicated to the craft of fan-making, brought over by settlers from Dao Xa village, also known as Dong Quat, in An Thi district of Hung Yen province.

The tradition of fan-making in Hang Quat Street began when a group of settlers from Dao Xa village migrated to this area, seeking new opportunities and establishing themselves as skilled artisans. They founded a communal temple, the Spring Fair Temple, located at number 4 on the street, to honor their patron saint and the origins of their craft. This temple, known as the Spring Fair Temple or "Xuan Phiến Thị," symbolizes the seasonal nature of the fan trade, with its peak activity during the spring months.

The fans sold on Hang Quat Street were sourced from various regions, each contributing unique styles and materials. For instance, the Lu fans, crafted in Kim Lu village of Thanh Tri district in Hanoi, featured intricate designs made from paper, thin silk, and even bone and ivory. Similarly, the Hoi fans from Hai Yen village in the district of Tien Lu, Hung Yen, were renowned for their bamboo ribs, while the Vac fans from Canh Hoach village in Thanh Oai district of Hanoi were distinguished by their meticulous assembly, appearing almost like silk fans when unfurled. Additionally, fans from Dong Lac village in Dong Nac district of Tu Liem, Hanoi, showcased a variety of shapes such as willow leaves and trapezoids, while those from Vo village in Gia Lam district of Hanoi were known for their rice grain patterns. The street also boasted fans adorned with goose feathers, crafted in Dong Ding village of Ha Dong district in Hanoi.

Over time, Hang Quat Street evolved beyond its original purpose of selling fans and musical instruments. Today, the shops along the street have diversified into other trades, offering a wide array of goods including large and small altars, embroidered paintings, calligraphy, and ceremonial decorations used in funeral and wedding ceremonies. These items reflect the deep-rooted traditions and cultural practices that continue to thrive in the area.

Historically, Hang Quat Street comprised three distinct sections: Hang Quat, Hang Dan, and Ma Vi. The section known as Hang Dan was particularly famous for its music shops, where various types of traditional musical instruments such as the moon lute, zither, monochord, and flute were crafted and sold. By the early 20th century, many of these shops had shifted towards producing ornate wooden carvings, including dragon heads, eight treasures, and other decorative elements used in temples and palaces. Later, some of these establishments transitioned again, focusing on more common furniture items like tables, chairs, cabinets, and altar tables.

The segment called Ma Vi was named for its association with the production and sale of theatrical costumes, embroidery, and stage props. The term Ma Vi translates to "horse tail," referring to the use of horsehair in creating flags, banners, and other decorative items used in traditional performances and festivals. This part of the street was a vibrant center for artisans who specialized in crafting elaborate costumes and accessories for traditional theater and folk performances.

Today, visitors to Hang Quat Street can explore a range of historical sites and cultural landmarks. One notable site is the Dau Temple, also known as Thuong My Temple, located at number 64. This temple was named after the extensive mulberry groves that once thrived in the area, providing a livelihood for the local inhabitants. Another significant landmark is the communal house at number 74, which honors the local guardian deity, the Village God.

Educational institutions also dot the landscape of Hang Quat Street, with the Nguyen Van To School, situated at number 43, being one of the oldest private schools in Hanoi. Originally established as the Tri Tri School, it has played a crucial role in the educational development of the region.

Among the notable figures associated with Hang Quat Street is the prominent businessman and artist Nghiêm Xuân Huyến, whose residence at number 21 is a point of interest. He was not only a successful entrepreneur, owning the Rang Dong printing house, but also a journalist and publisher, founding newspapers such as Bac Ky The Thao in 1930 and Con Ong in 1936, which served as platforms for satire and criticism against colonial rule and collaborators. His contributions extended beyond business and journalism, as he was a mentor and father-in-law to the renowned composer Van Cao.

Hang Quat Street remains a living museum of Vietnamese culture, where visitors can immerse themselves in the rich history and traditions of the area, experiencing firsthand the legacy of craftsmanship and cultural significance that has defined this historic street for generations.

description: Tucked away like a humble hyphen between the bustling Hàng Lược and Hàng Mã streets, Hàng Rươi street emerges like a pensive low note amidst the vibrant symphony of the ba mươi sáu phố phường. Going back in time, this small street used to be a bustling stop for traders bringing rươi specialty from the chiêm trũng region to kinh kỳ for trade every autumn. The rustic name Hàng Rươi was born from the fresh rươi vendors, carrying the renowned culinary flavor of Thăng Long land. Although today the sight of rươi baskets has given way to stalls selling silk flowers and colorful decorations, the breath of life here still fully retains its simple, warm charm. Every day, locals and travelers leisurely stroll, engrossed in choosing vibrant flower branches or tasting some rustic street food. Especially nearing Tết, the street suddenly becomes bustling, joining the vibrant rhythm of the traditional flower market nearby. Standing silently in the small street corner, one's heart is suddenly filled with a boundless nostalgia. The experience of breathing the rare quiet atmosphere brings a deep sense of peace, helping each person fully understand the hidden charm of this urban place.
description_vi: Nằm lẩn khuất như một nét gạch nối khiêm nhường giữa phố Hàng Lược và Hàng Mã nhộn nhịp, phố Hàng Rươi hiện lên tựa một nốt trầm bâng khuâng giữa bản nhạc phồn hoa của khu ba mươi sáu phố phường. Ngược dòng thời gian về thuở trước, con phố bé nhỏ này từng là bến đỗ tấp nập của những thương lái mang đặc sản rươi từ vùng chiêm trũng lên kinh kỳ buôn bán mỗi độ thu về. Cái tên Hàng Rươi mộc mạc đã ra đời từ những gánh rươi tươi rói, mang theo cả phong vị ẩm thực trứ danh của đất Thăng Long. Dẫu ngày nay hình bóng những thúng rươi đã nhường chỗ cho các gian hàng hoa lụa và đồ trang trí muôn màu, hơi thở đời sống nơi đây vẫn giữ trọn nét bình dị, ấm áp. Ngày ngày, người dân và lữ khách thong dong dạo bước, mải mê chọn những nhành hoa rực rỡ hay nếm thử chút quà vỉa hè mộc mạc. Đặc biệt khi giáp Tết, con phố bỗng rộn rã hòa chung nhịp đập tưng bừng của chợ hoa truyền thống kề bên. Đứng lặng yên giữa góc phố nhỏ, lòng ta bỗng dâng lên một niềm hoài niệm miên man. Trải nghiệm hít thở bầu không khí tĩnh lặng hiếm hoi mang lại cảm giác bình yên thẳm sâu, giúp mỗi người thấu hiểu trọn vẹn nét duyên ngầm ẩn giấu nơi chốn đô hội.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Ruoi Street
documents.content:
Hang Ruoi Street is a small ancient street located in Hoan Kiem district, Hanoi, stretching approximately 108 meters long and 6 meters wide. The street runs from the intersection with Hang Loc Street to Hang Ma Street. Historically, this area was a part of the western embankment of the ancient To Lich River, which facilitated the docking of boats and the handling of aquatic products. It was situated within the old administrative boundaries of the villages of Vinh Tru and An Phu (later renamed to Yen Phu), belonging to the Hau Tuc ward of the former Tho Xuan district.

During the lunar month of September each year, when the rươi (a type of soft-bodied worm) breeding season occurs in brackish water areas, farmers from regions such as Hai Duong, Hai Phong, Nam Dinh, and Thai Binh would row their boats up the Red River, enter the To Lich River, and set up temporary stalls along the riverbank to form a bustling wholesale market for rươi. This seasonal market attracted traders who distributed the rươi to various markets and alleys within the imperial city of Thang Long to meet the unique culinary demands of Hanoi residents, including dishes like rươi paste, steamed rươi with gac leaves, or braised rươi. Consequently, the street acquired its name "Hang Rươi."

Under French colonial rule at the end of the 19th century, the street was officially named Rue des Vers Blancs, translating the local term for rươi into French. During this period, the system of ponds and parts of the To Lich River were gradually filled in to create standardized roads. After the August Revolution in 1945, the Vietnamese government reinstated the original Vietnamese name "Hang Rươi," which has remained unchanged until today.

Despite its short length, Hang Ruoi Street features two significant historical landmarks: the ancient Yen Phu communal house at number 17, which serves as evidence of the long-standing settlement history of the area, and the revolutionary site at number 4, which commemorates important events during the resistance war in the capital.

The street's historical significance extends beyond its current function, as it no longer primarily serves as a marketplace for rươi. Today, fewer households engage in preparing rươi-based dishes, having shifted to other occupations that offer higher income.

Hang Ruoi Street, a charming and historically rich artery in Hanoi's bustling Old Quarter, is a testament to the city’s dynamic past and vibrant present. The street, known for its former association with the sale of a local delicacy called rươi, has undergone significant transformation over the years, evolving into a hub of floral crafts and vibrant commerce. Originally named Rue des Vers Blancs by the French during their colonial era, the street was later renamed Hang Ruoi, reflecting its historical connection to the white larvae of certain fish species, which were once sold here in abundance.

The street stretches for 108 meters and is 6 meters wide, connecting Hang Luoc Street at one end and Hang Ma Street at the other. Historically, it was part of the ancient town of Vinh Truc, which included the northern section, and An Phu, which comprised the southern portion. The street is also associated with the Tong Huu Tuc, now known as Xuan Street, and the Hue Xuong district. Notably, the ruins of the Vinh Truc Pagoda can be found at number 59 Hang Luoc Street, while the An Phu Pagoda is located at number 17 Hang Ruoi Street, now converted into a residential building.

In the past, Hang Ruoi Street was renowned for selling rươi, a seasonal delicacy that was harvested during two periods each year: the beginning of May and the end of September according to the lunar calendar. The tradition of selling rươi was so integral to the street’s identity that even today, during these brief periods, visitors can hear the distinctive calls of vendors selling this rare delicacy. The phrase "Tháng chín đò mưới, tháng mưới mang năm" encapsulates the seasonal nature of rươi, highlighting its importance in Vietnamese culinary culture.

Today, Hang Ruoi Street no longer primarily sells rươi but has transformed into a bustling center for floral crafts. Over two-thirds of the shops along the street now sell various types of artificial flowers, made from materials like plastic and nylon, offering a range of colors and styles. These flowers are often arranged in intricate designs, creating a visually appealing display that attracts both locals and tourists. Many shops also offer workshops where visitors can learn the art of flower arrangement, adding an educational dimension to the shopping experience.

The atmosphere of Hang Ruoi Street is particularly festive during the Lunar New Year celebrations, when the entire street transforms into a sea of red and gold decorations. As early as December, the shops begin to decorate their storefronts with vibrant red and golden hues, hanging strings of lanterns, paper chains, and other festive ornaments. This creates a warm and welcoming ambiance that invites visitors to explore the street and immerse themselves in the holiday spirit.

Visitors to Hang Ruoi Street will find a variety of attractions and activities. The street is lined with boutique shops selling unique handicrafts, including Hoa La Phuong Linh at number 10, Hoa La Ha Phuong, and Hoa La Chuoc An, among others. These shops not only sell beautiful artificial flowers but also offer a glimpse into the local craft traditions and the creativity of the artisans who create them. Additionally, there are several cafes and hair salons that cater to the needs of shoppers and visitors, providing a comfortable space to rest and enjoy a cup of coffee or a haircut.

The street’s architecture reflects its historical significance, with many buildings dating back to the colonial period. One notable structure is the house at number 4, which served as the residence of Tran Phu, a prominent figure in Vietnamese history, during his tenure as the head of the Central Committee of the Communist Youth Union. Although he later moved to number 90 on Thanh Nhuom Street, the house remains an important landmark, symbolizing the intersection of political and cultural life in Hanoi.

Surrounded by other historic streets such as Dao Duy Tu, Cau Go, and Ca Tho, Hang Ruoi Street forms part of a larger network of narrow, winding lanes that make up the heart of Hanoi’s Old Quarter. Each street offers its own unique character and charm, contributing to the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s urban landscape. Visitors can wander through these streets, exploring the myriad of shops, cafes, and cultural sites, immersing themselves in the city’s rich heritage and contemporary vibrancy.

In summary, Hang Ruoi Street is a fascinating destination that combines historical significance with modern commercial activity. Its transformation from a street dedicated to the sale of rươi to a vibrant center for floral crafts showcases the adaptability and resilience of Hanoi’s community. Whether you are interested in learning about the city’s culinary traditions, admiring the intricate designs of artificial flowers, or simply enjoying the lively atmosphere, Hang Ruoi Street offers a memorable experience that captures the essence of Hanoi’s dynamic culture.

Hang Ruoi Street, formerly known as Rue des Vers Blancs during the French colonial era, is a historic street located in the heart of Hanoi, Vietnam. The street's name is derived from its past as a bustling market for rươi, a rare and highly prized delicacy found only in the northern region of Vietnam. This unique culinary specialty has given Hang Ruoi Street its distinctive identity and cultural significance, making it a must-visit destination for food enthusiasts and tourists alike.

The origins of Hang Ruoi Street date back to the time when the area was a river port on the To Lich River. Every year, during the ninth month of the lunar calendar, people from nearby provinces such as Thai Binh, Hai Duong, Hai Phong, and Nam Dinh would converge here to sell and buy rươi, giving rise to the name "Hang Ruoi." Under French rule, the street was officially named Rue des Vers Blancs, which translates to "Street of White Worms," reflecting the local dialect term for rươi. In 1945, after the establishment of the Vietnamese government, the street was officially renamed Hang Ruoi Street.

One of the most significant landmarks on Hang Ruoi Street is the house numbered 4, which served as the headquarters for the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam from 1929 to 1930. This site holds immense historical importance as it was where Tran Phu, the first General Secretary of the Party, worked diligently to draft the first Political Platform of the Party. This historical legacy adds a layer of cultural richness to the street, making it not just a culinary destination but also a place of historical significance.

The annual appearance of rươi coincides with the ninth month of the lunar calendar, specifically around the 20th of September and the 5th of October. During this brief period, the street transforms into a vibrant hub of activity, attracting numerous visitors eager to experience the unique flavors of rươi. Despite its short availability, rươi is considered a delicacy that embodies the distinct culinary traditions of Northern Vietnam. Unlike elaborate dishes like nem công chả phượng (pheasant meat rolls), rươi offers a simple yet unforgettable taste that few have had the pleasure of enjoying.

Today, Hang Ruoi Street is home to several restaurants that specialize in preparing various dishes made from rươi. These include chả rươi (rươi sausage), rươi hấp (steamed rươi), rươi xào (stir-fried rươi), rươi nấu (cooked rươi), nem rươi (rươi spring rolls), rươi kho (braised rươi), and rươi rang (fried rươi). Each dish showcases the versatility and richness of rươi, contributing to the street's reputation as a culinary haven. Scientific studies have recognized rươi as a nutritious food source, rich in protein and safe for consumption, further enhancing its appeal among food lovers.

While Hang Ruoi Street no longer functions primarily as a market for rươi, it has evolved into a dynamic commercial center with a diverse range of businesses. Many of the original households that once sold rươi have transitioned to other trades to increase their income. Today, the street is renowned for its floriculture, adding a touch of beauty to the bustling city of Hanoi. The vibrant colors of flowers and the aromatic scents fill the air, creating a serene atmosphere that contrasts with the hustle and bustle of urban life.

During the Mid-Autumn Festival, Hang Ruoi Street becomes one of the three designated locations in Hanoi for organizing lantern festivals for children. About a month before the full moon in August, the street is adorned with colorful decorations, drawing hundreds of children each night to purchase traditional toys such as paper lanterns, masks, and spinning tops. This festive atmosphere not only brings joy to the young but also enriches the cultural tapestry of the street.

As the Lunar New Year approaches, Hang Ruoi Street begins to prepare for the celebrations early, typically starting in December. The shops along the street are festively decorated with red and gold hues, symbolizing good fortune and prosperity. Decorations such as golden coins, couplets, flower garlands, lanterns, and potted plants adorn the storefronts, creating a lively and festive ambiance that sets the tone for the upcoming holiday season.

Throughout the year, Hang Ruoi Street remains a vibrant part of Hanoi's cultural landscape. Its historical significance, combined with its current role in promoting floriculture and hosting cultural events, makes it a unique destination for visitors. Whether one comes to savor the rare delicacy of rươi, admire the beautiful floral arrangements, or participate in traditional festivals, Hang Ruoi Street offers a rich and immersive experience that reflects the enduring charm and cultural heritage of Hanoi.

description: Hidden amidst the bustling rhythm of the thirty-six streets, Hàng Thiếc emerges like a lively metal symphony right in the heart of Hanoi's Old Quarter. Tracing back history to the fifteenth century, skilled artisans from Phú Thứ tin casting village brought their traditional craft to the imperial capital to establish their livelihood. From crafting incense burners and candle holders offered to sacred places, they gradually shifted to shaping and welding tinplate and galvanized iron, and the name Hàng Thiếc thus deeply rooted itself in the consciousness of the people of Tràng An. The breath of life in this place carries a distinctive, unmistakable working atmosphere. Tourists and locals strolling through here are always captivated by the rhythmic clinking sound of hammers, engrossed in watching artisans deftly shaping shiny sheets of corrugated iron into buckets, basins, or household items. Especially during Mid-Autumn Festival, the street becomes even more bustling and lively as crowds flock to buy handmade molds for baked mooncakes and sticky mooncakes. Standing amidst that sound-filled space, one's heart is suddenly filled with admiration mixed with nostalgia. The experience of listening to the rustic street symphony brings a deep sense of connection, helping everyone fully understand the enduring craftsmanship of a thousand-year-old craft street in Thăng Long.

During the Mid-Autumn Festival, the street becomes even more bustling and lively as crowds flock to buy handmade molds for baked mooncakes and sticky mooncakes. As one stands amidst the sound-filled space, one's heart is suddenly filled with admiration mixed with nostalgia, a testament to the street's enduring cultural significance.

Nestled within the vibrant heart of Hanoi’s Old Quarter, Hang Thiec Street, also known as Phố Hàng Thiếc, stands as a testament to the enduring legacy of traditional craftsmanship. Emerging from the bustling tapestry of the thirty-six streets, this narrow thoroughfare has been a hub of metalworking since the fifteenth century. Originating from the skilled artisans of Phú Thứ tin casting village, who brought their traditional craft to the imperial capital of Thăng Long to establish their livelihood, Hang Thiec Street has become synonymous with the intricate art of tin and metalwork.

The street’s historical roots trace back to the mid-15th century when artisans from Phú Thứ began crafting incense burners and candle holders for religious offerings. Over time, these craftsmen shifted their focus to shaping and welding tinplate and galvanized iron, giving rise to the name Hang Thiếc, which translates to Tinware Street. This shift marked the beginning of a long-standing tradition that continues to thrive today, deeply embedded in the cultural consciousness of the people of Tràng An.

Visually, Hang Thiec Street is characterized by its narrow, straight path flanked by rows of倾斜的窄巷房屋（nhà ống），这些房屋之间悬挂着各种金属制品，如桶、盆和金属月饼模具。这些闪闪发光的银灰色锡片和铁板与岁月的尘埃交织在一起，构成了独特的视觉特征。街道上布满了错综复杂的电线网络，狭窄的人行道上总是挤满了来往的人流和车辆。

Hang Thiec Street not only serves as a center for metalworking but also holds significant cultural and historical importance. The rhythmic sounds of hammering and bending metal sheets create a distinctive atmosphere that draws both tourists and locals alike. Visitors are often captivated by the sight of artisans deftly transforming sheets of corrugated iron into functional household items, such as buckets and basins. During the Mid-Autumn Festival, the street transforms into a hive of activity as people flock to purchase handmade molds for baking mooncakes, adding a festive touch to the already bustling scene.

This vibrant street symphony, a blend of traditional craftsmanship and modern hustle, offers a glimpse into the rich heritage of Hanoi. It stands as a living museum, preserving the skills and traditions of generations past, and continues to be a vital part of the city’s cultural landscape.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Thiec Street
documents.content:
Hang Thiec Street is an ancient street located within Hang Gai ward, Hoan Kiem district, in the city of Hanoi. It is one of the few remaining historic streets in Hanoi that still preserves both the sounds and the traditional craft of metalworking. In the past, the name of the street originated from its role as a center for handmade tin and lead casting, serving the daily needs and spiritual requirements of the residents of the imperial capital.

Historically, the origins and settlers of Hang Thiec Street can be traced back to the village of Dan Hoi (formerly part of Ha Dong). According to the genealogies of long-standing families like the Tran clan, the founder of the tin-crafting profession was granted the title of "Tich cuc truong," or head of the Tin Management Bureau, by the royal court during the Le dynasty. Over time, artisans from nearby villages known for their metalwork, such as Phu Thu (now part of Hoai Duc), Thuan Tien, and Bac Ninh, migrated to Hang Thiec Street to establish their businesses, making it a bustling center for manufacturing household goods.

As time progressed, the materials used in the production shifted. Initially, all products were made from tin casting, primarily items associated with religious rituals and daily life, such as incense burners, candles, oil lamps, tea kettles, tea bags, and hat tips. By the mid-20th century, when pure tin products no longer had a large market, the craftsmen of Hang Thiec Street quickly adapted. They began recycling iron containers brought by the French, transforming them into washbasins, water scoops, and clothing chests. Despite changes in materials over time—from tin to iron, zinc, and now stainless steel—the traditional craft of handcrafted metalworking has remained intact.

The name of Hang Thiec Street has become deeply ingrained in the folk consciousness through classic folk songs about the streets of Hanoi:
"Let's play around Long City,
Thirty-six streets clearly named without error.
Street of Willow, Street of Silver, Street of Reed,
Sailor Street, Tin Street, Sandal Street, Tray Street..."

During the colonial period, the French authorities respected the local production identity and named the street Rue des Ferblantiers, meaning "Street of Tin Workers." In 1945, the then Governor of Hanoi, Tran Van Lai, officially restored the original Vietnamese name, Hang Thiec Street, which has been maintained until today.

Today, Hang Thiec Street retains a unique vibrancy within the old quarter. The most distinctive feature is the characteristic sound of hammering and clinking from small workshops along the street, creating a lively artisanal atmosphere amidst modern urban life.

Hang Thiec Street, a narrow lane nestled within the heart of Hanoi, is a testament to the enduring traditions of Vietnamese craftsmanship. This historic street, known for its centuries-old trade in metalwork, stretches over a length of 136 meters, starting from the bustling intersection of Bat Dan and Thuoc Bac streets, and ending at the junction of Hang Thiếc and Hang Nón streets, located in the Phuong Hang Gai district of Hoan Kiem, Hanoi. The origins of this street date back to the time when it was part of the village of Yen Noi, situated in the former district of Tien Tuc, Tho Xuan.

In the past, Hang Thiếc Street was renowned for its traditional craft of casting tin to produce household items such as incense burners, tea kettles, and trays. These products were highly esteemed and represented the pinnacle of local craftsmanship. However, by the mid-20th century, the demand for tinware had diminished, leading artisans to adapt their skills to work with iron goods brought by the French. Items like oil cans were transformed into washbasins, ladles, and water carriers, earning the street the French name Rue des Ferblanties, or "Street of Tin Workers." Despite this, the locals continued to call it Hang Thiếc, preserving its original identity.

Over time, the craftsmen of Hang Thiếc expanded their repertoire to include products made from zinc and steel, creating durable household items that were both functional and aesthetically pleasing. In recent years, many shops have begun selling modern materials like stainless steel, catering to contemporary needs while maintaining the essence of traditional craftsmanship. The period between the 1930s and 1940s marked the golden age of Hang Thiếc, where not only metalworking but also glass and mirror crafting flourished. The small street was a hive of activity, with workshops and stores operating side by side, contributing to a vibrant atmosphere that continues to attract visitors today.

Despite the challenges posed by modern plastic goods, which have impacted the traditional metalwork industry, Hang Thiếc remains resilient, continuing to thrive with its unique blend of old-world charm and modern adaptation. Today, the street no longer boasts many ancient houses, with only a few remnants like number 20 still standing as a reminder of its storied past. Most of the establishments are small family-run businesses, where the art of metalworking is passed down through generations. The production process is labor-intensive, relying more on the skillful hands of the artisans than on capital investment. 

Electric tools have replaced the traditional furnaces once used by the craftsmen, allowing them to maintain efficiency while preserving the quality of their work. Each house serves as both a workshop and a storefront, where women often participate in the demanding tasks alongside men. Within the confined spaces of these workshops, artisans diligently create a variety of products, from traditional tinware to modern stainless steel items. Visitors can witness the entire production process, from raw material preparation to the final product, offering a glimpse into the intricate world of Vietnamese metalwork.

Visitors to Hang Thiếc Street can explore a range of products, from handcrafted tinware to contemporary stainless steel goods. The artisans are also available for custom orders and installation services, providing a personalized touch to their offerings. Foreign tourists often find themselves captivated by the unique items on display, such as antique tin tea kettles or modern stainless steel kitchen utensils. The atmosphere of Hang Thiếc Street is one of timeless tradition interwoven with modern innovation, making it a must-visit destination for those interested in the rich cultural heritage of Hanoi.

Hang Thiec Street, a narrow lane nestled within the historic district of Old Quarter in Hanoi, is a testament to the city's rich cultural heritage and traditional crafts. This quaint street, stretching for 136 meters from the intersection of Bat Dan and Thuoc Bac streets to the junction of Hang Thiec and Hang Non, has maintained its identity as a hub for metalwork and tinware production, standing out among the many other streets that have lost their original trades over time.

The origins of Hang Thiec Street date back to a period when Hanoi was bustling with skilled artisans who migrated from various regions, bringing with them their families and establishing communities that eventually formed distinct neighborhoods or "pho" (streets). The presence of numerous streets named with the prefix "Hang," such as Hang Thiec, indicates that Hanoi was once a vibrant city filled with specialized craft villages. Over centuries, these artisanal communities thrived, each specializing in different crafts, contributing to the city’s economic and cultural vitality.

Hang Thiec Street specifically gained prominence due to its specialization in tinware crafting, particularly in producing household items like incense burners, tea kettles, and tea trays. These products were not only functional but also held significant cultural value, reflecting the artistic skills and traditions of the local craftsmen. As time progressed, the artisans of Hang Thiec expanded their repertoire to include items made from zinc and steel, creating durable and aesthetically pleasing household goods that continue to attract customers seeking quality and reliability.

One of the most distinctive products associated with Hang Thiec Street is the toy boats, which evoke fond memories of childhood for many Hanoians. These miniature vessels, crafted with meticulous care, serve as cherished souvenirs and toys, embodying the ingenuity and creativity of the local artisans. In addition to these charming toys, the street is renowned for its range of metal goods, including those made from tin, stainless steel, and iron, catering to both practical needs and decorative purposes.

Despite the modernization of Hanoi, Hang Thiec Street remains a vital part of the city’s cultural landscape, preserving the legacy of traditional craftsmanship. The cultural significance of Hang Thiec Street extends beyond its commercial activities, serving as a living museum where visitors can witness the intricate processes involved in crafting tinware and metal goods. Each piece produced here carries the imprint of the artisan’s hand, reflecting the dedication and artistry that have been passed down through the years. For tourists and locals alike, a visit to Hang Thiec Street offers a glimpse into the enduring traditions of Hanoi, where the past seamlessly blends with the present, creating a unique tapestry of history and contemporary life.

Nestled within the heart of Hanoi’s historic Old Quarter, Hang Thung Street stretches like a bridge connecting the bustling Red River dike bank to the vibrant core of the city. This narrow thoroughfare, known in Vietnamese as Phố Hàng Thùng, is a testament to the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s cultural heritage, blending ancient traditions with modern vibrancy. Historically, the street was a hub for skilled carpenters who specialized in crafting wooden barrels, tubs, and bathtubs, essential items for the daily life of the imperial capital during the Ly and Tran dynasties. The name “Hang Thung” itself, meaning “Street of Barrels,” was coined from the resonant sounds of sawing and chiseling that once echoed through the area, a sonic signature of the carpentry trade.

Though the days of bustling carpentry workshops have largely faded into memory, Hang Thung Street now thrives as a culinary haven, its vibrant nightlife drawing locals and tourists alike. As evening descends, the street transforms into a lively market where seafood stalls and steaming plates of boiled snails spill out onto the sidewalks, creating a festive atmosphere that permeates the air. The juxtaposition of moss-covered houses with the bright neon lights and colorful plastic tables and chairs adds a unique charm to the scene, making it a popular destination for those seeking a taste of authentic Hanoi street food.

The architectural landscape of Hang Thung Street is characterized by the iconic nhà ống, or tube houses, which line both sides of the street. These narrow, elongated structures, often painted in a faded yellow hue, reflect the traditional Vietnamese urban design. Adjacent to the main road leading to the winding Red River dike, the street is shaded by a canopy of trees, providing a cool respite from the summer heat. This natural cover, combined with the vibrant street life, creates a serene yet energetic ambiance that captivates visitors.

Culturally, Hang Thung Street serves as a microcosm of Hanoi’s enduring spirit, where the past and present coexist harmoniously. The street’s transformation from a center of carpentry to a culinary hotspot symbolizes the dynamic nature of Hanoi’s evolution. For tourists, exploring Hang Thung Street offers not only a feast for the palate but also a profound understanding of the city’s historical continuity and cultural richness. As one wanders through the narrow lanes, the sights, sounds, and flavors of the street evoke a deep sense of connection to the thousand-year-old legacy of Thang Long, now known as Hanoi, a city that continues to thrive with a blend of tradition and contemporary life.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Hang Thung Street
documents.content:
Hang Thung Street is located within the districts of Ly Thai To and Hang Bac in Hoan Kiem District, Hanoi. The street stretches approximately 216 meters in length and is 8 meters wide, running from Tran Quang Khai Street to its intersection with Hang Be Street (which continues to Cau Go Street), crossing through Hang Tre and Nguyen Huu Huan streets.

In the past, the name of the street originated from its role as the center for producing and selling wooden and bamboo barrels used to store fish sauce or water for daily use during an era when the city lacked a piped water supply system. Historically, this area was part of the village of So Trang (eastern half) and Dong Yen (western half), both belonging to the Tả Túc commune (later renamed to Hòu Túc), in the old Thọ Xương district. By the mid-19th century, So Trang merged with Tả Lâu to form Trang Lâu village. Remnants of this ancient area are still preserved in the Trang Lauer Temple at number 33 on the street. The Dong Yen Communal House, which once stood opposite the Trang Lauer Temple across Nguyen Huu Huan Street, was dismantled around 1970.

Due to its strategic location near the Dong Yen gate, leading directly to the Red River port, barges carrying logs and bamboo rafts from upstream regions such as Phu Tho and Tuyen Quang would dock here. The abundant and inexpensive local raw materials facilitated the thriving craft of making wooden barrels. Craftsmen in the area specialized in splitting wood from banyan and persimmon trees to construct barrels, then sealing them with tung oil to prevent leaks.

During the colonial period, the street was divided into two segments with different commercial characteristics and names:

The eastern segment, from Tran Nhut Duct Street to Nguyen Huu Huan Street, was called Phuc Chau Street (Rue Fou-tchéou) until 1919, when it was renamed Rongdoni Street (Rue Rondony). This section primarily housed large timber warehouses that imported logs, planks, and coffins.

The western segment, from Nguyen Huu Huan Street to Hang Be Street, was officially named Rue des Sceaux (Street of Barrels) by the colonial authorities, reflecting the local name "Hang Thung."

After the success of the August Revolution in 1945, the Viet Minh government renamed Rongdoni Street to Binh Chuan Street, after a feudal official responsible for foreign trade. By the end of 1945, the two segments were officially merged and reverted to the original Vietnamese name, Hang Thung Street. This name has remained unchanged throughout subsequent adjustments to the street's designation until today.

Hang Thung Street, a historic thoroughfare in the heart of Hanoi, stretches from Tran Nhat Duat Street to Hang Be Street, encompassing what was once the land of the villages of So Trang and Dong Yen. By the mid-19th century, these two villages merged into one, known as Trang Luan. The temple and shrine of the village of Ta Lau now reside on Pho Lo Su, while those of So Trang are located at number 33 Hang Thung. Despite this, both are collectively referred to as the Trang Luan Temple and Shrine. The temple of Dong Yen faces the Trang Luan Temple across Nguyen Huu Huan Street, serving as both house number 35 Hang Thung and house number 94 Nguyen Huu Huan, dedicated to Uy Linh Lang. This temple was demolished in 1970.

Historically, Hang Thung Street was renowned for its production and sale of various types of barrels made from bamboo and rattan, or wooden barrels coated with lacquer. During the French colonial period, the street was divided into two sections: from Tran Nhat Duat to Nguyen Huu Huan Street was called Phuc Chau (Fou-tchéou) Street, later renamed Rondony Street. This area was home to numerous wood shops, where carpentry flourished, leading many merchants to amass wealth quickly. The wood trade expanded into the inner part of the street, beyond the original gate. Besides planks and boards, artisans crafted finished wooden products such as beds, wardrobes, tables, chairs, and food storage cabinets, even coffins. Wealthier residents renovated their old houses, constructing new ones that were taller, wider, and more aesthetically pleasing.

The remaining portion of the street, from Nguyen Huu Huan to Hang Be, was known as Hang Thung Street (Rue des Sceaux). After August 1945, both segments were combined under the name Phuc Chuan Street. In 1947, the Vietnamese government unified the two streets, reverting to the name Hang Thung, which it retains to this day.

At number 22 Hang Thung Street stands the Tho Nam Shrine, a spiritual hub for the local community. In 2008, artist Vu Van Thao's sculpture "Ancient House No. 13 Hang Thung Street" was among the top ten works in the APB Foundation Signature Art Prize for Asia-Pacific.

Like other streets in the ancient quarter of Hanoi, Hang Thung Street's name reflects its historical specialization in producing and selling barrels. These barrels were used for carrying water or storing fish sauce. On the eastern side of Hang Thung Street, now known as Rondony Street, many families operated wood shops and sold household goods made of wood. The carpentry industry thrived, contributing significantly to the prosperity of the residents. Old, low houses were transformed into newer, larger, and more beautiful structures.

Over time, the number of households engaged in barrel-making has dwindled, and today, no one continues this traditional craft. However, the enterprising residents have adapted by diversifying their businesses to align with contemporary trends. Today, Hang Thung Street is bustling with various commercial activities, including restaurants, grocery stores, and fashion boutiques. Notably, Madame Hong's nem tai shop at number 37 Hang Thung Street has become a beloved fixture for locals and visitors alike, preserving the unique flavors and traditions of the past.

Visitors to Hang Thung Street can immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s history and culture. The street’s architecture, with its mix of old and new buildings, offers a glimpse into the evolution of urban life in Vietnam. The Tho Nam Shrine, with its serene atmosphere, provides a tranquil space for reflection and worship. The vibrant energy of the street, filled with the sounds of bustling commerce and the aromas of traditional cuisine, creates a memorable experience for tourists and locals alike.

Hang Thung Street, located in Hoan Kiem District of Hanoi, is a historic thoroughfare that stretches for 216 meters and is 8 meters wide. It runs from Tran Quang Khai Street to Hang Be Street, which connects with Cau Go Street, intersecting with Hang Tre Street and Nguyen Huu Huan Street. This street has a rich history dating back to the time when it was part of two separate villages, Sotrang and Dongyen, both belonging to the old Tatha district of Tho Xuong county. By the mid-19th century, these two villages merged into one, known as Tranglau, with their respective communal houses and temples still standing today.

During the French colonial period, Hang Thung Street was divided into two sections. The segment from Tran Nhut Duct Street to Nguyen Huu Huan Street was called Phuc Chau Street, later renamed Rondonny Street in 1919. The remaining portion retained its original name, Hang Thung Street, also known as Rue des Sceaux. After the revolution, Rondonny Street was renamed Binh Chuan Street, named after a former official responsible for foreign trade affairs. In 1945, the two streets were combined into one, retaining the name Hang Thung Street, which has remained unchanged since then.

Today, Hang Thung Street falls under the jurisdiction of Ly Thai To and Hang Bac wards in Hoan Kiem District. The street's cultural significance is evident in its historical landmarks, such as the communal house and temple of Tranglau village, located at number 33 on Hang Thung Street, though its main entrance faces Nguyen Huu Huan Street at number 77. Similarly, the communal house of Dongyen village, dedicated to the legendary hero Uy Linh Lang, stands at the intersection of Hang Thung and Nguyen Huu Huan Streets, specifically at number 35 Hang Thung Street and number 94 Nguyen Huu Huan Street. This structure was demolished around 1970, but its legacy remains deeply embedded in the local culture.

The origins of the street's name are rooted in the traditional crafts practiced here. Historically, this area was home to numerous workshops producing various types of wooden containers, such as water buckets and jars used for storing fish sauce. These products were made using bamboo and rattan, as well as wood joined with traditional lacquer, giving rise to the name "Hang Thung," meaning "Street of Buckets." The eastern end of the street was primarily occupied by timber merchants who sold planks and logs, while the junction with Hang Tre Street was a bustling market for bamboo and rattan products, known as the Hang Be Market.

The street's layout and architecture reflect its historical importance. It was once enclosed within the ancient walls of the Thang Long Citadel, with a gate called Dongyen Gate situated where Hang Thung Street meets Nguyen Huu Huan Street. This gate marked the eastern boundary of the citadel, and the area around it was a hub for artisans and traders involved in the production and sale of wooden containers and other goods. The preservation of these traditional crafts and the historical significance of the street make it a unique destination for visitors interested in the cultural heritage of Hanoi.

Visitors to Hang Thung Street can immerse themselves in the rich tapestry of Hanoi’s past, exploring the narrow lanes lined with old houses and shops that continue to carry on traditional crafts and trades. The atmosphere is one of quiet dignity, with the sounds of hammering and crafting echoing through the streets, reminiscent of the bustling activity of centuries past. The street's cultural significance extends beyond its physical presence, embodying the spirit of resilience and continuity that defines Hanoi's identity.

description: Lying along the windy dike road of the Red River, Hàng Tre street emerges as a bustling junction on the edge of Hanoi's Old Quarter. Going back in time, this alluvial plain was originally a bustling docking point for rafts of bamboo, luong, and nua from the upstream regions, flowing downstream to supply building materials for the entire imperial city. The rustic name Hàng Tre was born from that bustling, riverine trade scene, encapsulating memories of a time that was arduous yet prosperous. Nowadays, even though the bamboo rafts have completely faded into the past, the pace of life here still pulsates with energy, with a series of restaurants and eateries packed closely together. Locals and tourists often come here to gather, chatting lively over a cold beer or enjoying diverse culinary flavors when night falls. Lost amidst that vibrant pulse, one's heart is suddenly filled with a wistful feeling intertwined with wonderful relaxation. The experience of breathing in the cool, misty air from the river surface, mixed with the hustle and bustle, helps each person fully understand the subtle, ever-changing charm of the thousand-year-old Thăng Long.
description_vi: Nằm chạy dọc theo trục đường đê sông Hồng lộng gió, phố Hàng Tre hiện lên như một nốt giao thoa nhộn nhịp nơi rìa khu ba mươi sáu phố phường Hà Nội. Ngược dòng thời gian về thuở trước, bãi bồi nơi đây vốn là bến đỗ tấp nập của những bè tre, luồng, nứa từ miền ngược theo dòng nước xuôi về cung cấp vật liệu xây dựng cho cả kinh thành. Cái tên Hàng Tre mộc mạc ra đời từ chính cảnh tượng giao thương tấp nập mang đậm hơi thở sông nước ấy, gói trọn ký ức về một thời nhọc nhằn mà trù phú. Ngày nay, dẫu những bè tre đã hoàn toàn lùi vào dĩ vãng, nhịp sống nơi đây vẫn cuồn cuộn sức nóng với hàng loạt nhà hàng, quán ăn san sát. Người dân và du khách thường xuyên tìm đến tụ tập, rôm rả chuyện trò bên ly bia mát lạnh hay thưởng thức phong vị ẩm thực đa dạng khi màn đêm buông xuống. Lạc bước giữa nhịp đập phồn hoa ấy, lòng ta bỗng trào dâng một cảm giác bâng khuâng đan xen sự thư thái tuyệt vời. Trải nghiệm hít thở bầu không khí mang chút hơi sương mát lành từ mặt sông xen lẫn sự náo nhiệt giúp mỗi người thấu hiểu trọn vẹn nét duyên ngầm chuyển mình không ngừng của chốn Thăng Long ngàn năm.
