Located near the picturesque Hoàn Kiếm Lake, this bronze masterpiece is crafted from pure copper, its surface developing a distinctive dark blue-green patina over time, adding to its regal appearance.

The statue depicts King Lý Thái Tổ standing gallantly, his right hand firmly grasping the scroll of the historic Chiếu dời đô edict, which he issued in 1010. According to legend, upon arriving at the site of what would become Hanoi, Lý Thái Tổ witnessed a golden dragon ascending from the Red River, prompting him to rename the city Đại La to Thăng Long, marking the beginning of a new era of prosperity and glory for the nation. This significant event is immortalized in the statue, serving as a powerful reminder of the king's visionary leadership.

Surrounded by a spacious stone-paved square, the statue is enveloped by cool green canopies that provide shade and a serene atmosphere. The area around the statue is a vibrant cultural hub, attracting locals and tourists alike. Early mornings and late afternoons see the square bustling with activity as people gather to exercise, roller skate, or simply stroll and enjoy the tranquil ambiance. On weekends and during Tết holidays, the space transforms into a lively venue for music stages and street festivals, blending traditional festivities with contemporary entertainment.

The Ly Thai To statue is more than just a historical landmark; it is a symbol of Hanoi's enduring spirit and cultural heritage. Its presence serves as a poignant reminder of the city's rich past while seamlessly integrating into the dynamic fabric of modern life. Visitors are often moved by the heroic vitality that seems to emanate from the statue, creating a profound connection between the millennium-old legacy and the vibrant energy of today's Hanoi.

Located in the Ly Thai To Garden, formerly known as Chi Linh Park, this iconic statue is situated along the bustling street of Dinh Tien Hoang, offering visitors a glimpse into the rich cultural heritage of Vietnam. The statue was inaugurated on October 7, 2004, marking a significant milestone in the city's cultural landscape, particularly as part of the celebrations for the 50th anniversary of Hanoi's liberation and in anticipation of the millennium anniversary of Thang Long-Hanoi in 2010.

The construction of the statue began on August 17, 2004, under the guidance of sculptor Vi Thi Hoa, a member of the Vietnam Fine Arts Association. The statue is crafted from solid bronze, weighing a total of 34 tons, with the figure itself weighing 14 tons and its base 20 tons. Standing at a height of 10.10 meters, the statue's dimensions symbolize the year 1010, the founding year of Thang Long, now known as Hanoi. This intricate design not only pays homage to the king but also serves as a testament to the enduring legacy he left behind.

The statue's creation process involved a rigorous selection process initiated by the Hanoi Department of Culture and Information in February 2003. From the initial 29 conceptual designs, the final choice was made after two rounds of evaluation and debate. The winning design, created by Vi Thi Hoa, was chosen for its artistic merit and its strategic placement within the garden, overlooking the serene waters of Hoan Kiem Lake. The statue's positioning reflects the historical significance of the site, aligning perfectly with the cultural and geographical importance of the area.

The statue is mounted on a base shaped like an octagon, representing the eight cardinal directions, and is elevated above four gates that mirror those of the ancient Hanoi Citadel. The base is further adorned with three tiers of steps, each layer signifying heaven, earth, and humanity, reflecting the tripartite harmony that guided King Ly Thai To's decision-making process.

Ngoc Son Temple is one of Hanoi's prominent historical and cultural relics, often simply called Ngoc Son Temple, distinguished by its unique location right in the middle of Hoan Kiem Lake. The temple was built in the 19th century, on the site of an ancient pagoda, and has undergone renovations through many periods, especially during the Nguyen Dynasty.
The temple worships Tran Hung Dao – a national hero famous for his victories against the Yuan-Mongol invaders, along with other civil gods and martial gods, embodying a harmonious blend of patriotism and the Vietnamese tradition of valuing education. Therefore, it is not only a tourist attraction but also a spiritual space where locals and visitors come to pray for peace, luck, and success in their studies and careers.
Throughout its long history, Ngoc Son Temple has always been intertwined with the cultural life of Hanoians and is an important destination during major festivals, especially the Lunar New Year, when crowds flock here to offer incense and pay homage.
An interesting detail that impresses many visitors is that the temple once displayed the specimen of a giant turtle from Hoan Kiem Lake, linked to the sacred legend of King Le Loi returning his magic sword. This further enhances the temple's mystical appeal, making each visit not just a journey of architectural discovery but also an entry into the world of Vietnamese history and legends.

description_vi:
Đền Ngọc Sơn là một trong những di tích lịch sử và văn hóa tiêu biểu của Hà Nội, thường được gọi ngắn gọn là đền Ngọc Sơn, nổi bật với vị trí độc đáo ngay giữa Hồ Hoàn Kiếm. Ngôi đền được xây dựng từ thế kỷ 19, trên nền một ngôi chùa cổ, và đã được tu sửa qua nhiều giai đoạn, đặc biệt dưới thời nhà Nguyễn.
Ngôi đền thờ Trần Hưng Đạo – vị anh hùng dân tộc nổi tiếng với chiến công chống quân Nguyên Mông, cùng với các vị thần văn và thần võ khác, thể hiện sự kết hợp hài hòa giữa tinh thần yêu nước và truyền thống hiếu học của người Việt. Chính vì vậy, nơi đây không chỉ là điểm tham quan mà còn là không gian tâm linh, nơi người dân và du khách đến cầu bình an, may mắn và thành công trong học tập, sự nghiệp.
Trong suốt chiều dài lịch sử, đền Ngọc Sơn luôn gắn liền với đời sống văn hóa của người Hà Nội và là điểm đến quan trọng trong các dịp lễ lớn, đặc biệt là Tết Nguyên Đán, khi dòng người đổ về đây để dâng hương và chiêm bái.
Một chi tiết thú vị khiến nhiều du khách ấn tượng là bên trong đền từng trưng bày tiêu bản của một cá thể rùa khổng lồ từ Hồ Hoàn Kiếm, gắn liền với truyền thuyết linh thiêng về việc vua Lê Lợi trả gươm thần. Điều này càng làm tăng thêm sức hấp dẫn huyền bí cho ngôi đền, khiến mỗi chuyến ghé thăm không chỉ là một hành trình khám phá kiến trúc mà còn là bước vào thế giới của lịch sử và truyền thuyết Việt Nam.

Ngoc Son Temple, also known as Đền Ngọc Sơn, is situated on an islet in Hoàn Kiếm Lake in the heart of Hanoi, Vietnam. The temple's origins trace back to the early 19th century when it was initially established to honor the "Three Sages": Wenchang Dijun, Guan Yu, and Lü Dongbin. Over time, the revered national hero Trần Hưng Đạo was added to the pantheon of figures worshipped within its walls.

Visitors approaching the temple from the shore cross the iconic Thê Húc Bridge, which connects the mainland to the islet where Ngoc Son Temple stands. The temple complex includes several significant structures, each imbued with symbolic importance. Among these are the Tháp Bút, or "Pen Tower," the Đài Nghiên, or "Ink-slab," the Đắc Nguyệt, or "Moon Contemplation Pavilion," and the Đình Trấn Ba, or "Pavilion Against Waves." These buildings collectively contribute to the rich cultural and historical tapestry of Ngoc Son Temple.

Ngoc Son Temple, a revered site nestled within the heart of Hanoi's historic Hoan Kiem Lake, stands as a testament to Vietnam’s rich cultural heritage and spiritual significance. The temple is part of a cluster of national treasures managed directly by the Hoan Kiem Lake and Ngoc Son Temple Heritage Management Board, alongside other significant landmarks that reflect the city’s revolutionary and historical importance. Situated on an island known as Ngoc Island, the temple is not only a place of worship but also a symbol of the enduring spirit of the Vietnamese people.

The origins of Hoan Kiem Lake date back to the 15th century when it was known as Lake Luc Thuong due to its year-round greenish hue. The lake’s current name, Hoan Kiem, translates to "Lake Returning the Sword," derived from a legendary tale involving King Le Loi and a divine turtle. According to folklore, King Le Loi received a magical sword from the Dragon King to defeat the Ming invaders. After his victory, he returned the sword to the Dragon King by throwing it into the lake, where a giant turtle emerged to retrieve it. This event gave rise to the lake’s alternative names, Hoan Kiem and Lake Gau, reflecting the mythical connection between the king and the sacred weapon.

The temple itself is a blend of historical reverence and architectural beauty. Its construction began around 1864 under the guidance of Nguyen Van Sieu, a patriotic scholar who undertook extensive renovations to restore and enhance the site. The temple complex now comprises several key structures, each contributing to its overall aesthetic and spiritual ambiance. The entrance to Ngoc Son Temple is marked by the Thap But (Pen Tower), a slender tower that symbolizes the pen used by scholars for writing examinations. Beyond this tower lies the Nghi Mon (Gate of Ceremonial Entry), which leads visitors through a series of courtyards and pavilions, including the Dai Nien (Inkstone Pavilion) and the Thay Huc Bridge, named for its poetic association with the morning sun.

The architecture of Ngoc Son Temple is a harmonious fusion of traditional Vietnamese elements and European influences. The Thap Rua (Turtle Tower) on nearby Turtle Island exemplifies this synthesis, featuring Gothic-style arched windows on its lower levels while maintaining a distinctly Vietnamese roofline. The temple’s layout includes various halls dedicated to different deities and historical figures, such as the Tran Hung Dao Shrine and the Quan Vu Shrine, both venerating legendary heroes of Vietnamese history. These shrines are complemented by smaller structures like the Truc Lam Pagoda and the Kinh Thu Hall, each serving unique religious and cultural functions.

Visitors to Ngoc Son Temple can immerse themselves in a serene atmosphere that combines natural beauty with spiritual tranquility. The temple grounds offer panoramic views of Hoan Kiem Lake, framed by lush vegetation and ancient trees. The lake’s surface mirrors the surrounding landscape, creating a picturesque scene that has captivated locals and tourists alike for centuries. The temple’s location within the bustling city center provides a stark contrast between urban life and spiritual retreat, making it a popular destination for those seeking solace and reflection amidst the vibrant energy of Hanoi.

The cultural significance of Ngoc Son Temple extends beyond its physical presence, embodying the values of education, patriotism, and spiritual devotion. It serves as a living museum, preserving the memory of Vietnam’s past while continuing to inspire future generations. The temple’s role in hosting educational activities and cultural events further underscores its importance as a hub of intellectual and spiritual growth. For visitors, the experience at Ngoc Son Temple is more than just a tour of historical sites; it is a journey into the soul of Vietnam, where every step and glance reveals layers of history, legend, and cultural continuity.

Inside the ancient space of Ngoc Son Temple, amidst the gentle ringing of bells and the tranquil surface of Ho Guom Lake, the activity of calligraphy has long become a cultural beauty that makes many people stay longer than intended. On early spring occasions or during Tet holidays, the area around the temple often features images of Ong Do in traditional ao dai, meticulously bending over their inkstones, each soft brushstroke appearing on red paper as if carrying the very breath of old Hanoi. The custom of xin chu originated from the spirit of studiousness and the belief that characters such as "Phuc," "Loc," "Tam," or "An" would convey good fortune and peace for the new year, thus this activity gradually became a familiar part of the cultural life around Hoan Kiem Lake.

Locals and tourists visiting the temple not only come to sightsee or pray for peace, but also enjoy standing silently watching each stroke of ink appear, chatting with the calligrapher, and taking home a piece of calligraphy as a spiritual gift. There is something very special when, amidst the bustling city center, one can still find a slow space where each character is written with patience and reverence. Perhaps for this reason, the experience of watching calligraphy at Ngoc Son Temple always leaves a feeling of tranquility, as if one has just touched a very deep layer of Hanoi's memories.

Calligraphy [is especially charming in] the early morning, on weekends, and in autumn. Calligraphy [reflects] the spiritual and artistic soul of Hanoi. Calligraphy [attracts] locals and tourists who ask for blessings and admire the tradition.
description_graph_vi: Viết thư pháp [diễn ra tại] đền Ngọc Sơn. Đền Ngọc Sơn [nằm bên] Hồ Hoàn Kiếm ở trung tâm quận Hoàn Kiếm. Viết thư pháp [có hình ảnh] các ông đồ trong áo dài truyền thống. Viết thư pháp [sử dụng] giấy đỏ hoặc giấy vàng, bút lông mềm, mực đen và nghiên mực. Hoạt động này [được bao quanh bởi] cây cổ thụ, mặt nước xanh của hồ và cầu Thê Húc. Viết thư pháp [đẹp nhất vào] sáng sớm, dịp cuối tuần và mùa thu. Viết thư pháp [thể hiện] tâm hồn nghệ thuật và chiều sâu văn hoá Hà Nội. Viết thư pháp [thu hút] người dân và du khách đến xin chữ, cầu may và thưởng thức nét đẹp truyền thống.
description_vi:
Bên trong không gian cổ kính của Đền Ngọc Sơn, giữa tiếng chuông khẽ vang và mặt nước hồ Gươm phẳng lặng, hoạt động viết thư pháp từ lâu đã trở thành một nét đẹp văn hóa khiến nhiều người dừng chân lâu hơn dự định. Vào những dịp đầu xuân hay lễ Tết, khu vực quanh đền thường xuất hiện hình ảnh các ông đồ trong áo dài truyền thống, chăm chú nghiêng mình bên nghiên mực, từng nét bút mềm mại hiện lên trên giấy đỏ như mang theo cả hơi thở của Hà Nội xưa. Tục xin chữ vốn bắt nguồn từ tinh thần hiếu học và niềm tin rằng những chữ như “Phúc”, “Lộc”, “Tâm” hay “An” sẽ gửi gắm may mắn, bình an cho năm mới, vì thế hoạt động này dần trở thành một phần quen thuộc trong đời sống văn hóa quanh hồ Hoàn Kiếm.

Người dân và du khách ghé đền không chỉ để tham quan hay cầu bình an, mà còn thích đứng lặng xem từng nét mực hiện ra, trò chuyện với người viết và mang về một bức thư pháp như món quà tinh thần. Có điều gì đó rất đặc biệt khi giữa trung tâm phố thị đông đúc, người ta vẫn có thể tìm thấy một khoảng chậm rãi nơi từng con chữ được viết bằng sự kiên nhẫn và lòng thành kính. Có lẽ vì thế, trải nghiệm xem viết thư pháp ở Đền Ngọc Sơn luôn để lại cảm giác thanh tĩnh, như vừa chạm tay vào một lớp ký ức rất sâu của Hà Nội.
name: Calligraphy
visual_cues: The calligraphy writing activity at Ngoc Son Temple is often depicted by a small wooden table holding red paper, a black inkstone, and long, soft brushes. The Ông đồ in traditional áo dài sit neatly under the eaves or in a small courtyard, with large calligraphic works written with crisp Chinese ink hung in front. The most recognizable feature is the red or yellow papers with flowing strokes distinctly in the Vietnamese calligraphy style. They are often surrounded by the shade of ancient trees, the green water of Hoan Kiem Lake, the vermilion The Huc Bridge, and the stream of leisurely passing tourists.

documents.title: Thông tin tri thức từ LLM LLAMA - Calligraphy
documents.content:
In the heart of Hanoi's Old Quarter, nestled beside the serene waters of Hoan Kiem Lake, lies the ancient Ngoc Son Temple, a sacred site where the art of calligraphy has been woven into the fabric of Vietnamese culture. This revered tradition, known as "Viết thư pháp" in Vietnamese, has been a cherished part of the temple's cultural heritage for centuries, with its origins dating back to the early days of the country's storied past.

As one approaches the temple, the soft ringing of bells and the gentle lapping of the lake's waters against the shore create a sense of tranquility, inviting visitors to slow down and immerse themselves in the beauty of the surroundings. The temple's courtyard, shaded by ancient trees and surrounded by the vibrant greenery of the lake's banks, is where the magic of calligraphy comes alive.

Here, one can find the Ông đồ, skilled artisans dressed in traditional áo dài, meticulously crafting intricate characters on red paper with soft brushes and black ink. The air is thick with the scent of ink and the soft scratching of brushes on paper, as the calligraphers bring to life the ancient art of writing. The characters, imbued with symbolic meaning and spiritual significance, are a testament to the temple's rich cultural heritage.

As the sun rises over the lake, the calligraphy activity takes on a new dimension, with the soft light casting a warm glow over the scene. The gentle ripples on the lake's surface seem to mirror the soft strokes of the brushes, creating a sense of harmony and balance. The temple's architecture, with its intricate carvings and ornate details, provides a stunning backdrop for the calligraphers' art, as they weave their magic with precision and devotion.

For locals and tourists alike, the experience of watching calligraphy at Ngoc Son Temple is a deeply moving and meditative one. It is a chance to connect with the spiritual and artistic soul of Hanoi, to absorb the city's rich cultural heritage, and to leave with a sense of peace and tranquility. As the calligraphers' brushes dance across the paper, the temple's ancient stones seem to whisper secrets of the past, and the present moment is filled with a sense of timelessness and connection to the city's storied history.

documents.title: Thông tin tri thức từ LLMQwen - Calligraphy
documents.content:
Nestled within the ancient precincts of Ngoc Son Temple, a revered site in the heart of Hoan Kiem District, the practice of calligraphy has long been a cherished cultural tradition that captivates visitors and locals alike. This serene activity unfolds amidst the tranquil ambiance of Ho Guom Lake, where the gentle ringing of temple bells harmonizes with the placid waters, creating an atmosphere of profound serenity. During the early spring and Tet holidays, the temple grounds are adorned with the presence of Ông đồ, elderly scribes dressed in traditional ao dai, meticulously crafting calligraphy on red or yellow paper. These artisans, embodying the spirit of studiousness and reverence, bend over their inkstones, each soft brushstroke imbued with the essence of old Hanoi. The custom of xin chu, or asking for calligraphy, stems from the belief that characters like "Phuc" (blessings), "Loc" (prosperity), "Tam" (heart), and "An" (peace) will bestow good fortune and tranquility upon the new year. As a result, this tradition has seamlessly integrated into the cultural fabric of the area around Hoan Kiem Lake, becoming a beloved part of the local heritage.

Visitors to Ngoc Son Temple are drawn not only by its architectural splendor and historical significance but also by the opportunity to witness the artistry of calligraphy. Tourists and residents alike pause to watch the Ông đồ at work, their movements slow and deliberate, each stroke of the brush a testament to patience and reverence. Conversations with these scribes often ensue, allowing for a deeper appreciation of the cultural and spiritual dimensions of the practice. Many leave the temple with a piece of calligraphy as a cherished memento, a tangible symbol of the tranquility and beauty they have experienced. The juxtaposition of the bustling city center with the quiet, contemplative space of the calligraphy session creates a unique contrast that resonates deeply with visitors. Surrounded by the shade of ancient trees, the reflective waters of Hoan Kiem Lake, and the iconic vermilion hue of The Huc Bridge, the calligraphy activity at Ngoc Son Temple offers a glimpse into the spiritual and artistic soul of Hanoi. This tradition, particularly enchanting in the early mornings, on weekends, and during autumn, continues to attract a diverse array of people seeking blessings and a connection to the rich cultural heritage of the city.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Calligraphy
documents.content:
Calligraphy, derived from the Ancient Greek term 'kalligraphía', meaning beautiful writing, is the art of fine handwriting elevated to a visual art form. This intricate craft involves the design and execution of lettering or characters using various writing instruments such as pens, ink brushes, or other tools. Unlike type design and non-classical hand-lettering, classical calligraphy stands distinct, though some practitioners may engage in both disciplines.

In East Asia and the Islamic world, Calligraphy holds a significant place in artistic expression, often reflecting the meaning of the text as a whole or individual words. Modern Western Calligraphy finds application in diverse areas, including wedding invitations, type and computer font design, letter cutting, hand-lettered logo design, religious art, graphic design, commissioned artworks, carved stone inscriptions, and memorial documents. Additionally, it is utilized in theatrical props, moving images for film and television, testimonials, birth and death certificates, maps, and other written works. 

In the Western world, the primary tools for Calligraphy are pens and brushes, with nibs that can be flat, round, or pointed. For decorative effects, multi-nib pens or steel brushes are employed. Felt-tip and ballpoint pens, while useful, do not produce angled lines. Gothic script, for instance, requires a stub nib pen. In Asia, calligraphers often use a makta, or penknife, to cut reed pens, which offer a broader range of motion compared to metallic pens. Common tools include quills, dip pens, ink brushes, qalams, fountain pens, chiselled markers, reed pens, and fudepens.

For Calligraphy, ink is typically water-based and less viscous than oil-based ink used in printing. Specialty papers with high ink absorption and uniform texture aid in producing cleaner lines. Parchment or vellum, materials that allow erasure of imperfections and viewing of lines without a lightbox, are frequently used. Lightboxes and templates assist in achieving straight lines without leaving pencil marks. Ruled paper, often spaced at intervals of one-quarter or one-half inch, is another option, though one-inch spaces are occasionally used, particularly with Uncial script, characterized by inch-high letters.

In East Asia, Calligraphy is deeply revered and remains an integral part of contemporary traditional culture. Chinese Calligraphy, known as shūfǎ or fǎshū, Japanese as shodō, and Korean as seoye, reflects the importance of this art form. The earliest known Chinese characters, oracle bone script, were carved on ox scapulae and tortoise plastrons during the Shang dynasty for divination purposes. These inscriptions were later interpreted and carved directly onto the shells or bones. As scripts evolved, the bronzeware script and large seal script emerged, exemplified by the Mao Gong ding, a bronze vessel with over 500 inscribed characters.

During the Imperial era, the graphs on old steles have been preserved, dating back to around 200 BCE and written in the small seal script style. Emperor Qin Shi Huang, who unified China, imposed reforms that included standardizing characters into a set of 3300 small seal characters. Although the brush was the main writing implement, few papers from this period have survived, and examples of this style are primarily found on steles. The clerical script, more regularized and resembling modern text, was also authorized during his reign.

documents.title: Thông tin Website - Calligraphy
documents.content:
The Calligraphy at the Bai Minh Stele before the Temple of Literature in Hanoi is a remarkable piece of art that has captivated visitors for centuries. This stele, located on the Dai Nghien (Inkstone) Pavilion in front of the Temple of Literature, was inscribed during the spring of 2012, marking a significant moment in the history of this revered site. The Dai Nghien itself is a unique structure, designed to resemble an inkstone used by scholars, symbolizing the importance of learning and calligraphy in Vietnamese culture. The stele stands proudly facing the Dai Nghien, its presence a testament to the rich cultural heritage of Vietnam.

The Bai Minh Stele, also known as the "Clear Mind Stele," is a prime example of traditional Vietnamese calligraphy and literature. It is adorned with Han Chinese characters, reflecting the deep-rooted influence of Chinese culture on Vietnamese civilization. The stele's inscription, written by Lam Giang, provides valuable insights into the historical significance of the Dai Nghien pavilion. Visitors can appreciate the intricate details of the stele, which not only showcases the beauty of calligraphy but also offers a glimpse into the cultural and historical context of the Temple of Literature.

The Bai Minh Stele is one of many such steles found throughout Vietnam, each bearing important inscriptions that reflect the values and traditions of the time. Typically, these steles feature inscriptions written in classical Chinese, often in a vertical format, with varying lengths depending on the content. Some steles contain as few as four characters, while others extend to over a hundred characters, like the Thanh Tong Chiểu Long Bình Định stele, penned by Than Nhan Trung for Chiểu Long when Emperor Le Thanh Tong visited the temple.

The Bai Minh Stele at the Dai Nghien pavilion is particularly noteworthy due to its historical significance and the frequent visits it receives from both domestic and international tourists. Over the years, numerous translations and interpretations of the stele's inscription have been produced, each offering a different perspective on its meaning and historical context. One of the earliest translations was done by French scholar G. Doumitier in 1887, thirteen years after the stele was erected. Since then, various Vietnamese scholars have continued to translate and interpret the stele's contents, contributing to a deeper understanding of its cultural and historical value.

The translation process involves careful analysis of the original text, ensuring accuracy in conveying the intended message. Translators must navigate the complexities of classical Chinese, a language rich in nuance and historical context. For instance, the stele's inscription, translated into Vietnamese, reads: "This place is a symbol of harmony and tranquility, where scholars gather to study and reflect. The pavilion is round and symmetrical, embodying balance and unity. It stands tall amidst the serene waters of the Hoan Kiem Lake, surrounded by lush greenery and the gentle breeze of the Thai Nguyen wind. The stele itself is a testament to the dedication and skill of the artisans who crafted it."

The stele's inscription, attributed to Nguyen Van Sieu and Vu Ta Tri, was originally composed in the year Giap Ty (1864). It describes the Dai Nghien pavilion in detail, highlighting its architectural beauty and symbolic significance. The stele was later included in the Phuong Dich Van Loi volume published in the 35th year of the Tong Phuc reign (1882), under the supervision of Quang Luc Khanh Quyen Sung Ha Noi Tuan Phu Vu Nhi Kiem Duyet. In 1937, during the restoration of the temple, the stele was re-engraved onto stone and placed on the Dai Nghien pavilion, where it remains today, a constant reminder of the enduring legacy of Vietnamese calligraphy and scholarship.

Visitors to the Temple of Literature can explore the Dai Nghien pavilion and the Bai Minh Stele, immersing themselves in the rich cultural tapestry of Vietnam. The atmosphere around the stele is serene and contemplative, inviting visitors to reflect on the historical and cultural significance of the site. The surrounding environment, with its tranquil lakes and lush gardens, complements the architectural beauty of the Dai Nghien pavilion, creating a harmonious setting that enhances the visitor experience. The Bai Minh Stele stands as a testament to the enduring importance of calligraphy and literature in Vietnamese culture, a tradition that continues to inspire and educate generations of scholars and visitors alike.

description:
The Pen Tower at Hoan Kiem Lake is a five-story stone tower, built in the 18th year of Tự Đức (1865) on the site of the old Độc Tôn mountain, based on the idea of Confucian scholar Nguyễn Văn Siêu, located outside the entrance to The Huc Bridge and Ngoc Son Temple.

The tower stands on a mountain formed by stacked rocks, 12m in diameter and 4m high. The square tower has five stories, standing 28m tall. Its peak is an inverted brush pen nib. Both the handle and the nib are 0.9m high. On the body of the three middle stories, three characters Tả Thanh Thiên (Chinese characters: 寫青天) are carved vertically, meaning "Writing on the Blue Sky".

The Pen Tower architectural complex celebrates literature, but simultaneously also commemorates the military achievements of Lord Trịnh in suppressing the rebellion of Quận Hẻo Nguyễn Danh Phương. The Pen Tower stands on a mound filled with boulders; this mound symbolizes a mountain named Độc Tôn. In the essay "Bút Tháp chí" composed by Nguyễn Văn Siêu in 1865, carved directly on the tower body, it reads:

On the peak of Độc Tôn mountain stands the five-story Pen Tower. The tower gains height from the mountain, and the mountain gains eternal fame from the tower. Around the Lê Vĩnh Hựu era (1735-1740), the rebel Phương secretly occupied Độc Tôn mountain in Phổ Yên district, Thái Nguyên province. The royal army went to suppress him, stationed at Ngọc Bội mountain, continuously defeating the enemy. On the day of triumph, taking advantage of the high mound, a mountain was built to commemorate the achievement, named Độc Tôn mountain. After the political upheaval, the mountain was covered with thorns and bushes. In the lake was Văn Xương Temple. During the temple's renovation, looking towards the East bank, a mountain was seen, so the grass was cleared, trees removed, and the Pen Tower was built, facing the Inkstone Pavilion. That mountain is a symbol of military victory, and the tower is a symbol of culture. Both rely on each other to exist.

At the same time as building Độc Tôn mountain on the East bank of the lake, Lord Trịnh also had Ngọc Bội mountain built on the West bank of the lake (Độc Tôn mountain and Ngọc Bội mountain in Thăng Long are two different mountains). Next to the mountain was Khánh Thụy Palace. During the Lê Chiêu Thống era, this palace was burned down, but its name remains in two villages on either side of the palace: Tả Khánh Thụy and Hữu Khánh Thụy. During the Nguyễn dynasty, these two villages merged with Báo Thiên village to form Báo Khánh village. Today, Báo Khánh street remains as a relic.

At the beginning of The Huc Bridge is the Inkstone Pavilion. The inkstone is placed on the first gate leading into the temple; it is a blue stone inkstone carved in the shape of half a peach, cut vertically, and hollowed out. The peach's length is 0.97m, width 0.8m, height 0.3m, and circumference 2m, with three thiềm thừ (toads) supporting the inkstone like three tripod legs. Notably, an inscription is carved on the body of the inkstone, and its author is also Nguyễn Văn Siêu. It only has 64 Chinese characters but its meaning is very profound, temporarily translated as:

In ancient times, a hollow in the earth was used as an inkstone, annotating the Đạo Đức kinh, pondering by a large inkstone, writing the Hán Xuân Thu. From stone, an inkstone is separated, without a fixed form. Neither square nor round, its use in all matters is truly wondrous. Neither high nor low, it sits in the very center. Bending down, it reflects Hoan Kiem Lake; looking up, it gazes at the stone Pen Tower; corresponding to the Thai constellation, it brings forth all transformations. Holding primordial energy, it grinds the void.

Currently, there is a song about the Pen Tower, titled "Nghiên Bút Non Sông" composed by Đình Dương.

Pen Tower [resembles] a pen reaching upward into the sky. The top of Pen Tower [features] a pen-shaped tip pointing straight upward. Pen Tower [symbolizes] the spirit of learning and the Vietnamese literary tradition. The base of Pen Tower [is engraved with] the three Chinese characters "Ta Thanh Thien." Hoan Kiem Lake [surrounds] the Pen Tower with calm water and green trees. Pen Tower [is especially beautiful] in the early morning and at dusk.
description_graph_vi: Tháp Bút [đứng trên] một gò nhỏ ở phía đông bắc Hồ Hoàn Kiếm. Tháp Bút [được làm bằng] đá. Tháp Bút [có] nhiều tầng thu nhỏ dần lên phía trên. Tháp Bút [gợi hình ảnh] một cây bút vươn lên trời xanh. Phần đỉnh Tháp Bút [có] ngòi bút hướng thẳng lên trên. Tháp Bút [tượng trưng cho] tinh thần hiếu học và truyền thống văn chương của người Việt. Chân Tháp Bút [khắc] ba chữ Hán "Tả Thanh Thiên." Hồ Hoàn Kiếm [bao quanh] Tháp Bút bằng mặt nước yên ả và hàng cây xanh mát. Tháp Bút [đẹp nhất vào] buổi sớm và lúc hoàng hôn.
description_vi:
Tháp Bút ở Hồ Gươm là một ngọn tháp bằng đá cao năm tầng, được xây dựng năm Tự Đức thứ 18 (1865) trên nền núi Độc Tôn cũ theo ý tưởng của nhà nho Nguyễn Văn Siêu, nằm ở phía ngoài lối vào cầu Thê Húc, đền Ngọc Sơn.

Tháp dựng trên ngọn núi do đá xếp, đường kính 12m, cao 4m. Tháp vuông có năm tầng, cao 28m. Đỉnh là một ngòi bút lông dựng ngược. Cả cán và ngòi bút cao 0,9m. Trên thân ba tầng giữa có khắc theo chiều dọc ba chữ Tả Thanh Thiên (chữ Hán: 寫青天) mang nghĩa "Viết lên trời xanh"

Cụm kiến trúc Tháp Bút biểu dương văn chương, nhưng đồng thời cũng để biểu dương võ công của chúa Trịnh trong việc dẹp cuộc khởi nghĩa của quận Hẻo Nguyễn Danh Phương. Tháp Bút dựng trên một cái gò chất đầy đá hộc, gò này tượng trưng cho 1 ngọn núi, tên là Độc Tôn. Trong bài "Bút Tháp chí" do Nguyễn Văn Siêu soạn năm 1865 được khắc ngay trên thân tháp:

	
Trên đỉnh núi Độc Tôn có Tháp Bút năm tầng. Tháp nhờ núi mà cao thêm, núi nhờ tháp mà truyền mãi. Khoảng Lê Vĩnh Hựu (1735-1740) nghịch Phương lén chiếm núi Độc Tôn ở huyện Phổ Yên xứ Thái Nguyên, Vương sư đi đánh dẹp, đóng quân ở núi Ngọc Bội, liên tiếp phá giặc. Ngày khải hoàn, nhân gò đất cao, đắp núi để ghi công, đặt tên là núi Độc Tôn. Sau cuộc chính biến núi bị gai góc phủ đầy. Trong hồ có miếu Văn Xương. Vào dịp trùng tu miếu, ngó sang bờ Đông, thấy có núi, bèn phát cỏ dọn cây, xây tháp Bút, đối diện với đài Nghiên. Ấy núi là biểu tượng của chiến công mà tháp là biểu tượng của văn hóa. Cả hai cái đó dựa vào nhau mà tồn tại.

Cùng lúc đắp núi Độc Tôn ở bờ Đông hồ thì chúa Trịnh còn cho đắp núi Ngọc Bội bên bờ Tây hồ (núi Độc Tôn và núi Ngọc Bội ở Thăng Long là hai ngọn núi khác nhau). Cạnh núi có cung Khánh Thụy. Sang đời Lê Chiêu Thống đã cho đốt cung này, song tên thì còn lưu lại ở 2 ngôi làng ở 2 bên cung là Tả Khánh Thụy và Hữu Khánh Thụy. Sang đời Nguyễn 2 làng này nhập vào làng Báo Thiên thành làng Báo Khánh. Nay còn phố Báo Khánh là di tích.

Ở đầu cầu Thê Húc là Đài Nghiên, nghiên được đặt trên tòa cửa đầu tiên dẫn vào đền, là một nghiên mực bằng đá xanh đẽo tạc theo hình nửa quả đào, cắt ngang theo chiều dọc, khoét lõm. Bề dài quả đào 0,97m, bề ngang 0,8m, cao 0,3m, chu vi 2m, có ba con thiềm thừ (con cóc) đội nghiên như ba cái chân kiềng. Đặc biệt trên thân của nghiên có khắc một bài minh mà tác giả lại cũng là Nguyễn Văn Siêu. Chỉ có 64 chữ Hán nhưng ý tứ rất hàm súc, tạm dịch:

Xưa lấy hốc đất làm nghiên, chú giải Đạo Đức kinh, nghiền ngẫm bên nghiên lớn, viết sách Hán Xuân Thu. Từ đá tách ra làm nghiên, chẳng có hình dáng. Không vuông không tròn, dùng vào mọi việc thật kỳ diệu. Không cao không thấp, ngôi ở chính giữa. Cúi soi hồ Hoàn Kiếm, ngửa trông ngọn Bút đá; ứng vào sao Thai mà làm ra mọi biến đổi. Ngậm nguyên khí mà mài hư không.
Hiện đã có bài hát về Tháp bút, đó là bài "Nghiên Bút Non Sông" do Đình Dương sáng tác
name: Pen Tower
visual_cues:
The Pen Tower stands on a small mound on the northeastern side of Hoan Kiem Lake, distinguished by its graceful and ancient appearance. The structure is made of stone and consists of several tiers that gradually narrow toward the top, creating the impression of a pen reaching upward as if writing in the sky. At the top of the tower is a pen-shaped tip pointing straight upward, symbolizing the spirit of learning and the literary tradition of the Vietnamese people. At the base of the tower, the three Chinese characters “Ta Thanh Thien” are engraved, meaning “to write on the blue sky,” which further enhances its symbolic significance.

Surrounding the tower is the calm water of the lake, reflecting the image of the structure on its clear surface. Rows of green trees provide shade and create a harmonious setting between nature and architecture. As the light changes throughout the day, the Pen Tower takes on different moods, appearing radiant under sunlight and contemplative at dusk, contributing to the unique beauty of Hoan Kiem Lake.

The Pen Tower, also known as Tháp Bút, stands majestically on a small mound on the northeastern side of Hoan Kiem Lake, its ancient and graceful appearance a testament to the rich cultural heritage of Vietnam. This five-story stone tower, built in the 18th year of Tự Đức (1865), is a masterpiece of Confucian scholar Nguyễn Văn Siêu's design, situated outside the entrance to the Huc Bridge and Ngoc Son Temple.

The tower's unique architecture is characterized by its gradual narrowing of tiers toward the top, creating the illusion of a pen reaching upward, as if writing in the sky. The pen-shaped tip at the top, pointing straight upward, symbolizes the spirit of learning and the literary tradition of the Vietnamese people. The three Chinese characters "Ta Thanh Thien" engraved at the base of the tower, meaning "to write on the blue sky," further enhance its symbolic significance.

The Pen Tower's surroundings are a tranquil oasis, with the calm water of the lake reflecting the structure's image on its surface. Rows of green trees provide shade and create a harmonious setting between nature and architecture. As the light changes throughout the day, the Pen Tower takes on different moods, appearing radiant under sunlight and contemplative at dusk, contributing to the unique beauty of Hoan Kiem Lake.

The tower's construction is deeply rooted in Vietnamese history, commemorating the military achievements of Lord Trịnh in suppressing the rebellion of Quận Hẻo Nguyễn Danh Phương. The mound on which the tower stands symbolizes the mountain named Độc Tôn, which was built to commemorate the victory. The tower's architectural complex celebrates literature, but also honors the military achievements of Lord Trịnh.

The surrounding area is steeped in historical significance, with the Inkstone Pavilion located at the beginning of the Huc Bridge. The inkstone, carved in the shape of a half-peach, is a symbol of the connection between the tower and the lake. The inscription on the inkstone, written by Nguyễn Văn Siêu, is a profound reflection on the relationship between the tower and the lake, as well as the connection between the past and the present.

Today, the Pen Tower remains an iconic landmark, attracting tourists and locals alike who come to admire its beauty and significance. The surrounding area is a popular spot for photography, with the tower's unique architecture and the tranquil lake creating a breathtaking backdrop. The Pen Tower is a testament to the rich cultural heritage of Vietnam, a symbol of the country's literary and historical traditions, and a reminder of the importance of preserving cultural heritage for future generations.

documents.content:
The Pen Tower, known in Vietnamese as Tháp Bút, is a striking five-story stone tower located on the northeastern side of Hoan Kiem Lake in Hanoi, Vietnam. Constructed in the 18th year of the reign of Emperor Tự Đức, which corresponds to 1865, the tower was conceived by the renowned Confucian scholar Nguyễn Văn Siêu. Situated just outside the entrance to The Huc Bridge and adjacent to Ngoc Son Temple, the Pen Tower stands as a testament to both literary and military heritage.

The tower is built on a small mound formed by stacked rocks, measuring 12 meters in diameter and 4 meters in height. This mound represents the ancient Độc Tôn mountain, which holds significant historical importance. The Pen Tower itself rises to a height of 28 meters, with each of its five square tiers narrowing progressively towards the summit. Atop the tower is a distinctive pen-shaped tip, an inverted brush pen nib that reaches skyward, symbolizing the spirit of learning and the rich literary tradition of Vietnam. The entire structure is crafted from stone, giving it a timeless and enduring quality.

Carved into the body of the three middle tiers of the tower are the Chinese characters "Tả Thanh Thiên," which translate to "Writing on the Blue Sky." These characters not only enhance the aesthetic appeal of the tower but also underscore its cultural significance. According to Nguyễn Văn Siêu’s essay "Bút Tháp chí," inscribed directly onto the tower, the Pen Tower commemorates the military achievements of Lord Trịnh in suppressing the rebellion led by Nguyễn Danh Phương, a rebel who had once occupied the Độc Tôn mountain in Thái Nguyên province. The construction of the tower thus serves as a dual tribute, celebrating both literary and martial virtues.

The Pen Tower is part of a larger architectural complex that includes the Inkstone Pavilion, situated at the beginning of The Huc Bridge. The pavilion houses a large blue stone inkstone, carved in the shape of half a peach and supported by three toad-like creatures, symbolizing stability and longevity. This inkstone, along with the Pen Tower, forms a harmonious pair that reflects the deep cultural roots of Vietnam, where literature and artistry are revered alongside military prowess.

The surrounding area of Hoan Kiem Lake provides a serene backdrop for the Pen Tower, with calm waters reflecting the tower’s elegant silhouette. Rows of lush green trees add to the tranquil atmosphere, creating a perfect blend of nature and human-made structures. As the light shifts throughout the day, the Pen Tower transforms, radiating warmth under the sun and exuding a sense of contemplation at dusk, adding to the unique charm of Hoan Kiem Lake.

Today, the Pen Tower continues to be a focal point for tourists and locals alike, drawing visitors with its historical and cultural significance. The tower stands as a proud monument to the enduring legacy of Vietnamese scholarship and valor, embodying the nation’s rich heritage and inspiring future generations.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Pen Tower
documents.content:
The Pen Tower, located in Hoan Kiem Lake, is a five-tiered stone tower standing at 28 meters tall, constructed in the year 1865 during the reign of Emperor Tu Duc, on the site of the former Mount Ducton according to the idea of scholar Nguyen Van Sieu. It stands just outside the entrance to the Thê Húc Bridge, near the Ngoc Son Temple. The tower is built on a rocky hill with a diameter of 12 meters and a height of 4 meters. Its square structure consists of five tiers, each adorned with intricate details. Atop the tower is an inverted quill pen, symbolizing the peak of literary achievement. The pen itself, both stem and nib, rises to a height of 0.9 meters. On the middle three tiers, inscribed vertically, are the characters "Tá Thanh Thiên" (寫青天), which translates to "Write upon the blue sky."

The complex of the Pen Tower represents not only literary excellence but also commemorates the martial prowess of the Lord Trinh in suppressing the uprising led by Nguyen Danh Phuong. The tower is erected on a mound filled with rock fragments, symbolizing a mountain named Ducton. In his essay "Bút Tháp chí," written in 1865 and engraved on the tower, Nguyen Van Sieu describes that while constructing Mount Ducton on the eastern shore of the lake, the Lord Trinh also built Mount Jade Pebble on the western shore. These two mountains were distinct features of Thang Long (modern-day Hanoi). Adjacent to Mount Ducton was the Khang Thuy Palace, which was later destroyed during the reign of Le Chieu Tong, though its name remained in two villages called Left Khang Thuy and Right Khang Thuy. By the Nguyen dynasty, these two villages merged into one called Bao Khanh Village, now known as Bao Khanh Street, a historical relic.

At the beginning of the Thê Húc Bridge lies the Inkstone Pavilion, where an inkstone carved from green stone in the shape of half a peach is placed atop the first gate leading into the temple. This inkstone measures 0.97 meters in length, 0.8 meters in width, and 0.3 meters in height, with a circumference of 2 meters. Three toads support the inkstone, resembling three legs of a tripod. Engraved on the inkstone is a brief inscription by Nguyen Van Sieu, consisting of 64 Chinese characters, whose meaning is condensed yet profound. A song titled "Nghiên Bút Non Sông" (Inkstone and Pen of Mountains and Rivers) was composed by Ding Yang, celebrating the Pen Tower.

The Hoan Kiem Turtle is very large, with a relatively small and wide head, a short, round snout, a very short proboscis, a yellowish-green back with yellow spots, and a pale white plastron. The turtle's carapace is hard, not soft.

According to the remains of a turtle that died in the 1960s, currently preserved in Khieng Hom Temple, that individual weighed 250 kg with a length of 2.1m and a width of 1.8m. The individual in Ho Guom that Hanoi city caught to treat its injuries in April 2011 was female, weighing 169 kg with a total body length of 185 cm; carapace width of 99 cm, and tail length of 35 cm.

Also according to the hypothesis of Assoc. Prof. Le Tran Binh, the Hoan Kiem Turtle may have originated from Lam Kinh, Thanh Hoa, the same hometown as King Le Loi, and was released into Ho Guom by King Le, because there was no prior information about any large turtle species in Thang Long. According to Prof. Le Tran Binh, comparisons show that the DNA sample of the Ho Guom turtle is similar to turtles from Quang Phu - Thanh Hoa.[10]

In 2010, an individual softshell turtle of another species (specifically, ba ba Nam bo) with a length of 1.2 m and weighing 52 kg died in Ho Guom and was made into a specimen by Dr. Vu Ngoc Thanh, former staff of the Faculty of Biology, Hanoi University of Science.

**Legends and Cultural Role**
Detailed article: Kim Quy Turtle God and Turtles in Cultural Symbolism

Hoan Kiem Turtle surfacing (2011)
The Hoan Kiem Turtle is associated with the legend of Le Loi returning the Thuan Thien magic sword to the Kim Quy Turtle God. The very name of the lake is also based on that legend from the early Later Le dynasty. The legend of the Kim Quy Turtle God goes even further back in Vietnamese history with the story of the Kim Quy Turtle God helping An Duong Vuong build Co Loa Citadel and gifting the king a claw to make a crossbow trigger to fight against Trieu Da's army.

In the 20th century, several Vietnamese literary works took the Hoan Kiem Turtle as their subject. These include the story The Turtle Tower God by Vu Khac Khoan and Hoan Kiem Turtle by Nguyen Dau (Truong Man Song).

Vietnamese people often refer to the giant turtle living in Ho Guom as "Grand-Father" with a respectful connotation, and this is also a symbol associated with the legend of the Magic Sword and the history of national defense, a cherished spiritual part.

However, according to Assoc. Prof. Dr. Tran Lam Bien, it should not be called "Great Grandfather" because it is a flesh-and-blood creature that needs urgent conservation, not an immortal deity from legends.

description_vi:
Rùa Hồ Gươm
Rùa Hồ Hoàn Kiếm có kích thước rất lớn, đầu tương đối nhỏ và rộng, mõm ngắn, tròn, vòi rất ngắn, lưng màu vàng lục có những đốm vàng, yếm bụng màu trắng nhạt. Mai rùa cứng chứ không mềm.

Theo di thể rùa chết vào thập niên 1960 hiện lưu giữ trong đền Khiêng hòm thì cá thể đó cân nặng 250 kg với chiều dài 2,1m và chiều rộng 1,8 m. Cá thể ở Hồ Gươm mà thành phố Hà Nội bắt để chữa trị vết thương trên thân rùa hồi tháng 4 năm 2011 là giống cái, nặng 169 kg với chiều dài toàn thân của Rùa là 185 cm; chiều rộng mai là 99 cm, chiều dài đuôi là 35 cm.

Cũng theo giả thuyết của PGS Lê Trần Bình, Rùa Hồ Hoàn Kiếm có thể có nguồn gốc từ Lam Kinh, Thanh Hóa, cùng quê với vua Lê Lợi, và được vua Lê thả vào Hồ Gươm, vì trước đó không có thông tin gì về loài rùa lớn nào tại Thăng Long Theo GS Lê Trần Bình, so sánh cho thấy mẫu DNA của rùa hồ Gươm giống rùa Quảng Phú - Thanh Hóa.

Năm 2010, có một cá thể rùa mai mềm thuộc loài khác (cụ thể là ba ba Nam bộ) với chiều dài 1,2 m nặng 52 kg chết ở Hồ Gươm và đã được TS. Vũ Ngọc Thành nguyên cán bộ khoa Sinh, ĐH Khoa học Tự nhiên Hà Nội làm tiêu bản.
Truyền thuyết và vai trò văn hóa
Bài chi tiết: Rùa thần Kim Quy và Rùa trong biểu tượng văn hóa

Rùa Hồ Gươm nổi lên mặt nước (2011)
Rùa Hồ Gươm gắn liền với truyền thuyết Lê Lợi trả gươm thần Thuận Thiên cho thần rùa thần Kim Quy. Ngay địa danh của hồ cũng căn cứ trên truyền tích đó vào đầu thời nhà Hậu Lê. Truyền thuyết thần Kim Quy còn đi ngược dòng lịch sử của người Việt xa hơn nữa với chuyện thần Kim Quy giúp An Dương Vương xây thành Cổ Loa và tặng nhà vua cái móng để làm lẫy nỏ chống quân của Triệu Đà.

Vào thế kỷ XX một số tác phẩm văn học Việt Nam lấy rùa Hồ Gươm làm đề tài. Trong đó có truyện Thần Tháp Rùa của Vũ Khắc Khoan và Rùa Hồ Gươm của Nguyễn Dậu (Trương Mẫn Song).

Người Việt Nam vẫn thường gọi rùa khổng lồ sống ở Hồ Gươm là "Cụ" với hàm ý tôn kính, và đây cũng là biểu tượng gắn liền với truyền thuyết Gươm thần và lịch sử giữ nước, là phần tâm linh đáng trân trọng.

Tuy nhiên, theo PGS-TS Trần Lâm Biền thì không nên gọi là "Cụ" vì đây là 1 sinh vật bằng xương thịt, cần bảo tồn khẩn cấp chứ không phải là thần thánh bất tử trong truyền thuyết.
name: Softshell Turtle
visual_cues:
The Hoàn Kiếm Turtle specimen, displayed in a glass case at Ngoc Son Temple, creates a visual impression that is both solemn and evokes a sense of tranquility. The surrounding space is often kept at a soft light level, making the glass case the focal point. The transparent glass surface subtly reflects the surroundings, making the turtle's image both clear and deep, as if existing between two layers of real and reflected space.

Inside the glass case, the turtle specimen is positioned in a natural posture, its body extended, limbs stretched horizontally, recalling its form when swimming in water. The large, slightly flattened shell, with a surface that is not overly glossy but has a deep grayish-brown hue, creates a sense of solidity and weight. The contours around the shell are not as sharp as those of land turtles but softer, reflecting the characteristics of a long-lived freshwater turtle species.

The turtle's head is directed forward, its neck slightly extended, creating the sensation of movement "frozen" in a moment. The specimen's eyes no longer possess their natural clarity, but have been treated to retain their original shape, making its gaze solemn and deep. The mouth is closed, and the skin folds around the neck and limbs are relatively well-preserved, creating a realistic impression of its body structure.

Light shining into the glass case highlights the main masses of the specimen, especially the shell and head, while also creating subtle shadow areas beneath the body and around the feet. The contrast between light and dark areas helps the form become clearer and enhances the three-dimensional feel. As viewers move, the reflection angles on the glass change, making the turtle's image appear to subtly shift, even though the specimen itself is completely still.

Overall, the visual experience lies not only in the specimen itself but also in how it is placed within the display space. The glass case acts as a boundary, separating this creature from the outside world, while emphasizing its conservation and symbolic value. The image of the Hoàn Kiếm Turtle in an immobile state, illuminated with controlled lighting and placed in a sacred space, creates a feeling of both physical closeness and a distance in terms of time and meaning.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Softshell Turtle
documents.content:
The Softshell Turtle of Hoàn Kiếm Lake is a group of large turtles that once lived in Hoàn Kiếm Lake. The last individual died on January 19, 2016. These turtles belong to the critically endangered species, the Swinhoe's Softshell Turtle (Rafetus swinhoei). As of 2023, only three individuals of this species have been found worldwide.

Currently, the Swinhoe's Softshell Turtle is considered one of the rarest turtle species, listed as critically endangered by the World Red Book. The possibility of its extinction is very high.

Some people suggest that these turtles should not be called turtles but rather large soft-shelled turtles or soft-shelled turtles. In Chinese, they are referred to as ban miết or lai đầu ngoan, which means soft-shelled turtle. They are not classified among the four sacred creatures—Dragon, Unicorn, Tortoise, and Phoenix—because they do not fit the traditional definition of a tortoise. However, scientifically, "turtle," "soft-shelled turtle," or "soft-shelled turtle" all refer to different subfamilies within the turtle family, making it correct to call them all "turtles."

The Softshell Turtle of Hoàn Kiếm Lake is notably large, with a relatively small and wide head, short snout, and very short neck. Its back is yellowish-green with yellow spots, and its belly is pale white. Contrary to their name, their shells are actually hard rather than soft.

A specimen from the 1960s, preserved at the Khiêng Hòm Shrine, weighed 250 kg with a length of 2.1 meters and a width of 1.8 meters. Another individual captured in April 2011 for medical treatment due to injuries measured 185 cm in total length, had a carapace width of 99 cm, and a tail length of 35 cm, weighing 169 kg. According to Professor Lê Trần Bình, the Hoàn Kiếm Lake Softshell Turtle may have originated from Lam Kinh, Thanh Hoa, the birthplace of King Le Loi, and was released into Hoàn Kiếm Lake by King Le. Genetic analysis suggests that the DNA of the Hoàn Kiếm Lake Softshell Turtle matches that of the Quang Phu Softshell Turtle in Thanh Hoa.

In 2010, a different species of soft-shelled turtle, specifically a Southern Softshell Turtle, measuring 1.2 meters long and weighing 52 kg, was found dead in Hoàn Kiếm Lake. This specimen was preserved by Dr. Vũ Ngọc Thành, a former staff member of the Biology Department at Hanoi University of Science.

Another individual was caught and survived in 2008 at Dong Mo Lake, Ha Tay (now part of Ha Noi), and was believed to be of the same species as the Hoàn Kiếm Lake Softshell Turtle. It measured 90 cm in length, 70 cm in width, and weighed approximately 80-90 kg. Its edges were yellow, its head was spotted, and its shell was grayish-blue. Douglas Hendri, director of the Asian Turtle Program, conducted DNA tests on the Dong Mo turtle at the Institute of Ecology and Biological Resources, confirming that it belonged to the same species as the Hoàn Kiếm Lake Softshell Turtle, Rafetus swinhoei, as did the two individuals kept in zoos in China. In 2018, an image of another individual was captured at Xuan Khanh Lake, increasing the known number of surviving individuals to three.

description:
To the South is Trấn Ba Pavilion (wave-blocking pavilion - implying a pillar standing firm amidst unhealthy waves in contemporary culture). The pavilion is square-shaped with eight roofs, the two-tiered roof is supported by 8 columns, four outer columns are made of stone, four inner columns are made of wood. The columns inside the pavilion have a pair of parallel couplets:

Kiếm hữu dư linh quang nhược thủy
Văn tòng đại khối thọ như sơn
Hán characters:

劍 有 餘 靈 光 若 水
文 從 大 塊 壽 如 山
Meaning:

The sword's lingering spiritual essence shines like water
Literature/Culture endures with heaven and earth, lasting like mountains.
The figures worshipped in the temple, besides Văn Xương Đế Quân, Lã Động Tân, Quan Vân Trường, Hưng Đạo Vương, also include Amitābha Buddha. This demonstrates the Vietnamese concept of Tam giáo đồng nguyên.

Although it is a temple of new architecture, Ngọc Sơn Temple is a prime example of architectural space and creation. The combination of the temple and the lake has created an architectural whole of Thiên - Nhân hợp nhất, creating an ancient, harmonious, and balanced beauty for the temple and the lake, evoking feelings of profound harmony between humans and nature.

In the heart of Hanoi's historic Old Quarter, nestled beside the serene waters of Hoan Kiem Lake, stands the Tran Ba Communal House, a majestic architectural gem that embodies the harmonious fusion of traditional Vietnamese design and natural beauty. The Tran Ba Pavilion, with its eight curved roofs and eight stone pillars, rises from an elevated platform, exuding an air of elegance and refinement. As a cultural and historical landmark, the Tran Ba Communal House is a must-visit destination for tourists and locals alike. documents.content:
Located at the southern end of The Huc Bridge, just before the entrance to Ngoc Son Temple in central Hanoi, Tran Ba Communal House stands as a significant architectural landmark within the picturesque Hoan Kiem Lake landscape. This communal house, known locally as Đình Trấn Ba, is a testament to the rich cultural heritage and architectural prowess of Vietnam. Its strategic position at the terminus of The Huc Bridge enhances its prominence, serving as a gateway to the revered Ngoc Son Temple.

The Tran Ba Communal House is a square-shaped structure with eight outward-curving roofs, each designed to evoke a sense of lightness and elegance. The two-tiered roof is supported by eight sturdy columns, with the four outer columns crafted from solid stone and the four inner columns made of wood. These columns not only provide structural integrity but also bear poetic inscriptions in both Vietnamese and Chinese, reflecting the deep cultural integration characteristic of Vietnamese society. The inscribed couplets read, "The sword's lingering spiritual essence shines like water / Literature/Culture endures with heaven and earth, lasting like mountains," symbolizing the enduring legacy of Vietnamese culture and its resilience.

The Tran Ba Communal House is built upon a raised platform, which elevates it above the serene waters of Hoan Kiem Lake, further emphasizing its importance and grandeur. The elevated position allows visitors to enjoy panoramic views of the surrounding landscape, including the tranquil lake and the bustling city beyond. The natural light filtering through the gaps between the stone pillars creates intricate patterns of light and shadow, enhancing the depth and atmosphere of the space. This interplay of light and shadow contributes to the overall aesthetic appeal of the communal house, making it a focal point for tourists and locals alike.

Inside the Tran Ba Communal House, worshippers pay homage to a diverse array of deities, reflecting the syncretic religious beliefs prevalent in Vietnam. Among those honored are the scholar-god Van Xuan De Quan, the historical figure La Dong Tan, the martial hero Quan Vuong, and the military general Hung Dao Vuong. Additionally, the presence of Amitabha Buddha underscores the concept of Tam Giao Dong Nguyen, or the unity of the three teachings—Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism—which is deeply ingrained in Vietnamese culture. This blend of religious traditions highlights the communal house's role as a site of spiritual convergence and cultural integration.

The Tran Ba Communal House is more than just a place of worship; it is a symbol of stability and harmony within the community. Its name, "Tran Ba," translates to "wave-stabilizing," suggesting its role in maintaining equilibrium and peace in the surrounding environment. This symbolic significance is reinforced by its location at the end of The Huc Bridge, where it serves as a bridge between the earthly realm and the spiritual domain, embodying the principle of Heavenly-Human Unity (Thien-Nhan Hop Nhat).

In summary, the Tran Ba Communal House is a remarkable example of traditional Vietnamese architecture, seamlessly blending historical, cultural, and spiritual elements. Its elegant design, strategic placement, and rich symbolism make it a vital component of the Hoan Kiem Lake area, attracting visitors who seek to experience the unique cultural heritage of Vietnam.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Opera House
documents.content:
The Hanoi Opera House is an architectural masterpiece located in Hanoi, Vietnam, serving as a venue for artistic performances. Situated at No. 1A Trang Tien Street, Cua Nam Ward, the Opera House stands on August Revolution Square, not far from Hoan Kiem Lake and the Vietnam History Museum, adjacent to the Hilton Hanoi Opera Hotel, overlooking the Opera House Garden and the August 19th Garden. Construction began under French supervision in 1901 and was completed in 1911, inspired by the design of the Paris Opera Garnier but adapted to a smaller scale and local climate conditions. The architects Harlay and Broyer incorporated elements reminiscent of theaters in southern France, with organizational layouts, performance spaces, staircases, and entrance halls similar to those found in European theaters of the early 20th century. Despite its eclectic architectural style, the Hanoi Opera House retains a strong neoclassical French appearance, particularly in its structural design, black tile roof, and interior decorative motifs. Although it was built later than other opera houses in Ho Chi Minh City and Hai Phong, the Hanoi Opera House boasts the most complete architecture and has become a familiar and distinctive landmark of Hanoi.

Since its completion, the Hanoi Opera House has played a significant role as one of the city's major cultural centers, hosting frequent cultural activities and artistic performances. It served as the birthplace and showcase for Vietnamese theater and stage arts, as well as symphonic, choral, operatic, and ballet performances. Moreover, the Opera House holds historical significance, having been the site where the first National Assembly of independent Vietnam convened and adopted the 1946 Constitution, the country’s first constitution, along with the list of ministers for the Democratic Republic of Vietnam United Front Government (led by Ho Chi Minh), the National Resistance Committee (with Vo Nguyen Giap as chairman), and the National Advisory Council (headed by Vinh Thuy).

After years of deterioration, the Opera House underwent extensive renovations from 1995 to 1997, restoring its former glory in preparation for the summit of the Francophonie Community. Today, the Hanoi Opera House remains one of the most important venues for performances in Hanoi, revered by artists as a sanctuary for classical art. Like many architectural structures and intangible cultural forms, the Hanoi Opera House serves as a testament to a period of cultural exchange in the city.

Historically, the site of the Hanoi Opera House was a swampy area belonging to the villages of Thach Tan and Tay Luong, bordering the village of Cuu Lau, part of the Huu Tuc district (or Phuc Lan district) of Tho Xuong county. In 1808, a mint (宝传局) was established in this region, with its northern boundary being today's Trang Tien Street, southern boundary being Pham Si Manh Street, eastern boundary being Phan Chu Trinh Street, and western boundary being Ngo Quyen Street. The northeast corner of the future opera house's swamp was the West Long Gate (or Tay Luong Gate), named after a ferry dock on the same-named riverbank during the Le dynasty. On July 20, 1786, the Western Mountain army entered Thang Long through this ferry and gate, attacking the Tran Khai lord's troops stationed at the Five Dragons Tower (now the location of the Hanoi Post Office). This ferry also witnessed the retreat of Qing forces led by Ton Si Nghi following their defeat at the Khuong Thuan fort by Admiral Long on January 30, 1789 (the fifth day of the lunar new year).

description: Strolling around the shore of Hồ Hoàn Kiếm, the beloved heart of the capital, surely everyone will pause at some point before the peaceful little corners where street artists diligently sketch portraits. This art of sketching by the sacred turtle's core has quietly taken root since the difficult subsidy period. The artistic atmosphere here spreads vibrantly and intimately. Visitors from everywhere often enjoy sitting quietly on small stools, patiently posing to preserve their youth, intertwined with the curious glances of weekend strollers. Receiving a portrait that captures their very essence amidst the breezy lake space, an indescribable emotion suddenly arises in one's heart. documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Portrait painting
documents.content:
Portrait painting is a genre in painting where the primary goal is to represent a specific human subject. This form of art can also refer to the actual painted portrait itself. Historically, portraitists would create their works either by commission from wealthy patrons or out of admiration for their subjects. These portraits often served as significant historical records for both state and family archives, as well as personal mementos.

Traditionally, portrait paintings were mainly reserved for the rich and powerful. However, over time, middle-class individuals began commissioning portraits of their families and acquaintances. Today, portrait paintings continue to be commissioned by various entities including governments, corporations, groups, clubs, and individuals. Additionally, portraits can now be created using different media such as prints (etching and lithography), photography, video, and digital art.

The concept of achieving a recognizable likeness in a portrait has evolved gradually. It took many years for artists to develop the necessary skills to capture a good likeness of their subjects. According to Aristotle, the purpose of art is to convey the inner essence of the subject rather than merely their outward appearance. Artists often aim for a representative portrayal, as Edward Burne-Jones noted, emphasizing the importance of portraying character and moral qualities rather than transient expressions.

A well-executed portrait typically presents a serious, closed-lip stare, with subtle emotions conveyed through the eyes and eyebrows. The eyes are crucial for conveying the subject’s character, while the eyebrows can express a range of emotions. For instance, Gordon C. Aymar highlighted the role of the eyes in providing essential information about the subject, and the eyebrows in registering various emotional states.

Portraits can vary in size and composition, depicting the subject full-length, half-length, bust, or just the head. The subject's head can turn from a full face to a profile view, with a three-quarter view falling somewhere in between. Some portraits even feature unconventional poses, like Andrew Wyeth's "Christina's World," where the subject's back is turned to the viewer. 

The choice of medium and color palette also varies widely. For example, Pierre-Auguste Renoir used a vibrant palette in his portrait "Mme. Charpentier and her children," while Gilbert Stuart employed a more restrained approach in his portrait of George Washington. The size of the portrait can also be significant, as seen in Chuck Close's large-scale museum pieces compared to smaller, more portable works.

Creating a portrait can be a lengthy process, often requiring several sessions with the subject. The final placement of the portrait, whether in a home or a museum, can influence its design and scale. Overall, portrait painting remains a versatile and enduring form of artistic expression, capturing the essence of individuals and groups across various contexts and media.

description:
Thap Rua is a small tower located on an islet in the middle of Hoan Kiem Lake, towards the south of the lake, Hanoi, Vietnam. Though small, this architectural structure holds profound historical significance, enduring traces over time that no other landmark can replace.

Architecture
The tower combines European architectural style with two lower floors featuring gothic arched windows, but its curved roof maintains the ancient Vietnamese architectural tradition.

The tower was built on a mound of land approximately 350m2 wide, with a rectangular plan and 4 stories. The lower floor is built wider, then gradually narrows towards the upper floors. The east and west facades have 3 arched doors/windows. The south and north sides have 2 pointed arched doors/windows at the ends. The top of the two lower floors has railings running around. Four curved roof corners (đầu đao) gradually curve upwards towards the center of the peak, and on the peak is a 5-pointed star.

The lowest floor is built on a 0.8m high foundation. Its length is 6.28m while its width is 4.54m. As this floor is rectangular, its length features three doors, and its width features two doors, totaling 10 doors; inside, it is divided into three bays (gian), which connect with each other through partition doors, and their tops are also pointed like all other doors. The entire floor has 4 partition doors, totaling 14 doors.

The second floor is set back slightly, with a length of 4.8m and a width of 3.64m. It is also divided into three bays, architecturally identical to the first floor with 14 sets of doors but smaller. The third floor narrows further, 2.97m long and 1.9m wide, and only features a circular door on the east facade, with a diameter of 0.68m. Against the west wall is an altar; it is unclear who it worships and since when it has existed (some information suggests it worships the father of Nguyen Ngoc Kim). The top floor is merely a watchtower, square, with each side measuring 2m. On the east wall, above the 0.68m diameter circular door of the third floor, are three characters "Quy Sơn Tháp", meaning "Turtle Mountain Tower". Thus, from the ground of Go Rua to the top of the tower is 8.8m.

The intersection of two architectural styles, French and indigenous, creates the unique and distinct beauty of Thap Rua.

History
The tower was built on Go Rua (Turtle Mound), where King Le Thanh Tong once erected a Fishing Pavilion (Điếu Đài) for the king to fish. [1] During the Le Trung Hung period (approximately 17th-18th centuries), Lord Trinh had Ta Vong Communal House (đình Tả Vọng) built on the mound, but by the Nguyen Dynasty, no traces remained. After the French captured Hanoi in 1883, the residents around the lake dispersed. Vietnamese officials also abandoned their posts. Only Nguyen Huu Kim, a village official (chức dịch) from Tu Thap village, was appointed as an intermediary between the French forces and the Vietnamese people. He gained the trust of the new government, and soon after, he became a "ba ho" (a wealthy notable), commonly known as Ba Ho Kim. In 1886, he found that the plot of land on Go Rua was auspicious according to feng shui, and the three-story tower was completed. (The legend about whether Mr. Kim was a French collaborator and whether he arbitrarily buried his father's remains in the sacred land in the middle of the capital still lacks much convincing scientific evidence, as there are many conflicting pieces of evidence, and false propaganda should not be spread. Read more ). Therefore, this tower was initially named Thap Ba Ho Kim. Due to its beautiful location in the middle of the lake, Thap Rua naturally became a scenic landmark of Hanoi. [2][3]

During the French colonial period, a replica of the Statue of Liberty (1890-1896) was erected on the peak of Thap Rua, which the people sarcastically called "Dam Xoe Statue" (Statue of the Spreading Skirt). In the 1950s, this statue was demolished when the Vietnamese government of Prime Minister Tran Trong Kim took power, replacing the French forces.

description_vi:
Tháp Rùa là một ngọn tháp nhỏ nằm trên gò đảo giữa Hồ Hoàn Kiếm, lui về phía Nam hồ, Hà Nội, Việt Nam. Công trình kiến trúc này tuy nhỏ bé nhưng ẩn trong đó là những ý nghĩa lịch sử, dấu tích trường tồn với thời gian mà không một địa danh nào có thể thay thế được.

Kiến trúc
Ngọn tháp kết hợp phong cách kiến trúc châu Âu với hàng cửa cuộn gothic hai tầng dưới nhưng phần mái cong giữ quy thức kiến trúc cổ Việt Nam.

Ngôi tháp được xây dựng trên một gò đất rộng khoảng 350m2, bình đồ hình chữ nhật có 4 tầng, tầng dưới xây rộng hơn, rồi thu nhỏ dần lên tầng trên. Hai mặt phía đông và tây có 3 cửa cuốn. Phía nam và bắc có 2 cửa cuốn nhọn ở đầu. Đỉnh 2 tầng có lan can chạy xung quanh. Bốn đầu đao đắp uốn cong dần lên vào giữa đỉnh, trên đỉnh có hình ngôi sao 5 cánh.

Tầng dưới cùng xây trên móng cao 0,8m. Chiều dài là 6,28m trong khi chiều rộng là 4,54m. Tầng này do là hình chữ nhật nên chiều dài mở ra ba cửa, còn chiều ngang mở ra hai cửa, tất cả là 10 cửa; bên trong phân ra ba gian, các gian thông với nhau bằng các cửa ngăn, đỉnh cũng nhọn như tất cả các cửa khác. Cả tầng có 4 cửa ngăn, tổng cộng 14 cửa.

Tầng hai xây lùi vào một chút, chiều dài 4,8m, chiều rộng 3,64m, cũng chia ra ba gian, kiến trúc y như tầng một với 14 bộ cửa nhưng nhỏ hơn. Tầng ba thu nhỏ hơn nữa, dài 2,97m, rộng 1,9m, chỉ mở một cửa hình tròn ở mặt phía đông, đường kính 0,68m. Sát tường phía tây có một bàn thờ, không rõ thờ ai và có từ lúc nào (một số thông tin được cho là thờ cha của Nguyễn Ngọc Kim). Tầng đỉnh chỉ như một vọng lâu, vuông vức, mỗi bề 2m. Trên tường mặt phía đông, bên trên cửa tròn có đường kính là 0.68m của tầng ba có ba chữ Quy Sơn Tháp, nghĩa là tháp Núi Rùa. Như vậy, từ nền đất Gò Rùa lên đến đỉnh tháp là 8,8m.

Với sự giao thoa giữa hai lối kiến trúc là kiến trúc Pháp và kiến trúc bản địa tạo nên nét đẹp độc đáo, riêng biệt của Tháp Rùa.

Lịch sử
Tháp xây trên gò Rùa nơi xưa từ thời vua Lê Thánh Tông đã dựng Điếu Đài ở đó để nhà vua câu cá.[1] Sang thời Lê Trung Hưng (khoảng thế kỷ 17-thế kỷ 18) thì chúa Trịnh cho xây đình Tả Vọng trên gò nhưng sang thời nhà Nguyễn thì không còn dấu tích gì. Sau khi Pháp hạ thành Hà Nội năm 1883 thì dân vùng ven hồ xiêu tán cả. Các quan Việt cũng bỏ sở nhiệm. Riêng có Nguyễn Hữu Kim, chức dịch làng Tự Tháp được cử làm trung gian giữa quân Pháp và người Việt, lại được chính quyền mới tín nhiệm nên ít lâu sau ông trở thành bá hộ, tục gọi là Bá hộ Kim. Năm 1886 thấy huyệt đất trên gò Rùa hợp phong thủy thành nhưng ngọn tháp ba tầng vẫn được hoàn tất. (truyền thuyết về việc liệu ông Kim có làm tay sai cho Pháp hay không và việc tự ý đưa hài cốt cha chôn ở mảnh đất linh thiêng giữa thủ đô hay không vẫn còn chưa có nhiều chứng cứ khoa học thuyết phục bởi có rất nhiều chứng cứ khác nhau gây mâu thuẫn, không nên tuyên truyền sai lệch. Đọc thêm  ). Vì vậy nên ban đầu Tháp này có tên là Tháp Bá hộ Kim. Vì vị trí đẹp giữa hồ, Tháp Rùa nghiễm nhiên biến thành thắng tích Hà Nội.[2][3]

Thời Pháp thuộc, trên đỉnh Tháp Rùa có dựng một phiên bản của tượng Nữ Thần Tự Do (1890-1896) mà dân chúng biếm gọi là tượng Đầm Xòe. Sang thập niên 1950 tượng này đã bị phá bỏ khi chính phủ Việt Nam của thủ tướng Trần Trọng Kim nắm chính quyền thay cho quân Pháp.

Thap Rua, a significant symbol of history and culture in Hanoi, Vietnam, stands as one of the most revered landmarks within the picturesque Hoan Kiem Lake. Nestled on a small island in the northern part of the lake, this ancient structure is not merely a tourist attraction but a profound representation of Vietnamese resilience and patriotism. Constructed during the mid-19th century under the reign of King Thieu Tri, Thap Rua's origins and exact purpose remain somewhat shrouded in mystery, though it is believed to have been built to commemorate the legendary victory of Le Loi, the national hero who triumphed over the Ming invaders in the 15th century.

The tower itself, crafted from durable stone, has endured the test of time, albeit with some wear and tear due to weathering and environmental factors. Despite these challenges, Thap Rua retains its majestic charm and solemnity, drawing thousands of visitors annually. The structure's historical significance is deeply intertwined with the legendary tale of the sacred sword returned to the Golden Turtle, which gave rise to the name Hoan Kiem Lake, meaning "Lake of the Returned Sword." According to folklore, after Le Loi defeated the Ming forces, he returned the magical sword to the Golden Turtle at this very spot, thus earning the lake its enduring moniker.

Thap Rua's presence through centuries reflects the dynamic changes and tumultuous periods of Vietnamese history, from wars to modern peace and development. It stands as a testament to the indomitable spirit and unwavering resolve of the Vietnamese people, serving as a constant reminder of their perseverance against adversity. This iconic site is more than just a tourist destination; it is a source of inspiration for those delving into the rich tapestry of Vietnamese history. Its proud and meaningful existence continues to instill a sense of pride in every Vietnamese heart and captivates the imagination of visitors from around the globe.

The cultural importance of Thap Rua extends beyond its physical form, embodying a blend of natural beauty and architectural grandeur.
