Nestled in the heart of Hanoi’s Dong Da District, at the address 58 Van Mieu Street, stands the majestic Van Mieu Gate, a monumental entrance to the revered Temple of Literature complex. Established in 1070 during the reign of Emperor Ly Thanh Tong of the Ly Dynasty, the gate was constructed concurrently with the founding of the temple, which was intended to honor Confucius and serve as a symbol of the nation's commitment to education and cultural heritage. The gate's architectural design reflects traditional Vietnamese craftsmanship, featuring a two-story tam quan structure with three imposing arched vaults, each archway framed by intricately carved wooden lintels. The red-brick body, now covered in a layer of moss, contrasts beautifully with the solemn yin-yang tiled roof system, adding a touch of antiquity and serenity to its appearance.

The gate's most distinctive feature is the embossed hoanh phi plaque, prominently displayed on the upper floor, inscribed with the Chinese characters "Văn Miếu Môn," signifying its role as the main entrance to the sacred site. This plaque not only marks the gateway but also serves as a testament to the enduring legacy of Confucian learning in Vietnam. The gate itself is situated on a brick courtyard, surrounded by the shade of ancient trees whose branches stretch out towards the bustling street nearby, creating a harmonious blend of tranquility and urban vibrancy.

Today, the Van Mieu Gate remains a focal point for both cultural reverence and tourism. It is a common sight to see eager tourists and groups of students, often dressed in traditional ao dai, queuing up to enter the complex. During the Tet holiday season, the area around the gate becomes particularly lively, with streams of visitors arriving to partake in the festivities and imbibe the spirit of knowledge and tradition. The gate acts as an invisible time wall, separating the noisy, bustling world outside from the serene scholarly space within, offering visitors a moment of reflection and a profound sense of connection to the rich cultural and spiritual heritage of Vietnam.

Hồ Văn Mười, born on August 10, 1969, in Thu Bồn, Danang City (formerly Duy Hòa, Duy Xuyen, Quang Nam Province), is a police officer and political figure in the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. He currently serves as a member of the Central Committee of the Communist Party of Vietnam's 14th term, Deputy Secretary of the Provincial Committee of Lam Dong Province, Secretary of the Party Committee, and Chairman of the People's Council of Lam Dong Province, concurrently holding administrative leadership positions in the province.

Previously, Hồ Văn Mười was Deputy Secretary of the Provincial Committee of Dak Nong Province, Secretary of the Party Committee, Chairman of the People's Council of Dak Nong Province, Secretary of the Party Committee, Director of the Dak Nong Provincial Police Department, Deputy Chief of the Financial and Economic Security Bureau under the Ministry of Public Security, and Deputy Chief of the Internal Security Bureau under the Ministry of Public Security.

Born in Thu Bồn, Đà Nẵng, he grew up and completed his secondary education there. In 1987, he moved to Hanoi to study at the University of Public Security (now the People's Security Academy), where he earned a Bachelor’s degree in Public Security. Subsequently, he obtained additional Bachelor’s degrees in Economics and State Administration, as well as a Master’s degree in Law. Hồ Văn Mười joined the Communist Party of Vietnam on December 28, 1993, becoming a full member on December 28, 1994. Throughout his career, he attended various courses at the Ho Chi Minh National Political Academy and received a Master’s degree in Political Theory. Currently, he resides in Nam Gia Nghĩa Ward, Lam Dong Province.

In July 1993, after graduating from university, Hồ Văn Mười began his career as an officer and investigator at the First Political Protection Bureau under the Ministry of Interior. In March 1993, the Third Political Protection Bureau was established within the Counterintelligence General Corps, and he transferred to become an officer and investigator there. Following the separation of the Ministry of Public Security, he joined the Security General Corps, rising to Deputy Head of the Department and Assistant Deputy Chief of the Security General Corps. In October 2006, he was reassigned to Dong Nai Province, joining the Party Committee of the Dong Nai Provincial Police Department, where he served as Secretary of the Party Branch and Head of the Economic Security Department for six years.

In September 2012, Hồ Văn Mười was transferred to Ho Chi Minh City, assuming the position of Deputy Secretary of the Party Branch and Deputy Chief of the Financial and Economic Security Bureau under the Security General Corps in Ho Chi Minh City. In September 2015, he was appointed Secretary of the Party Committee and Deputy Chief of the Fifth Political Protection Bureau under the Security General Corps. In August 2018, following organizational restructuring within the Ministry of Public Security, he was assigned as a member of the Standing Committee, Secretary of the Party Committee, and Deputy Chief of the Internal Security Bureau in Ho Chi Minh City. On December 6, 2019, Minister of Public Security To Lam reassigned him to the Dak Nong Provincial Police Department, where he assumed the role of Director of the Dak Nong Provincial Police Department.

Upon his transfer to Dak Nong Province in December 2019, Hồ Văn Mười was elected to the Standing Committee of the Dak Nong Provincial Party Committee at the 11th term. At the 12th term Dak Nong Provincial Party Congress in October 2020, he was re-elected to the Standing Committee

Van Lake, nestled within the UNESCO World Heritage site of the Van Temple - National Academy, is emerging as a vibrant cultural hub that seamlessly blends traditional heritage with contemporary creativity. This picturesque body of water, located opposite the main entrance of the Van Temple, is transforming into a dynamic space where ancient traditions meet modern life through a variety of innovative and engaging activities.

According to Dr. Le Xuan Kieu, Director of the Van Temple - National Academy Cultural and Scientific Activities Center, the area around Van Lake has undergone significant renovations aimed at preserving and enhancing its historical significance while fostering a rich cultural experience. Over the past year, the center has developed Van Lake into a multifaceted destination that integrates elements of heritage, artisanal crafts, artistic performances, culinary delights, exhibitions, and educational workshops.

Van Lake's strategic location within the Van Temple complex provides it with a unique advantage, offering visitors a serene and culturally rich setting. The lake's surroundings feature a harmonious blend of natural beauty and historical charm, making it an ideal venue for a wide array of cultural events and community activities. Regularly scheduled workshops showcase traditional crafts such as Dong Ho paintings, lacquerware, Bat Trang pottery, silk weaving from Meo Village in Hung Yen, bamboo and rattan weaving from Phu Vinh, and traditional paper-making techniques. These hands-on demonstrations not only preserve local crafts but also offer tourists an immersive experience into Vietnamese artistry.

In addition to these craft workshops, Van Lake hosts a diverse range of cultural programs including folk music and dance performances, modern art exhibitions, and educational sessions focused on heritage preservation. The lake's ambiance is further enhanced by a variety of food stalls serving traditional dishes like lotus tea from Tay Ho, herbal teas, Hanoi rice cakes, bun oc (snail noodle soup), bun cha (grilled pork and noodle bowl), and other regional specialties. This culinary diversity reflects the rich gastronomic heritage of Vietnam, providing visitors with a taste of local flavors.

The cultural significance of Van Lake extends beyond individual exhibits to create a cohesive ecosystem of experiences. It serves as a platform for various organizations, schools, embassies, and businesses to host large-scale events, fostering a collaborative environment that enriches the cultural landscape of Hanoi. The lake's evening activities are particularly noteworthy, offering a different set of experiences compared to daytime visits. Visitors can explore over thirty traditional-style booths arranged around the lake, each offering unique insights into Vietnamese culture and craftsmanship.

Van Lake's development aligns with the broader vision of the Van Temple complex to become a new cultural industry center in Hanoi. This ambitious goal aims to transform Van Lake into a distinctive cultural experience zone, attracting both domestic and international tourists. To achieve this, the center plans to organize regular themed events starting from July 2026, focusing on themes such as "Strolling Around Van Lake – Living with Heritage." These events will run daily from 8 AM to 8 PM, with extended hours during Hanoi's nighttime economy period. Every Saturday, visitors can participate in workshops and cultural experience programs, while the last Sunday of each month will feature special events showcasing artisans and traditional crafts.

The integration of Van Lake with the Inner Temple and Van Lake itself creates a seamless cultural journey for visitors. This interconnectedness enhances the overall experience of exploring the Van Temple complex, allowing tourists to transition smoothly between historical sites and interactive cultural spaces. The addition of Van Lake as an experiential zone complements the traditional reverence of the Inner Temple, offering a more dynamic and engaging visit for both domestic and international travelers.

With nearly one million visitors to the Van Temple complex in the first six months of the year, approximately 60% of whom were international tourists, Van Lake's expansion is expected to significantly boost tourist interest. The cultural activities and interactive experiences at Van Lake provide a fresh perspective on Vietnamese heritage, making it a must-visit destination for those interested in understanding the rich cultural tapestry of Hanoi.

Van Lake, also known as Ho Van or Ho Minh Duong, is a significant historical site nestled within the heart of Hanoi, Vietnam, specifically at Number 58 Quoc Tu Giam Street, Phuong Van Mieu, Dong Da District. This tranquil body of water is not only a testament to the rich cultural heritage of Vietnam but also a living museum that encapsulates the essence of Vietnamese scholarly traditions and intellectual pursuits. The lake's serene presence is a direct reflection of its historical importance, serving as a venue for scholars to engage in literary critiques and discussions during the feudal era.

Van Lake is situated within the expansive grounds of the Van Mieu - Quoc Tu Giam complex, a UNESCO World Heritage Site that has been a cornerstone of Vietnamese education since the early days of the Le dynasty in the 15th century. The lake's original purpose was to host gatherings where scholars would convene to critique poetry and prose, thereby upholding the tradition of academic excellence and scholarly discourse. At the center of the lake lies a small hill called Kim Chau, which once housed a pavilion known as Phan Thuy Dien, where scholars would gather to discuss literature and Confucian philosophy. Although the pavilion no longer stands, two stone steles remain on the hill, commemorating the beauty and significance of the lake. One of these steles, erected in 1865 during the reign of Emperor Tu Duc, documents the restoration of the Van Mieu and the dredging of the lake in 1863.

The lake itself is rectangular in shape, covering an area of approximately 12,000 square meters, surrounded by sturdy walls that protect its historical integrity. The central feature of the lake is the small hill, Kim Chau, which serves as a focal point for visitors and a reminder of the scholarly activities that once took place there. The surrounding area is adorned with ancient trees that provide shade and contribute to the tranquil atmosphere of the lake. The pathways around the lake are wide and well-maintained, ensuring easy access for visitors while preserving the natural beauty of the site. The lake's waters are kept clear through regular maintenance and drainage systems, enhancing its aesthetic appeal and ecological balance.

Throughout its history, Van Lake has undergone various transformations and restorations, each aimed at maintaining its historical value and cultural significance. During the Nguyen dynasty, the lake continued to serve as a cultural space for organizing examinations, traditional festivals, and folk art performances. Despite the passage of time and the changes brought about by modernization, Van Lake retains its original charm and remains a vital part of the educational and cultural landscape of Vietnam.

Today, Van Lake is a vibrant hub of cultural activities, hosting events such as calligraphy exhibitions, traditional book fairs, and folk art performances. These events attract both locals and tourists, offering a unique opportunity to experience the rich cultural heritage of Vietnam. Calligraphy exhibitions showcase works from renowned artists, providing insight into the art of calligraphy and the reverence for learning that has been a hallmark of Vietnamese culture. Traditional book fairs feature stalls selling antique and contemporary books, author signings, and discussions with prominent writers, appealing to readers of all ages. Folk art performances include traditional music, puppetry, and dance, bringing to life the cultural traditions of Vietnam in a dynamic and engaging manner.

In addition to these cultural events, Van Lake also hosts educational programs and guided tours designed for students and scholars. These initiatives aim to preserve and promote the historical and cultural significance of the site, ensuring that future generations can appreciate and learn from the legacy of Van Mieu - Quoc Tu Giam. The lake's serene ambiance and historical significance make it a must-visit destination for anyone interested in the rich tapestry of Vietnamese history and culture. Visitors can immerse themselves in the tranquil surroundings, reflecting on the scholarly traditions that have shaped the nation's intellectual heritage over centuries.

The theatre's performances have captivated audiences from more than forty countries across Asia, Europe, America, and Australia, leaving an indelible mark on the global stage.

Water puppetry, a distinctive art form exclusive to Vietnam, traces its origins back to the eleventh century, emerging from the rural villages of the Red River Delta region in northern Vietnam. This ancient tradition was born out of the agricultural lifestyle, where villagers would entertain themselves by playing with puppets during the rice harvest season when fields were flooded. The theatre's performances today showcase a carefully curated selection of over 400 traditional water puppet routines, each one meticulously crafted and performed by skilled artists who have honed their craft over generations.

The theatre itself is a vibrant hub of cultural activity, featuring a unique stage setup designed specifically for water puppetry. Large bamboo poles support the puppets beneath the water surface, allowing puppeteers to manipulate them from behind a curtain, creating the illusion that the puppets are moving gracefully across the water. This ingenious method of performance combines traditional Vietnamese music played on instruments such as the dan nguyet (two-stringed fiddle), sao (flute), dan tranh (zither), tam thap luc (36-string zither), dan bau (monochord), and cheo folk songs, which infuse the performances with a sense of nostalgia and cultural richness.

Among the many captivating performances, the theatre presents a variety of acts that reflect different aspects of Vietnamese culture and folklore. One of the most beloved characters is the humorous figure known for his witty remarks and ability to bridge the gap between the audience and the puppet world. Another highlight is the dragon and phoenix dance, symbolizing the importance of these mythical creatures in Vietnamese folklore, representing ancestral spirits and marital fidelity respectively. 

The theatre also showcases scenes depicting the tranquil life of a Vietnamese village, where the gentle sounds of a flute evoke a deep sense of longing for one’s homeland among those far from home. Other performances illustrate the daily lives of Vietnamese farmers, showcasing their diligent work in the fields, reflecting the hardworking spirit of the Vietnamese people. Additionally, there are performances that recount historical legends, such as the tale of King Le Loi returning the magic sword to the Golden Turtle, an event that gave rise to the name Hoan Kiem Lake, now the central landmark of Hanoi.

A Performance is an act or process of staging or presenting a play, concert, or other forms of entertainment. It can also be understood as the action or process of carrying out or accomplishing an action, task, or function. In the workplace, job performance is the hypothesized conception or requirements of a role, divided into two types: contextual and task. Task performance is dependent on cognitive ability, while contextual performance is influenced by personality. Task performance relates to behavioral roles recognized in job descriptions and remuneration systems, directly impacting organizational performance. Contextual performance, on the other hand, involves value-based contributions that are not explicitly covered by job descriptions or compensation, adding indirect support to organizational performance. Citizenship performance, similar to contextual performance, refers to individual activities that support organizational culture.

In the realm of performing arts, a Performance generally involves an event where a performer or group of performers present one or more works of art to an audience. In instrumental music and drama, a Performance is often referred to as a "play." Performers usually participate in rehearsals beforehand to practice the work. An effective Performance is determined by the achieved skills and competency of the performer, also known as the level of skill and knowledge. In 1994, Spencer and McClelland defined competency as a combination of motives, traits, self-concepts, attitudes, cognitive behavior skills, and content knowledge that differentiates superior performers from average ones. Additionally, a Performance describes the way in which an actor performs, and in a solo capacity, it may refer to a mime artist, comedian, conjurer, magician, or other entertainer.

Another aspect of Performance that gained popularity in the early 20th century is performance art. Originating with Dada and Russian constructivism groups, this form focuses on avant-garde poetry readings and live paintings meant to be viewed by an audience. It can be scripted or completely improvised and may include audience participation. The emergence of abstract expressionism in the 1950s, with artists like Jackson Pollock and Willem de Kooning, led to action painting, a technique that emphasizes the dynamic movements of artists as they apply paint and other media to canvas or glass. For these artists, the motion of putting paint on canvas was as valuable as the finished painting, leading them to document their work in film, such as the short film "Jackson Pollock 51" (1951).

Situationists in France, led by Guy Debord, combined avant-garde art with revolutionary politics to incite everyday acts of anarchy. Their "Naked City Map" (1957) fragmented the 19 sections of Paris, using techniques like détournement and abstraction to deconstruct the geometry and order of a typical city map. At the New School for Social Research in New York, John Cage and Allan Kaprow developed happening performance art, which included the audience in chaotic and spontaneous acts. These happenings challenged traditional art conventions and encouraged artists to consider the role of the audience. In Japan, the 1954 Gutai group, led by Yoshihara Jiro, Kanayama Akira, Murakami Saburo, Kazuo Shiraga, and Shimamoto Shozo, brought the materials of art-making to life through body movement, blurring the lines between art and theater. Kazuo Shiraga's "Challenging Mud" (1955) exemplifies this approach, as he rolled and moved in mud, using his body as the art-making tool, emphasizing the temporary nature of performance art.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Boat Racing
documents.content:
The UIM E1 Series, an all-electric international offshore powerboat racing series sanctioned by the Union Internationale Motonautique, made its debut in February 2024 with the E1 Jeddah GP in Saudi Arabia. This series was conceived in early 2020 by Rodi Basso, a former Formula One engineer and McLaren Applied business director, and Alejandro Agag, the founder of Formula E and Extreme E. They approached Sophi Horne, who had previously focused on electric leisure boats, to design the race boat. The series was officially announced at the Monaco Yacht Club on September 25, 2020, and the boat was unveiled in June 2021, along with a partnership with Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

Testing of the RaceBird, the all-electric hydrofoil boat, commenced on April 21, 2022, when Luca Ferrari, a former powerboat champion, piloted the prototype on the River Po in Italy. The boat then made its public debut at the Venice Boat Show in June 2022, where model Cara Delevingne assisted with the launch. The first public race occurred in September 2022 during the World Port Days in Rotterdam, with Sam Coleman piloting the RaceBird. In September 2023, the series returned to Rotterdam, this time featuring four RaceBirds in competition, with Oban Duncan emerging as the champion.

The inaugural 2024 season featured 9 teams and 18 pilots, with Team Brady winning the championship. The second season in 2025 began in January in Jeddah, with the debut of a new team led by LeBron James. Despite the addition of new talent, Team Brady retained its championship title after seven races.

Each race weekend consists of free practice and qualifying sessions on the first day, followed by group races, a race-off, a place race, and finals on the second day. Pilots alternate driving duties throughout these sessions. Each race lasts six laps, including a mandatory short lap and long lap that can be taken at any point during the race. The course boundaries are marked by electronic anchorless buoys called SmartMarks, which are less invasive than traditional buoys.

The Blue Impact championship, introduced during the inaugural season, challenges teams to work towards a better future through activism such as aquatic conservation and restoration programs and marine habitat research. Fans and an expert jury vote for the champion at the end of the season. Team Brady won the inaugural Blue Impact Championship.

The RaceBird, designed by SeaBird Technologies and manufactured by Victory Marine, features a 150kW electric motor and a 35kWh battery capacity, allowing it to reach a top speed of 50 knots (58 MPH/93 KPH). The boat is 7.5 meters long and uses carbon fiber hydrofoils that lift the vessel when it reaches 17 knots. The cockpit is designed for a single pilot, equipped with a steering wheel and pedals similar to those found in a single-seater race car. The electric powertrain is developed by Mercury Racing, and the rechargeable batteries come from Kreisel Electric. Currently, all teams run identical boats, but the goal is to allow teams to design their own vehicles in future years.

The series initially aimed to represent various cities and countries, starting with the Venice Racing Team. However, it evolved to feature celebrity owners such as Tom Brady, Will Smith, Virat Kohli, and Rafael Nadal. Each team must include both male and female pilots, mirroring the regulations of Extreme E. The UIM E1 Pilot Academy trains a new generation of racers, inviting athletes with experience in motors

In the charming city of Hội An, nestled along the picturesque coastline of central Vietnam, a unique cultural experience awaits visitors in the form of Children Playing with Water, also known as the traditional art of water puppetry. This ancient performance art has its roots in the fertile plains of northern Vietnam, emerging around the 10th century, and has since spread to various regions across the country, including the historic town of Hội An.

The year 2014 marked a significant milestone for Hội An when the local government, supported by the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, initiated a project to develop and showcase traditional water puppetry performances specifically tailored for tourists visiting the ancient town. The program was designed not only to entertain but also to preserve and promote the rich cultural heritage of Hội An.

The performances feature a range of traditional acts that have been enjoyed for generations, such as "Bơi bắt cá" (Fishing), "Đua thuyền" (Boat Racing), "Múa tứ linh" (Dance of the Four Mythical Beasts), and "Nhi đồng hí thủy" (Children Playing with Water). These captivating shows are complemented by new segments that reflect the distinct cultural identity of Hội An, including "Múa Apsara" (Dance of the Apsaras) and "Truyền thuyết con Cù" (Legend of the Turtle).

Each performance is a testament to the intricate craftsmanship and artistic skill required to bring these puppets to life. The puppets themselves are meticulously crafted from wood, often painted with vibrant colors and adorned with delicate costumes that reflect the traditional attire of Vietnamese people. They are manipulated by skilled puppeteers standing behind a waist-high rectangular pool of water, using long bamboo rods to control the movements of the puppets beneath the surface. The puppeteers must possess great dexterity and coordination to perform complex maneuvers while remaining hidden from the audience's view.

The water puppetry performances in Hội An offer more than just entertainment; they serve as a window into the cultural traditions and historical narratives of the region. The shows are performed in a specially constructed venue that blends seamlessly with the surrounding architecture of Hội An, creating an immersive experience for visitors. The atmosphere is one of enchantment, where the sounds of traditional music and the graceful movements of the puppets transport spectators back in time to a world of folklore and legend.

Visitors to Hội An can witness these performances as part of their cultural exploration of the town, which is renowned for its well-preserved ancient streets, historic temples, and vibrant markets. The water puppetry shows provide a unique opportunity to engage with the local culture, offering insights into the daily life and traditions of the Vietnamese people. The performances are particularly popular among families, as they captivate both children and adults alike with their lively storytelling and colorful visuals.

Overall, the water puppetry performances in Hội An represent a harmonious blend of artistry, history, and community spirit. They not only entertain but also educate visitors about the rich cultural heritage of the region, making them an essential part of any visit to this enchanting town.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Dragon Dance
documents.content:
The Dragon Dance, a traditional Chinese cultural performance, is often seen during festive celebrations, particularly during Chinese New Year. This dance involves a team of skilled dancers manipulating a long, flexible dragon puppet using poles placed at regular intervals along its length. The dragon, a symbol of China's rich culture, is believed to bring good fortune and luck to the community, with longer dragons signifying greater blessings. Historically, the dragon embodies qualities such as power, dignity, fertility, wisdom, and auspiciousness, and its movements in the dance symbolize these attributes.

The origins of the Dragon Dance can be traced back to the Han dynasty, where ancient texts describe various forms of the dance. During times of drought, rain dances featuring dragon figures were performed, as the dragon was associated with rain in ancient China. For instance, the dragon Yinglong was considered a rain deity, and the Shenlong could control the amount of wind and rain. Dong Zhongshu’s “Luxuriant Dew of the Spring and Autumn Annals” mentions a ritual where clay dragon figures were used in dances to appeal for rain, with the number of dragons, their length, and color varying according to the season. Additionally, during the Han dynasty, dragon dances were part of the popular baixi variety shows, where performers dressed as dragons or other creatures entertained audiences.

Zhang Heng’s “Lyric Essay on Western Capital” describes performances where dancers dressed as green dragons played flutes, and another act where fish transformed into dragons. One such dance, known as "fish-dragon extending," featured a mythical creature transforming from a flounder into a dragon, entertaining foreign guests at the Han court. However, these ancient dances differed significantly from the modern Dragon Dance, which uses lightweight, maneuverable dragons.

References to dragon dances continued into the Tang and Song dynasties. The Song dynasty work “Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital” describes dragon lanterns used during the Lantern Festival, which were constructed from grass and cloth and illuminated with candles. These lanterns were carried and paraded by performers through the streets at night. Over time, various regional dragon dances developed, such as the Fenghua Cloth Dragon from Zhejiang, which dates back to the 1200s, and the Tongliang County dragon dance, which evolved from snake totem worship during the Ming dynasty and gained popularity in the Qing dynasty.

In the modern era, the government of the People's Republic of China promoted traditional folk dances, contributing to the widespread popularity of the contemporary Dragon Dance. Today, the popular form features a smaller, lighter dragon that can be controlled more easily, contrasting with the heavier, longer Southern Dragon designed for processions rather than agile movements. There are many regional variations, including the Zhanjiang dragon dance, where the dragon's body is formed by a human chain of dozens to hundreds of performers, and the Pujiang County dragon dance, where the dragon is made from wooden stools. Over 700 different dragon dances exist across China and Chinese communities worldwide.

Traditionally, retired dragon puppets are burned, but some historical remnants are preserved. The head of the oldest surviving dragon, dating back to 1878 and named Moo Lung, is displayed at the Bok Kai Temple in Marysville, California. Fragments of similarly aged dragons are also kept at the Sweetwater County Historical Museum in Green River, Wyoming.

In the vibrant heart of Hanoi, the Dragon Dance, a cherished tradition steeped in history and culture, was set to captivate audiences once again in 2020. The event, organized by the Hanoi Cultural Center, aimed to celebrate the rich heritage of the city and its people, while also serving as a significant cultural and social activity that would invigorate the local community and attract tourists from both within Vietnam and abroad. This was the sixth time that Hanoi had hosted such a grand spectacle, each iteration dedicated to showcasing the unique artistry and cultural significance of the Dragon Dance.

Scheduled for October 3rd, the Dragon Dance festival was to take place from 9:00 AM to 12:00 PM at the picturesque venue of the Lý Thái Tổ statue garden, located along Đinh Tiên Hoàng Street and the serene shores of Hoàn Kiếm Lake. The event promised to be a visual feast, blending traditional dance with the majestic movements of the dragon, a symbol deeply rooted in Vietnamese folklore and history.

The Dragon Dance, a performance that embodies the spirit of strength, nobility, and divine protection, has been a cornerstone of Vietnamese culture for centuries. According to legend, the decision by King Lý Công Uẩn to move the capital from Hoa Lư to Đại La, renaming it Thăng Long, signified a profound belief in the future prosperity and might of the nation. This act not only reflected the king's visionary leadership but also established the dragon as a symbol of the city's enduring legacy and the aspirations of its people.

For the 2020 festival, thirteen teams from various districts and counties across Hanoi were invited to participate, each bringing their own unique interpretation of the dragon dance. These teams included representatives from Ba Đình, Hoàng Mai, Tây Hồ, Hoàn Kiếm, Long Biên, Cầu Giấy, Nam Từ Liêm, Phúc Thọ, Đông Anh, Thường Tín, Thanh Trì, Đan Phượng, and Thanh Oai. Each team was tasked with presenting a five to seven-minute performance that featured one or more dragons alongside other mythical creatures like the phoenix, tortoise, and unicorn, all set to music and accompanied by narration that conveyed the themes and messages of their respective acts.

The performances were designed to evoke a sense of pride and unity among the participants and spectators alike, celebrating the rich tapestry of Vietnamese history and culture. Through intricate choreography and dynamic movements, the dancers aimed to recreate historical events and highlight the resilience and spirit of the Vietnamese people. The dragon, with its fluid motions and powerful presence, served as a metaphor for the nation's journey through time, embodying the strength and determination required to overcome challenges and thrive.

The organizers emphasized the importance of preserving traditional elements while allowing for innovation and creativity in the performances. Teams were encouraged to incorporate advanced techniques such as formation displays, water effects, and acrobatic maneuvers to enhance the visual impact of their dances. Additionally, the costumes and decorations were required to reflect the cultural norms and aesthetic values of the Vietnamese people, ensuring that the performances remained authentic and respectful of the traditions they sought to honor.

As the festival approached, anticipation grew among the local population and visitors alike. The Dragon Dance festival was not just a showcase of artistic talent but also a platform for cultural exchange and community engagement. It provided an opportunity for artists and performers to share their skills and insights, fostering a sense of camaraderie and mutual respect among the participating teams. Moreover, the event served as a testament to the enduring appeal of traditional arts in modern times, bridging the gap between past and present and reinforcing the cultural identity of Hanoi.

Visitors to the festival could expect to witness a series of captivating performances that combined the grace and power of the dragon dance with the vibrant energy of the local community. The atmosphere around Hoàn Kiếm Lake was sure to be electric, with the sounds of traditional music and the rhythmic movements of the dancers creating a lively and festive ambiance. As the dragon dancers moved through their routines, they brought to life stories of heroism, resilience, and national pride, offering a glimpse into the soul of Vietnam and its people.

In summary, the Dragon Dance festival in Hanoi was much more than a simple performance; it was a celebration of cultural heritage, a display of artistic excellence, and a testament to the enduring spirit of the Vietnamese people. Through this event, the city of Hanoi continued to honor its storied past while looking towards a future filled with promise and possibility.

documents.content:
Fishing for Fishies is the fourteenth studio album by the Australian psychedelic rock band King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, released on April 26, 2019, through Flightless and ATO Records. The album's existence was first hinted at on January 21, 2019, when the band shared a photograph on social media of themselves in the studio with the caption "new music coming soon." This teaser came over a year after the release of their previous album, Gumboot Soup, which was one of five albums they had released in 2017.

Following the teaser, the band released the album's first single, "Cyboogie," as a 7-inch single with "Acarine" as the B-side, accompanied by a music video. In March 2019, details of the album, including the title, cover art, and track listing, were leaked to various online stores. The band confirmed the leak on March 11 and officially announced the album through their social media channels. The next day, the title track "Fishing for Fishies" was released as a music video on YouTube. On March 28, the album's third single, "Boogieman Sam," was also released.

Band frontman Stu Mackenzie described the album as an attempt to create a blues record, but noted that the songs took on their own unique directions. He explained, "We tried to make a blues record. A blues-boogie-shuffle kinda-thing, but the songs kept fighting it—or maybe it was us fighting them. Ultimately though we let the songs guide us this time; we let them have their own personalities and forge their own path. Paths of light, paths of darkness."

During the recording process, sections of the album were recorded at a house owned by members of Tropical Fuck Storm. At these sessions, both bands recorded a large jam session known as the "Hat Jam." Parts of this jam were later used in the first single of King Gizzard's 2022 album, Omnium Gatherum, titled "The Dripping Tap," and in Tropical Fuck Storm's joint EP with King Gizzard, Satanic Slumber Party.

Before the official release of Fishing for Fishies, the band uploaded a short behind-the-scenes documentary titled "How to Gut a Fishie" to YouTube, featuring clips from the recording sessions of the album and the Hat Jam.

The album received generally positive reviews, although some critics found it less compelling than others. Sophie Kemp of Pitchfork rated it 4.8 out of 10, commenting that the album "is vaguely about the environment, but mostly about goofing off with expensive equipment in service to the concept of 'boogie oogie ooging'." NME, however, rated it four stars, praising it as "their most accessible and immediate album to date." DIY's Connor Thirlwell gave the album three and a half stars, noting that "King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard still know how to kick ass."

Fishing for Fishies was nominated for Best Blues and Roots Album at the ARIA Music Awards of 2019, though it ultimately lost to The Teskey Brothers for their album Run Home Slow.

The Four Sacred Beasts Dance, a vibrant and culturally significant tradition, has been a cherished part of Vietnamese festive celebrations for centuries. This dance, which draws its inspiration from the four sacred beasts—Thanh Long (Azure Dragon), Bạch Hổ (White Tiger), Huyền Vũ (Black Tortoise), and Chu Tước (Red Phoenix)—embodies the essence of ancient beliefs and traditions. These mythical creatures symbolize the four cardinal directions and the elements of fire, water, earth, and wind, respectively, reflecting a deep connection to the natural world and celestial bodies.

Originating from the ancient capital of Thang Long, the Four Sacred Beasts Dance was initially performed at the imperial court during various ceremonies under the Nguyen dynasty. It was later adapted into a more widespread folk tradition, celebrated during festivals and community gatherings. The dance is not only a form of entertainment but also a spiritual practice that brings blessings and harmony to the land and its people.

The preparation of the costumes for the dancers is a meticulous process that involves crafting elaborate headpieces and body coverings. The heads of the dragons, tigers, tortoises, and phoenixes are made from paperboard, intricately painted with vibrant colors and adorned with decorative elements. The bodies are fashioned from silk or brocade, embroidered with metallic threads and colorful yarns, creating a dazzling display of traditional craftsmanship. Each dancer dons these elaborate costumes, embodying the spirit of their respective beast through graceful and dynamic movements.

The performance itself is a harmonious blend of music and movement, guided by the rhythms of traditional eight-tone music. There are no lyrics sung along with the dance; instead, the dancers move in sync with the musical beats, executing a series of choreographed gestures that reflect the characteristics of each animal. The azure dragon's fluidity, the white tiger's strength, the black tortoise's stability, and the red phoenix's elegance are all conveyed through precise and expressive motions.

In modern times, the tradition of the Four Sacred Beasts Dance continues to thrive, particularly in rural areas where it remains an integral part of local culture. One notable example is the village of Huong Son in My Duc district, Hanoi, which boasts three teams dedicated to this art form. Notably, the team at Den Duc Khe temple comprises exclusively elderly performers who have dedicated their lives to preserving this heritage. According to Mr. Pham Van Hai, a member of the Duc Khe team, the tradition was introduced by General Cao Viet Minh during the Hung kings' era, teaching villagers not only agricultural practices but also the art of the Four Sacred Beasts Dance. This legacy has been passed down through generations, with each new cohort learning from their elders to ensure the continuity of this cultural treasure.

During the Lunar New Year festivities, the teams are especially active, performing throughout the villages and at significant sites such as the Temple of Literature and Chua Huong (Perfume Pagoda). The dancers can be seen in action from the fifth day of the lunar new year onwards, participating in various temple fairs and community events until the end of the first lunar month. The Duc Khe team, in particular, has gained recognition beyond their local area, having been invited to perform at numerous festivals across different provinces including Nam Dinh, Thanh Hoa, Hoa Binh, Vinh Phuc, and Ninh Binh.

The oldest member of the Duc Khe team, Mr. Pham Van Thuong, aged 87, exemplifies the dedication and passion that drives these performances. Despite his advanced age, he continues to participate, playing a crucial role in providing musical accompaniment for the dancers. His commitment to preserving the ancient dances and bringing joy to audiences during the festive season is a testament to the enduring spirit of the Four Sacred Beasts Dance.

Each team member plays a vital role in maintaining the tradition, whether through performing, making costumes, or passing on skills to younger generations. For instance, Mr. Pham Van Hai, aged 68, carries on the legacy of his father, ensuring that the intricate costumes are crafted according to traditional methods. These costumes take nearly a month to complete, reflecting the time-intensive nature of the craft. The dancers also train rigorously, often practicing together for one or two weeks before joining the main group to perform at various events.

The physical demands of the dance are considerable, requiring stamina and flexibility. For example, Mr. Trinh Van Binh, aged 70, is responsible for controlling the dragon's head, a task that requires significant strength and agility. He explains that the dragon's head, weighing between 15 to 20 kilograms, must be maneuvered skillfully to create lifelike movements, enhancing the visual appeal of the performance.

The Four Sacred Beasts Dance not only showcases the artistic talents of the performers but also fosters a sense of community and cultural pride. As the dancers weave through the streets and temples, they bring joy and festivity to the people, reinforcing the bonds within the community and celebrating the rich cultural heritage of Vietnam. Through their tireless efforts, the dancers ensure that this ancient tradition remains alive and vibrant, connecting past and present generations in a shared celebration of cultural identity and communal spirit.

The Four Sacred Beasts Dance, a traditional dance ensemble deeply rooted in Vietnamese culture, has been performed in the land known as "Ngũ phụng tề phi" for over a century. This ancient dance, which includes the mythical creatures Lân (ox), Long (dragon), Quy (turtle), and Phụng (phoenix), has captivated audiences with its vibrant performances and rich cultural significance. Over time, the once bustling scenes of the dance have faded into the memories of the elderly, leaving behind only cherished recollections of its former glory.

Among the four characters, Lân is the most beloved, often captivating the audience with its dynamic movements and lively presence. The dance's origins trace back to a time when it was first introduced by a group led by Master Nhung, who later passed the torch to his son, Master Nha, after his passing. Following the historic victory at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, Master Nha organized a grand performance of the Four Sacred Beasts Dance to celebrate this significant event, marking the expansion of the dance to various regions within the province.

Despite the passage of time and the challenges faced by the dance, the original choreography and traditions have gradually diminished. Today, only a few senior artists still remember parts of the dance, each preserving fragments of the intricate routines that once defined the performance. These artists, such as Mr. Đinh Quýt and Mr. Nguyễn Huệ, continue to pass down their knowledge, ensuring that the essence of the Four Sacred Beasts Dance remains alive.

The musical accompaniment for the dance is a blend of traditional instruments including the nhị (a type of flute), sáo (flute), kèn (trumpet), and chập chõa (a small drum). The primary instruments used are the trống (drum) and phèng la (a large gong), which create the rhythmic beats that drive the dance forward. To enhance the atmosphere and highlight the characteristics of each character, the artists have devised a unique form of firework called pháo xì, which produces smoke and flame without causing an explosion. This special effect is created using a mixture of diêm tiêu (matches) and tro cây dâu (mulberry ash) or tro cây sắn (cassava ash), carefully blended in proportions that reflect the personality of each character.

During performances, the stage lights flicker as the dancers emerge from the backstage area. A loud signal from the pháo xì marks the beginning of the dance, followed by the appearance of the Lân character, who emerges confidently to the beat of the drums, his head adorned with a flaming horn that spews smoke and fire. Each character then takes center stage, showcasing their unique movements and engaging the audience with their distinctive visual elements. The crowd roars with excitement, the festive atmosphere intensifying with every moment.

One of the most popular segments of the Four Sacred Beasts Dance is the "Lân mẫu xuất Lân nhi" (Mother Lân giving birth to Child Lân). In one memorable performance, Mr. Đinh Quýt played the role of Child Lân, lying on his back while being held by the performer playing Mother Lân. During a particularly enthusiastic performance, the two performers holding Mother Lân became so engrossed in the dance that they accidentally dropped Child Lân onto the ground beside a fake bush. The audience watched in anticipation as Mother Lân pretended to go through labor pains, but Child Lân did not appear. Sensing the tension, the organizers quickly covered the stage lights, allowing Child Lân to run out onto the stage and rejoin Mother Lân, much to the delight of the audience.

In 1990, with financial support from a businessman, Mr. Đinh Quýt and Mr. Nguyễn Huệ established a new troupe of dancers in Đà Nẵng. Over the next three years, the troupe performed extensively throughout Quảng Nam, especially during the Mid-Autumn Festival, entertaining children and adults alike. The Four Sacred Beasts Dance, with its rich cultural heritage, was warmly received wherever it was performed. Unfortunately, in 1993, a tragic fire destroyed all the props and costumes of the troupe, bringing an abrupt end to their performances.

Today, the legacy of the Four Sacred Beasts Dance continues to be celebrated and preserved by a handful of dedicated artists. Despite the challenges faced by the dance, it remains a testament to the enduring spirit of traditional Vietnamese culture, captivating audiences with its vibrant performances and deep cultural significance.

In recent years, visitors to Côn Sơn have been captivated by a unique and enchanting spectacle known as frog fishing, a charming activity that has become a significant part of the local tourism scene. This peculiar tradition involves frogs performing acrobatic feats such as jumping through hoops, dancing to music, and engaging in playful competitions, all of which are designed to entertain both children and adults alike. The practice of training frogs to perform these tasks is a relatively new addition to the region's cultural offerings, having emerged as a novel attraction in response to the growing interest in local tourism.

Mr. Lê Văn Cang, a member of the Côn Sơn Agricultural Cooperative, has taken it upon himself to contribute to the enrichment of the area’s tourist offerings. His vision is to create a more diverse range of activities that can engage visitors during their stay at Côn Sơn, particularly during the summer season. Inspired by the natural agility and playfulness of frogs, Mr. Cang began experimenting with the idea of training them to perform various tricks, which eventually evolved into the popular frog fishing performances.

The process of training frogs to perform these intricate maneuvers requires meticulous attention to detail and patience. Mr. Cang carefully selects young frogs that exhibit qualities such as agility, responsiveness, and a certain level of curiosity. These chosen frogs are then subjected to a rigorous training regimen that includes conditioning them to respond to commands, learning to jump through hoops, and even dancing to music. It takes approximately 30 days for a frog to become proficient enough to perform these tasks reliably.

One of the most challenging aspects of this training is maintaining the vibrant colors of the frogs, which are crucial for the visual appeal of the performances. The frogs tend to lose their bright hues over time due to their natural tendency to adapt to their surroundings. Therefore, Mr. Cang must ensure that the frogs are kept in environments that preserve their colorful appearance, which adds another layer of complexity to the training process.

Visitors from various regions, including tourists from Nghệ An, have expressed great enthusiasm and delight in witnessing these performances. The sight of trained frogs leaping through hoops in a coordinated manner is truly mesmerizing. Each hoop is painted with vibrant colors and arranged in a sequence that encourages the frogs to compete and showcase their agility. The performance typically consists of six rounds, each round featuring different colored hoops that the frogs must navigate through.

During the performances, the frogs demonstrate remarkable coordination and flexibility, jumping through hoops of varying sizes and heights. The training sessions involve not only physical exercises but also auditory cues, ensuring that the frogs can respond accurately to musical rhythms and vocal commands. This synchronization between the frogs and the trainers creates a harmonious and entertaining display that captivates audiences of all ages.

As the summer approaches, Mr. Cang plans to expand the repertoire of frog performances, introducing new routines that cater specifically to the interests of children visiting Côn Sơn. These performances are designed to be educational and fun, providing a memorable experience that combines entertainment with a touch of cultural insight into the local fauna and traditions.

The success of these frog fishing performances has not only enhanced the appeal of Côn Sơn as a tourist destination but also contributed to the preservation and promotion of local culture. By showcasing the unique abilities of the frogs, Mr. Cang and his team have created an engaging and interactive experience that resonates with visitors, making their stay at Côn Sơn all the more memorable.

documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Lion Dance
documents.content:
The Lion Dance, a traditional Chinese performance, involves mimicking a lion's movements in a lion costume to bring good fortune and ward off evil. This dance is typically performed during the Lunar New Year and other significant cultural and religious festivals. Additionally, it is featured at business openings, special celebrations, and wedding ceremonies, often to honor distinguished guests within Chinese communities. 

The Lion Dance is distinct from the Dragon Dance, which requires multiple performers holding a long dragon on poles. The Lion Dance usually involves two dancers, one controlling the lion's head and the other its tail. Accompanied by a vigorous drumbeat and the sounds of gongs and cymbals, the Lion Dance includes movements that are also found in Chinese martial arts.

In China, there are various forms of the Lion Dance, with the Northern Lion and Southern Lion being the most prominent. The Southern Lion, prevalent in Southeast Asia due to the historical migration of Southern Chinese communities, is particularly widespread. Variations of the Lion Dance, inspired by the Chinese version, are also practiced in Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam. Other forms of lion dancing exist in India, Indonesia, and East Africa.

The tradition of dancers wearing animal or mythical beast masks dates back to ancient China. References to such performances can be found in texts like the Shujing, where wild beasts and phoenixes are described as dancing. During the Qin and Han dynasties, dancers wore bear masks for exorcism rituals, and mime performers represented fish, dragons, and phoenixes.

Although lions are not native to China, the Lion Dance likely originated from countries like India or Persia and was introduced through Central Asia. The term "shi," meaning lion, might have been derived from the Persian word "šer." The earliest use of "shizi" to denote a lion appears in Han dynasty texts, with lions being gifted to the Han court by emissaries from Central Asia and the Parthian Empire.

Detailed descriptions of the Lion Dance emerged during the Tang dynasty, when it was recognized as a foreign dance by writers and poets. However, references to "lion acts" date back to the third century AD, as noted by a Three Kingdoms scholar, Meng Kang, in his commentary on Hanshu. Early in its history, the Lion Dance was linked to Buddhism, with records indicating that a lion led parades for Buddha statues to ward off evil spirits. This suggests that the dance could have evolved from a local tradition that adopted Buddhist symbolism.

During the Tang dynasty, several versions of the Lion Dance existed. At the Tang court, it was known as the "Great Peace Music" or the "Lion Dance of the Five Directions," featuring five lions of different colors and expressions, each controlled by two individuals and accompanied by 140 singers. Another version involved five lions over three meters tall, each with twelve assistants who teased the lions with red whisks. A poem by Tang poet Bai Juyi describes a Lion Dance performed by two Central Asian dancers wearing a wooden-headed, silk-tailed, and furry-bodied lion costume with golden eyes, silver teeth, and moving ears, similar to today’s Lion Dance. By the eighth century, this Lion Dance had reached Japan. During the Song dynasty, the Lion Dance became common in festivals and was known as the Northern Lion during the Southern Song period.

The Southern Lion, originating in Guangdong province, represents a later development. Several myths surround its origins, including one where villagers celebrated after driving away a mythical monster named Nian. Another legend attributes its creation to an auspicious dream experienced by the Qianlong Emperor.

The Lion Dance, a vibrant and culturally significant performance, is widely recognized for its ability to bring joy and excitement to various events across Vietnam. This traditional dance form, often accompanied by the rhythmic beats of drums and cymbals, is meticulously choreographed to create a spectacle that captivates audiences and adds a festive atmosphere to celebrations. The Lion Dance, also known as "Múa Lân" in Vietnamese, is not merely a display of acrobatic prowess but a deeply rooted cultural tradition that holds symbolic meanings and brings good fortune to those who witness it.

Incorporating elements of Chinese influence, the Lion Dance has been adapted into a unique Vietnamese style, reflecting the country's rich cultural heritage. The dance is performed during important occasions such as business openings, Lunar New Year celebrations, and community festivals. It is particularly popular during the Mid-Autumn Festival, where the dance is tailored to entertain children and foster a joyful, communal spirit. The Lion Dance can take on different forms depending on the event's requirements, ranging from simple performances suitable for small venues to elaborate shows featuring intricate movements and impressive feats of agility.

For business openings, the Lion Dance serves as a grand opening ceremony, symbolizing prosperity and good luck. The dance typically involves a team of performers dressed in lion costumes, accompanied by drummers and cymbal players. The lion dancers perform a series of synchronized movements, including jumping, spinning, and leaping, which are designed to attract attention and generate excitement among passersby. The dance often culminates in a symbolic act of "plucking the greens," where the lion reaches up to pluck a green vegetable or other auspicious item, signifying the start of a prosperous venture.

During the Mid-Autumn Festival, the Lion Dance takes on a more playful and interactive nature. Performances are designed to engage children, with the lion dancers interacting with young spectators, creating a fun and safe environment. The dance includes gentle movements and humorous interactions, often involving the character of the Earth God (Ông Địa), who adds a touch of humor and charm to the performance. The inclusion of drumming and cymbals enhances the festive mood, while the overall atmosphere is one of joy and celebration.

The Lion Dance can also be adapted for corporate events, where it serves as a highlight within larger programs. For these events, the dance is carefully integrated into the schedule to ensure it complements the overall flow of activities. The performance might include a combination of traditional lion dancing and modern elements, such as incorporating contemporary music or innovative choreography. The goal is to create a memorable moment that resonates with the audience and aligns with the event's theme.

One of the key aspects of the Lion Dance is its adaptability to different settings and requirements. For smaller venues, a compact team consisting of two lions, an Earth God figure, and accompanying musicians is sufficient to create a lively atmosphere. In larger spaces, such as corporate showrooms or outdoor festivals, the team can expand to include additional performers like dragons, gods of wealth, and larger drum ensembles. This flexibility allows the Lion Dance to be tailored to fit the specific needs of each event, whether it is a small shop opening or a grand festival.

The Lion Dance also comes in various styles, each suited to different types of events. The "Lân Địa Bửu" style, for instance, is ideal for smaller venues and community events, where the lion dancers perform on the ground, engaging with the audience through playful interactions and dynamic movements. This style is particularly popular for school events, family gatherings, and community festivals, where the focus is on creating a warm and welcoming atmosphere.

Another notable style is the "Mai Hoa Thung" or pole dance, which showcases the lion dancers' acrobatic skills as they perform complex maneuvers on poles and columns. This style is especially captivating when used for large-scale events, such as grand openings, festivals, or ceremonies requiring a visually striking performance. The dancers demonstrate their agility and strength by performing high jumps, balancing acts, and intricate movements that are both awe-inspiring and entertaining.

The Lion Dance also incorporates elements of fortune-telling and blessings, particularly in the form of the "Lân Hái Lộc" or "Lân Phát Lộc" dances. These performances involve the lion dancers collecting symbolic items such as red envelopes, couplets, or lucky vegetables, which are then presented to the host or guests as a gesture of good wishes and prosperity. This ritual is particularly meaningful during business openings or celebratory events, where the lion dancers' actions are seen as bringing good fortune and success to the enterprise.

Overall, the Lion Dance is a multifaceted performance that combines traditional cultural elements with modern adaptations, making it a versatile and beloved part of Vietnamese culture. Whether performed at a small shop opening or a grand festival, the Lion Dance continues to captivate audiences and embody the spirit of joy, prosperity, and community.

The Lion Dance, a vibrant and culturally significant performance, is widely recognized for its profound symbolism and dynamic presence at various festive events, particularly during the year-end celebrations known as Tet Nguyen Dan, or simply "Tet," in Vietnamese culture. This traditional dance, which includes the lion, dragon, and tiger performances, is not merely an artistic spectacle but also a deeply rooted ritual that carries immense spiritual and social significance.

The Lion Dance, often accompanied by the Dragon and Tiger dances, symbolizes prosperity, good fortune, and success in the coming year. These performances are meticulously choreographed to convey a sense of harmony and balance, reflecting the ancient belief that such acts can bring about positive energy and ward off evil spirits. The lion, in particular, is seen as a guardian spirit that brings luck and protection, while the dragon represents power and wealth, and the tiger signifies courage and strength.

During these performances, the lion dancers, dressed in elaborate costumes, perform intricate movements that require great skill and coordination. The lion's movements are fluid and graceful, yet they also exhibit moments of fierce determination, especially when the lion leaps onto high beams to pluck a sprig of green lettuce, symbolizing good fortune and prosperity. This act of the lion ascending a tall bamboo pole to retrieve the lettuce, known as "Lion Climbing Tree to Pick Fortune," is a highlight of the performance, embodying the idea that despite life's challenges, one can achieve success through perseverance and good fortune.

Another notable performance is the "Heavenly Dragon Descending," where the dragon, a mythical creature from Eastern and Western folklore, is portrayed as a powerful and auspicious being. The dragon's appearance in the Lion Dance signifies the arrival of divine blessings and good fortune. Dragons come in various colors, each representing different meanings: red dragons bring strength and luck, golden and silver dragons symbolize wealth and prosperity, and blue dragons represent peace and tranquility.

The inclusion of the tiger in the Lion Dance adds another layer of symbolism. Unlike the lion, which brings good fortune, the tiger is depicted as a fierce protector, capable of driving away evil spirits and ensuring safety and peace. This dual representation of the lion and tiger in the dance reflects the belief that both benevolence and strength are necessary to maintain harmony and protect against misfortune.

The Lion Dance is not only a visual feast but also a testament to the performers' dedication and skill. Each movement, from the rhythmic drumming that accompanies the dance to the precise footwork of the dancers, is carefully crafted to convey a message of hope and prosperity. The performances are designed to engage the audience, creating a lively and festive atmosphere that is integral to the celebration of the new year.

In corporate settings, the Lion Dance is often featured during year-end parties and business gatherings, serving as a symbolic gesture of goodwill and prosperity for the company and its employees. The dance is believed to bring about a successful and prosperous new year, making it a popular choice for businesses looking to enhance their year-end festivities. The Lion Dance is performed by skilled dancers who undergo rigorous training to master the complex movements and rhythms required for the performance.

Overall, the Lion Dance is more than just an entertaining performance; it is a cultural tradition that embodies the hopes and aspirations of the community. It serves as a reminder of the importance of unity, resilience, and the pursuit of prosperity in the face of life's challenges. As the Lion Dance continues to be a beloved part of cultural celebrations, it remains a vivid expression of the enduring values and traditions of the people.

description:
In a water puppetry performance, if the puppets are the main characters on the water, the instrumentalists and voice actors are the ones who breathe soul into each story. They usually sit in a corner of the stage, in front of or next to the thủy đình, where the sounds of drums, flutes, đàn nhị, and folk chèo melodies blend with the sound of water, creating a very unique atmosphere of Vietnamese water puppetry. Water puppetry originated around the 12th century in the Bắc Bộ delta, and since then, folk music has always been an inseparable part of every performance.

The artists not only play music but also take on the roles of narrating, voicing dialogues, and creating sound effects. When chú Tễu appears, when the army goes to battle, or when the countryside harvest scene takes place, it is their singing, shouting, laughing, and drumbeats that help the audience understand the characters' emotions, even though the puppets cannot speak for themselves. The seamless coordination between the puppeteers behind the bamboo screen and the orchestra in front brings life to the entire stage.

What many tourists remember forever is not only the puppets dancing on the water, but also the emotional folk sounds echoing. It is where the artists quietly tell stories, connecting the past of the Bắc Bộ countryside with today's audience through their own singing and traditional musical instruments.
description_vi:
Trong một buổi biểu diễn múa rối nước, nếu những con rối là nhân vật chính trên mặt nước thì các nghệ sĩ chơi nhạc cụ và lồng tiếng chính là những người thổi linh hồn vào từng câu chuyện. Họ thường ngồi ở một góc sân khấu, phía trước hoặc bên cạnh thủy đình, nơi tiếng trống, tiếng sáo, tiếng đàn nhị và những làn điệu chèo dân gian hòa quyện với tiếng nước, tạo nên bầu không khí rất riêng của nghệ thuật rối nước Việt Nam. Múa rối nước vốn xuất hiện từ khoảng thế kỷ XII ở vùng đồng bằng Bắc Bộ, và từ đó âm nhạc dân gian luôn là phần không thể tách rời của mỗi vở diễn.

Các nghệ sĩ không chỉ chơi nhạc mà còn đảm nhận vai trò dẫn chuyện, đối thoại và tạo hiệu ứng âm thanh. Khi chú Tễu xuất hiện, khi đoàn quân ra trận hay khi cảnh làng quê vào mùa gặt diễn ra, chính tiếng hát, tiếng hô, tiếng cười và nhịp trống của họ giúp khán giả hiểu được cảm xúc của nhân vật dù những con rối không thể tự cất lời. Sự phối hợp nhịp nhàng giữa người điều khiển rối phía sau màn tre và dàn nhạc phía trước tạo nên sức sống cho toàn bộ sân khấu.

Điều khiến nhiều du khách nhớ mãi không chỉ là những con rối nhảy múa trên mặt nước, mà còn là âm thanh dân gian vang lên đầy cảm xúc. Đó là nơi người nghệ sĩ âm thầm kể chuyện, kết nối quá khứ của làng quê Bắc Bộ với khán giả hôm nay bằng chính tiếng hát và nhạc cụ truyền thống của mình.

The art of Vietnamese water puppetry has its roots in the 12th century, when it originated in the Bắc Bộ delta. As the puppets dance on the water, the sounds of the instruments and the voices of the performers blend with the gentle lapping of the water, creating an immersive experience that transcends time and space.

In the heart of Vietnam’s cultural heritage, the musicians and vocal performers play a pivotal role in the enchanting art form of water puppetry, which originated around the 12th century in the fertile plains of the Bắc Bộ delta. This ancient tradition seamlessly blends the grace of puppetry with the soul-stirring melodies of traditional Vietnamese folk music, creating a unique auditory experience that resonates deeply with audiences both local and foreign.

These artists, often seated in a designated area near the thủy đình—a small pavilion built over the water—bring to life the narratives of Vietnamese folklore through their mastery of various traditional instruments. The stage, framed by the curved roof of the thủy đình, serves as a backdrop for the harmonious interplay between the puppeteers hidden behind bamboo screens and the musicians positioned in front. The musicians, dressed in vibrant traditional attire that contrasts beautifully against the red wooden backdrop of the stage, are responsible for more than just playing music; they also narrate the stories, provide voiceovers for the characters, and create sound effects that enhance the overall theatrical experience.

Among the instruments commonly used are the trống (drums), đàn nhị (two-stringed fiddle), sáo trúc (bamboo flute), mõ (gong), and thanh la (clapper). Each instrument contributes uniquely to the soundscape, blending seamlessly with the gentle splashes of water to evoke a sense of nostalgia and connection to the rural landscapes of northern Vietnam. The musicians’ performances are meticulously synchronized with the movements of the puppets, ensuring that the emotional nuances of each scene are conveyed effectively to the audience.

When the character Chú Tễu, a beloved figure in Vietnamese folklore, makes his appearance, or during scenes depicting battles or harvest festivals, the musicians’ voices and instruments become the conduits through which the characters’ emotions are expressed. Their singing, shouting, laughter, and rhythmic beats help the audience understand the complex emotions and actions of the puppets, even though the puppets themselves remain silent. This seamless coordination between the puppeteers and the musicians transforms the stage into a living tableau, where the past and present converge in a celebration of Vietnamese culture.

Tourists visiting Vietnam often leave with vivid memories of the water puppetry performances, not just because of the graceful dances of the puppets on the water, but also due to the emotive folk sounds that echo throughout the venue. These sounds serve as a bridge, connecting the rich cultural heritage of the Bắc Bộ countryside with contemporary audiences, allowing visitors to experience firsthand the enduring traditions of Vietnamese folk music and storytelling. Through their performances, the musicians and vocal performers quietly yet powerfully convey the essence of Vietnamese culture, making each water puppetry show a memorable and culturally enriching experience.

On the evening of August 24th, the Trung tâm hội nghị tỉnh Bình Định hosted a special artistic program titled "Ký ức quê hương" with the theme "Giai điệu ân tình - quê hương Bình Định." This event was organized by the People's Committee of Binh Dinh Province in collaboration with the Vietravel Group, the Association of Binh Dinh Compatriots in Ho Chi Minh City, the Nutifood Corporation, and the creative company Mãnh Hổ. The purpose of this night was to honor and express gratitude towards musicians and vocal performers from Binh Dinh who have left significant marks in the Vietnamese music scene.

The event not only celebrated the contributions of these artists but also underscored commitments to environmental protection and sustainable development. It was free for attendees and live-streamed online, making it accessible to people across the country. Musicians and vocal performers from Binh Dinh, such as Phạm Thế Mỹ, Giao Tiên, Trần Long Ẩn, Hàn Châu, Tô Quốc Cơ, Ngô Tín, and Vũ Thanh, among others, performed songs they had composed, which resonated deeply with the audience. These compositions were interwoven with popular contemporary tunes favored by young people and the general public on social media platforms.

The evening featured a blend of musical performances and fashion shows, showcasing the creativity and cultural richness of Binh Dinh. Two renowned designers, Hoàng Tony and Hà Thanh Việt, presented their collections inspired by the colors and life of their hometown. Their designs went beyond mere clothing, serving as messages about the culture and people of Binh Dinh. Models including supermodel Anh Thư, Mr World Vietnam 2024 finalist Võ Minh Toại, Miss Beauty Nguyễn Thảo Vy, Mạc Huyền Trân, and nearly twenty models from Binh Dinh participated in the runway show.

During the event, the People's Committee of Binh Dinh Province and the Vietravel Group announced ambassadors for the "Go Green" campaign, aimed at promoting responsible tourism that is environmentally friendly. They emphasized the importance of concrete actions in developing tourism and festivals in Binh Dinh, advocating for zero waste policies. This initiative aligns with broader efforts to preserve the natural beauty and cultural heritage of the region while fostering sustainable growth.

The atmosphere at the Trung tâm hội nghị was vibrant and filled with nostalgia, as the performances evoked memories of childhood and the unique charm of "the land of martial arts." The event highlighted the deep connection between music, fashion, and the cultural identity of Binh Dinh, offering visitors a rich tapestry of local traditions and modern expressions. Through the lens of music and fashion, the evening celebrated the enduring legacy of musicians and vocal performers from Binh Dinh, reinforcing their impact on the cultural landscape of Vietnam.

Since the theatre's inauguration in 1969, this dance has emerged as a symbol of peace and tranquility, embodying the historical legacy of the city's ancient name, Thăng Long, which was bestowed upon it by King Lý Thái Tổ when he relocated the capital here in the early 11th century. A highlight of the show is the tender moment when two phoenix puppets delicately touch their beaks, creating a poignant and graceful tableau that floats on the water's surface, framed by a rustic bamboo screen.

The theatre itself, a testament to Vietnamese architectural ingenuity, combines traditional elements with modern design, offering visitors a unique blend of cultural heritage and contemporary entertainment. The performance not only showcases the exceptional skill of puppeteers but also provides a profound cultural experience, immersing spectators in the rich tapestry of Vietnamese history and folklore. As the music of the bamboo flute and gentle drumbeats fill the air, the entire space transforms into an elegant festival atmosphere, drawing in both tourists and local residents who are drawn to the enchanting spectacle.

Visitors from around the world and the bustling streets of Hanoi are entranced by the rhythmic water-parting movements of the sacred creatures, each gesture a testament to the perfection of beauty and the enduring spirit of Vietnamese culture. The performance concludes with a lingering sense of peace and uplifted spirits, leaving a lasting impression of boundless pride in the cultural heritage of Vietnam. documents.title: Thông tin Wikipedia - Phoenix Dance
documents.content:
Phoenix Dance Theatre, originally known as Phoenix Dance Company, was founded in 1981 in the inner-city Harehills area of Leeds by three young men—David Hamilton, Donald Edwards, and Vilmore James—who had started dancing at Harehills Middle School. Their teacher, Nadine Senior, would later become the first principal of the Northern School of Contemporary Dance. By the summer of 1982, Phoenix had expanded its roster with two additional dancers, Merville Jones and Edward Lynch, both members of the Harehills Youth Dance Theatre. In 1985, the company relocated to its first permanent base in Chapeltown.

David Hamilton left Phoenix in 1987 to pursue a solo career, and Neville Campbell took over as Artistic Director. Under Campbell's leadership, Phoenix achieved significant milestones, including winning the Grand Prize at the International Choreographic Competition in Bagnolet in 1990 for Aletta Collins' piece "Gang of Five," and receiving a Laurence Olivier Award nomination for the Most Outstanding Achievement of the Year in Dance.

Margaret Morris joined Phoenix as Artistic Director in 1991, and during her tenure, the company became well-established on the UK touring circuit and began performing internationally, particularly in the United States. Following Morris's departure in 1997, Thea Narissa Barnes led the company until 2000. In 1998, Phoenix was commissioned by the BBC to perform with Roni Size at the Windrush Gala concert, which was broadcast nationally.

In 2002, Darshan Singh Bhuller was appointed as Artistic Director and initiated a rebranding of the company, officially renaming it Phoenix Dance Theatre. He also directed the company towards larger venues, enhancing its profile. Bhuller was succeeded by Javier de Frutos, who led Phoenix to win the "Company Prize for Outstanding Repertoire (Modern)" in the Critics' Circle National Dance Awards in 2006. That same year, Phoenix was invited to perform at the 5th International Festival of Contemporary Dance - La Biennale di Venezia, where they closed the festival with their final performance.

Sharon Watson became the seventh Artistic Director of Phoenix Dance Theatre in May 2009, having been associated with the company since 1989 when she joined as a dancer under the stage name Chantal Donaldson. She choreographed pieces such as "Shaded Limits" and "Never Still" during this period. After leaving the company in 1997, Watson returned in 2000 as Rehearsal and Tour Director, and continued her involvement through various roles, including a fellowship with the Clore Leadership Programme and directorial positions at Northern Ballet Theatre.

In 2010, Phoenix Dance Theatre moved into a new, purpose-built dance center in Leeds, alongside Northern Ballet, marking a significant milestone in the company's history. This facility, the largest outside London, houses both a national classical and a national contemporary dance company.

Phoenix Dance Theatre's current repertoire includes a variety of performances, such as "BERNSTEIN DOUBLE BILL" choreographed by Dane Hurst, "THE RITE OF SPRING" by Jeanguy Saintus, and "Windrush: Movement of the People" by Sharon Watson. These performances reflect the diverse and evolving nature of the company's artistic output, showcasing the talents of both established and emerging choreographers.
